title: Einer der ältesten Bräuche – «Fürio de Bach brönnt»: Aarau feiert Jubiläum des Bachfischet
content:
Es ist dunkel, wo sonst Strassenlaternen die bekannten bemalten Giebel beleuchten und in Schaufenstern Uhren glitzern. Am Strassenrand der Altstadt drängen sich die Menschen. Trommelschläge der Tambouren kündigen den nächtlichen Umzug an. Ein Raunen geht durch die Menge. Die Kinder ziehen durch die Stadt, der Schein ihrer selbst gebastelten Lampions erhellt die Gesichter und Fassaden. In Aarau ist Bachfischet.
-
Bild 1 von 5. Mit Lampions und Gesang ziehen die Aarauer Schulkinder durch die abgedunkelte Stadt. Fische sind ein beliebtes Motiv. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 2 von 5. «De Bach isch do, de Bach isch do», singen die Kinder am Bachfischet. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 3 von 5. Schulklassen und Jugendvereine basteln eigene Lampions. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 4 von 5. Der Bach ist eines der Themen, die immer wieder auftauchen. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 5 von 5. Am Ende des Umzugs wird ein Teil der Lampions verbrannt. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
Der Bachfischet wird dieses Jahr wohl schon zum 500. Mal gefeiert. Bereits 1526 wurde der Bachfischet nämlich erstmals in einem Ratsprotokoll der Stadt Aarau erwähnt. Aarau hat keinen natürlichen Fluss, das Gewässer wurde künstlich angelegt. «Der Stadtbach war die Lebensader der Stadt, bis die ersten Quellen gefasst werden konnten», betont Historikerin Stefanie Mahrer. Eine mittelalterliche Stadt konnte ohne Bach nicht überleben. Man habe Trinkwasser, Löschwasser und Wasserkraft für das Gewerbe gebraucht.
-
Bild 1 von 2. Der Bachfischet-Umzug zieht durch die Rathausgasse in der Aarauer Altstadt. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
-
Bild 2 von 2. Die Lampions erleuchten die sonst stockfinstere Stadt. Bildquelle: SRF/Mario Gutknecht.
Einmal jährlich musste die Stadt Aarau das Bachbett des Stadtbachs reinigen. Dafür wurde der Bach gestaut. Die Reinigung dauerte in der Regel vier Tage und wurde als Fronarbeit erledigt. Vier Tage ohne Trink- und Löschwasser – eine Herausforderung für die Bewohnerinnen und Bewohner. Deswegen legten Haushalte einen Wasservorrat in Kesseln und Zubern an.
Der Bachfischet 1950
-
Bild 1 von 4. Einmal jährlich wurde der Aarauer Stadtbach gestaut und geputzt, wie die Aufnahmen der Schweizer Filmwochenschau von 1950 zeigen. Bildquelle: Schweizer Filmwochenschau 1950.
-
Bild 3 von 4. Für vier Tage musste die gesamte Stadt ohne Wasser auskommen, bis der Brunnenmeister die Schleuse wieder öffnete und der Bach wieder in die Stadt fliessen konnte. Bildquelle: Schweizer Filmwochenschau 1950.
-
Bild 4 von 4. In Suhr schickten die Kinder Kerzen mit dem Stadtbach nach Aarau. Bildquelle: Schweizer Filmwochenschau 1950.
September sei für das Putzen des Bachs die ideale Zeit gewesen, sagt Stefanie Mahrer. Nach der Ernte und vor der Weinlese, weil da die Arbeitskräfte und die Kessel zur Verfügung gestanden hätten.
1784 musste die Bachreinigung frühzeitig abgebrochen werden – wegen eines Grossbrands. Daraufhin wurde der Stadtbach «notfallmässig vorzeitig geflutet», wie die Heinerich Wirri-Zunft schreibt, die sich der Pflege der Aarauer Bräuche verschrieben hat, insbesondere des Bachfischet. Zahlreiche Gebäude seien niedergebrannt, der Brandstifter habe seine Tat vor der Hinrichtung gestanden.
Heute gilt der Bachfischet laut der Heinerich Wirri-Zunft «als ältester dauernd gelebter Brauch in der Schweiz». Dass der Brauch so lange überlebt hat, ist nicht selbstverständlich. Im Laufe des 19. Jahrhunderts sei er in Vergessenheit geraten, der Bach habe wegen der modernen Wasserleitungen an Bedeutung verloren, erklärt Historikerin Stefanie Mahrer. «1922 muss der absolute Tiefpunkt gewesen sein, als nur noch ein paar Vereinzelte am Bachfischet teilgenommen haben.»
Daraufhin wurde die Heinerich Wirri-Zunft gegründet, die sich des Brauchs annahm. Initiiert wurde die Zunft vom Arzt und rechtsnationalen Aarauer Politiker Eugen Bircher. Zwar seien die Anfänge klar im rechtsbürgerlichen Milieu. Der Bachfischet sei aber absolut unpolitisch, betont Mahrer, die als Co-Autorin die Geschichte der Stadt Aarau erforscht. «Ohne die Heinerich Wirri-Zunft hätten wir das wunderbare Fest, wie wir es heute haben, nicht mehr.»
Wenn am Ende der Reinigung der Stadtbach wieder in sein Bett geleitet wurde, war das ein feierlicher Moment: Die Kinder in Suhr setzten Schiffchen mit Kerzen auf den Bach, die Kinder in Aarau empfingen diese, zogen in einem Umzug durch die Stadt und sangen das Bachfischet-Lied.
Früher trugen die Kinder ausgehöhlte Kürbisse oder Räbeliechtli, heute sind es selbst gebastelte Laternen an Haselruten. Beendet wird der Umzug mit dem «Mords-Chlapf», einem grossen einzelnen Böllerschuss. Auf einem grossen Feuer werden die Haselruten und teilweise auch die Lampions verbrannt.

title: Maasai culture: Keeping pace with change
content:
Dar es Salaam. While many modern societies have traded traditional ecological knowledge for rapid industrialisation, the Maasai people of East Africa remain one of the most culturally resilient communities on the planet.
This comes even amid reports from human rights organisations and Indigenous advocates warning that their traditional pastoral lifestyle and ancestral culture face an unprecedented existential threat, primarily driven by forced displacements, state-led conservation policies, and climate change.
Further, governments argue that human and livestock populations create environmental pressure on vital wildlife and UNESCO World Heritage ecosystems.
Conversely, advocates state that displacing pastoralists severs their spiritual and economic reliance on cattle, summarizing the process as "killing culture"
But even so, the Maasai’s ability to withstand the encroaching pressures of climate change and land loss is not a matter of luck, but the result of a "sophisticated system" of living that treats the environment and human existence as a single, inseparable unit.
At the heart of this resilience are three fundamental pillars or "legs" as explained in an exclusive interview by one of the renowned elders, defining the Maasai philosophy of being, belonging, and becoming.
According to an adjunct faculty member at the Arusha Climate and Environmental Research Centre (ACER), Mr Alais Morindat and a respected Maasai elder, the community’s life is balanced on three vital legs.
The first pillar is Natural Resources, encompassing the trees, water, pasture, and the diverse landscapes of the highlands and lowlands.
“This pillar is viewed as a divine gift, maintained through a deep understanding of the relationship between the sky and the ground,” he said.
The second pillar is Livestock, the primary livelihood and symbol of wealth that depends entirely on the health of the rangelands.
The third pillar, he said, is Society and Culture, the human element that interprets and manages the other two.
The resilience of the Maasai stems from the absolute interdependency of these pillars. Mr Morindat warns that if the pillar of natural resources collapses due to factors like climate change or land grabbing, the livestock pillar will inevitably fall, leading to the total collapse of Maasai society, history, and culture.
“Unlike communities that have abandoned their traditional roots, we the Maasai recognise that our survival is tied to the physical land we occupy; to lose the land is to lose the very "mark" that makes us a distinct people,” he explained.
The sacred bond with the land
A key reason the Maasai believe so fiercely in their specific land—and not "anywhere else"—is their spiritual interpretation of the ecosystem, often described as "God above and God below".
In this worldview, the sky (God above) is the source of influence, while the ground (God below) is where the divine responds through moisture and rain.
“This philosophy creates a closed loop of accountability and reverence; we do not see the land as a commodity to be traded, but as the literal manifestation of God’s response to our needs. This spiritual connection fosters a "conserving community" by nature,” he said.
Director of ACER, Dr Emmanuel Sulle, notes that the Maasai protect trees and natural resources because they know their entire livelihood depends on them. “They have even developed scientific methods for cutting trees and managing pastures through oral knowledge passed down through generations,” he told The Citizen. This, the researcher said, is why mobility was historically their key strategy; “if rain failed in one area, they moved to another, always following the "response" of God on the ground.”
Today, however, as borders and land laws restrict movement, their resilience has shifted toward restoration and "staying put" to heal the land they still hold.
Many outsiders have historically viewed the Maasai as "rigid" or "people of the bush" who are difficult to change. However, Mr Morindat insisted, the reality is that they are "intelligent creatures" who use their three-pillar system to survive under "huge constraints" that would break less organised societies.
“Our resilience is not about refusing to change, but about changing in a way that preserves our core,” insisted Mr Morindat.
Working with ACER, the Maasai are now bridging the gap between indigenous knowledge and modern science. They are adopting more resilient livestock breeds, such as the Sahiwal, which can thrive in smaller geographical areas while providing higher yields.

title: Darwin soccer club helps migrants find community and a place to call home
content:
One of the city's oldest soccer clubs, Darwin Olympic SC, helping to connect migrants from more than 30 nations
In short:
A family who fled Myanmar after a military coup says joining soccer club Darwin Olympic is helping them settle into life in the Northern Territory.
Founded by Greek migrants in 1967, Darwin Olympic now has players and members from more than 30 nationalities.
What's next?
The club says migrants are continuing to shape the Darwin soccer scene as players, volunteers, coaches and supporters.
When Kaung Zayar-Thaw kicked a soccer ball for the first time at age 13, he was displaced in Thailand.
His father, Zaw Zaw Htoo, had been a member of Myanmar's parliament with the National League for Democracy and in 2021, the military junta seized their home in a military coup.
The family was forced to make the dangerous journey into Thailand, hiding in a forest for several days in fear of being caught and deported.
Soon after arriving in Thailand, Kaung said he spotted some people kicking a ball around and was intrigued.
From there, the so-called "world game" went on to play a role in helping him cope with adversity.
"Football is the only thing that helped me get through stuff," he says.
When he arrived in the Top End in 2024, Kaung joined the Darwin Olympic Sporting Club, where his teammates helped him practise his English as well as soccer.
Now 15, Kaung plays as a defender for Darwin Olympic, and he says football has become much more than a sport.
"Football is the only way out of things when I'm under stress from all the pressure from the schoolwork and stuff," he says.
"It's fun, and it just teaches me how to … communicate with my teammates.
"My teammates help me. I just feel [like I] belong, [and] I really like being a part of this Olympic team."
A club shaped by migration
The Darwin Olympic Sporting Club was founded in 1967 by Greek migrants to the city as a place for their community to come together through soccer.
Almost 60 years later, the club has grown into a multicultural community representing more than 30 nationalities.
Club president Yianni Prouzos believes the club's home base in Darwin's multicultural northern suburbs has made it a natural meeting place for migrant communities.
"Football is the world's most common language," Yianni says.
"You come here, you don't have to speak the same language — you just have to know how to kick the ball and pass the ball."
Yianni, who moved to Australia as a child, says migrants now contribute to the club well beyond the playing pitch.
"We've got a lot of our migrants that come and help us," he said.
"Every person has different experiences, has different cultures … so what do they bring? Knowledge."
A family starting again
After a period of uncertainty, Kaung's mother, Kyi Nwe Oo, says the family has felt safe since arriving in Darwin, but that adjusting to their new home has been challenging.
"The difficulty we faced is that people speak a different language, culture, and the food is really difficult for us," she said.
But football has given the family a reason to get involved in the community.
"When we are seen in the community engaging with others in activities, it makes us feel that we're involved in the community and part of the community as well," Kyi Nwe Oo says.
According to Charles Darwin University senior lecturer Devaki Monani, Darwin's small and diverse population can make those connections easier to build.
"You can actually really get a multicultural experience and … you're not excluded," she said.
"Sport has great potential in connecting communities and breaking down those language and political barriers.
"In a place like Darwin, sporting activities are critical for families to engage with other families, whether migrants or not."
Soccer brings sense of belonging
Football Northern Territory chief executive Jaime Monteith says for many migrants, their first preference when it comes to sport is soccer.
He says the game can give people a sense of belonging while also opening doors to volunteering, coaching and refereeing.
"What it does is it breaks down barriers, breaks down the ability for new arrivals, migrants, to find a home or a sense of belonging," Jaime says.
For Kaung's family, those connections are helping to turn Darwin from somewhere they arrived into somewhere they can call home.
"We are trying our best to look after each other and be welcoming and make this place our home," Kyi Nwe Oo said.

title: Gebärdensprache: Kaum Lehrkräfte
content:
Spanisch, Italienisch, Latein – oder Gebärdensprache: Mit dem Schuljahr 2026/27 ist die Österreichische Gebärdensprache (ÖGS) erstmals als zweite lebende Fremdsprache im Lehrplan der AHS-Oberstufe verankert. Wählen können das Fach alle Schülerinnen und Schüler, unabhängig davon, ob sie hören oder nicht, und auch ohne Vorkenntnisse. Ab dem Schuljahr 2029/30 soll die Matura in ÖGS möglich sein.
In der Praxis ist von der Reform in Vorarlberg allerdings noch nichts zu sehen. „Derzeit wird an keiner Vorarlberger AHS-Oberstufe Österreichische Gebärdensprache als zweite lebende Fremdsprache oder als Wahlpflichtfach angeboten“, teilte Christian Kompatscher vom pädagogischen Dienst der Bildungsdirektion auf Nachfrage des ORF Vorarlberg mit. Laut ORF-Recherchen bildet Vorarlberg damit gemeinsam mit dem Burgenland das Schlusslicht.
ÖGS steht für Österreichische Gebärdensprache – die eigenständige Sprache der Gehörlosengemeinschaft in Österreich.
Andere Länder starten in Etappen
Anderswo läuft der Unterricht zumindest punktuell an: In Linz startet das Körnergymnasium, in Wien ist der Bildungsdirektion ein Standort bekannt, in der Steiermark gibt es einen ÖGS-Kurs am WIKU Graz. In Tirol wird die Entscheidung den Schulen selbst überlassen, Kärnten und Salzburg wollen ein Jahr später starten – dort sind Lehrkräfte noch in Ausbildung.
Der Grund für die Zurückhaltung ist überall derselbe: Es fehlt an qualifiziertem Personal. Ein eigenes Lehramtsstudium für Gebärdensprache gibt es in Österreich nicht, auch Unterrichtsmaterial für Kinder und Jugendliche ist rar. Am LZH haben viele Lehrkräfte und Pädagoginnen und Pädagogen eine Zusatzqualifikation im Bereich ÖGS, ein Lehramt hat im Dienststand der Bildungsdirektion aber nur eine einzige Person.
Ausbildung in Vorarlberg wenig attraktiv
„Wie bei allen Spezialisierungen, die nur einen kleinen Teil der Schülerinnen und Schüler unmittelbar betreffen, sind die Aus- und Fortbildungsangebote in Vorarlberg wenig attraktiv, da oft lange Anreisen in Kauf genommen werden müssen“, erklärt Kompatscher. Dazu komme: Unterrichtet eine gehörlose ÖGS-Lehrkraft, braucht es unter Umständen eine zweite sprechende Person mit ÖGS-Kenntnissen in der Klasse. Konkrete Planungen für das kommende Schuljahr liegen nicht vor, das Thema soll bei der Dienstbesprechung der AHS-Schulleitungen im Herbst zur Sprache kommen.
Kindergarten am LZH wird eingestellt
Während an den Gymnasien nichts weitergeht, wird das bestehende Angebot am LZH umgebaut: Der Kindergarten für Hör- und Sprachbildung in Dornbirn wird mit dem Kindergartenjahr 2027/28 eingestellt und in ein mobiles Unterstützungsangebot übergeführt. Das haben Land und LZH am Dienstag bekanntgegeben. Derzeit werden dort sieben Kinder begleitet – Kinder mit schweren Hörbeeinträchtigungen, Kinder mit zusätzlichen Behinderungen sowie hörende Kinder gehörloser Eltern.
Ein Teil der bisherigen Mittel soll künftig rund 1.970 zusätzliche Stunden audiopädagogischer Frühförderung ermöglichen. „Unser Ziel ist, dass Kinder mit Hörbeeinträchtigungen möglichst selbstverständlich am Bildungs- und Betreuungsangebot in ihrer Gemeinde teilhaben können“, sagt Soziallandesrätin Martina Rüscher (ÖVP). Die Mittel des Sozialfonds würden gezielt in den Ausbau der mobilen Frühförderung überführt, das sei „ein weiterer konkreter Schritt in Richtung eines inklusiven Bildungssystems“.
„Bedauern“ am LZH
Am LZH fällt die Reaktion gemischt aus. „Wir bedauern, dass der Kindergarten künftig nicht mehr in seiner bisherigen Form an unserem Standort weitergeführt wird“, sagt Johannes Mathis vom Landeszentrum für Hörgeschädigte. Man werde die Neuausrichtung aber „konstruktiv mitgestalten“. Angebote, die es bisher unter einem Dach gab – Psychologie, Therapie, Soziale Arbeit, HNO und Hörtechnik – stehen den Kindergartenkindern künftig nicht mehr direkt am Standort zur Verfügung. Die mobile Unterstützung werde dennoch „in hoher Qualität“ erbracht.
Vorbild ist „JUMI – Jupident mobile Inklusion“: Seit dem Betreuungsjahr 2023/24 unterstützt ein mobiles Team der Stiftung Jupident Kinder und Fachkräfte direkt in den Kindergärten. Das Land beruft sich zudem auf Artikel 24 der UN-Behindertenrechtskonvention und auf die Sozialfondsstrategie 2030.
Eine Wochenstunde in Dornbirn
Die Schule am LZH bleibt bestehen: Sie steht Kindern von sechs bis 14 Jahren aus ganz Vorarlberg offen, unterrichtet wird bei Bedarf bilingual, dazu kommt eine Wochenstunde ÖGS-Kurs. Rund 60 Kinder mit Hörbeeinträchtigung besuchen die Schule von der ersten bis zur achten Schulstufe, weitere rund 50 werden in Regelklassen an Volks- und Mittelschulen begleitet. Jährlich erhalten fünf bis zehn Jugendliche mit Hörbeeinträchtigung an AHS, BMHS und Berufsschulen eine Förderung.

title: ¿Quién llegó primero? Los dos significados de “indígena” en Europa
content:
Esta entrada es parte de la serie «Spotlight» de Global Voices de agosto de 2026, «Derechos indígenas«. Esta serie ofrece una visión de las vidas y experiencias de los pueblos indígenas con el fin de establecer vínculos entre regiones, destacar las experiencias indígenas y contar historias de líderes, activistas, miembros de la comunidad y otras personas. Puedes apoyar esta cobertura con una donación.
Para muchos europeos, la palabra “indígena” evoca dos significados muy distintos. Uno refiere a comunidades lejanas, en parte ficticias y profundamente romantizadas, que defienden sus tierras de los colonizadores; una imagen adquirida a través de relatos de aventuras de la literatura popular, novelas, películas e historietas europeas y estadounidenses. El otro significado es mucho más cercano a su realidad: reclamos nacionalistas de ser “autóctonos”, supuestos descendientes de los habitantes “originales” cuya sangre está ligada al suelo de su país, acompañados de argumentos de que los “otros” (por lo general, pueblos vecinos o migrantes recientes) llegaron después y, por ende, tienen menos derechos sobre el mismo territorio. Los Balcanes son un ejemplo especialmente contundente de cómo estas ideas pueden coexistir y ser objeto de abusos, aunque no constituyen una excepción exclusiva de tal región.
Una distinción importante suele perderse con facilidad en la traducción. En el uso internacional de los derechos humanos, los pueblos indígenas no son simplemente aquellos que pueden demostrar que sus antepasados llegaron primero. No existe una definición universal única, pero el concepto abarca autoidentificación, continuidad histórica con sociedades precoloniales, instituciones culturales o políticas diferenciadas, un vínculo estrecho con la tierra y experiencias de conquista o marginación.
Según explican los científicos sociales Maykel Verkuyten y Jochem Thijs de la Universidad de Utrecht, la autoctonía y el nativismo político funcionan de manera distinta: dividen a los habitantes en una población “anfitriona” natural y “huéspedes” condicionales. La creencia en la autoctonía —que un país pertenece a sus primeros habitantes— “puede ser una razón aceptable para exigir la propiedad colectiva de un territorio, y este reclamo puede tener consecuencias negativas para los recién llegados”, explicaron. “Los niños podrían razonar que un lugar pertenece a su grupo porque ‘nosotros’ llegamos primero y, por lo tanto, desarrollar actitudes negativas hacia otros grupos”.
Un ejemplo clave de cómo la cultura popular moldea la percepción en este ámbito es el caso de los nativos o indios norteamericanos.
Una versión europea del Lejano Oeste
Mucho antes de la televisión por cable e internet, los europeos ya habían construido su propio Oeste norteamericano, en parte gracias a las novelas de Karl May (1842-1912), que leían adultos y niños, que se convirtieron en un elemento infaltable en las bibliotecas familiares en Alemania y Austria, y en toda Europa, incluida Yugoslavia. May no había visitado el Oeste americano antes de escribir sus historias más famosas; y aun así, su héroe apache Winnetou moldeó las ideas sobre los nativos norteamericanos durante generaciones. Por ejemplo, en Macedonia del Norte muchas mujeres que nacieron en la década de 1970 se llaman Vineta en su honor.
Las adaptaciones cinematográficas basadas en la coproducción de varios países europeos, así como festivales y parques temáticos, ayudaron a mantener vivo este mundo imaginario, tal como se retrata en el siguiente video que acompaña al artículo de The New York Times “Perdidos en la traducción: La fascinación de Alemania por el Viejo Oeste norteamericano”:
Las representaciones de los nativos norteamericanos creadas por Hollywood no respondían a una fórmula única e inmutable. Muchos de las primeras películas del Oeste retrataban a los pueblos indígenas como anónimos “salvajes indios despiadados” (expresión extraída de la Declaración de Independencia de Estados Unidos), al punto de llegar a la caricatura. Películas posteriores los presentaron como víctimas de la conquista o como grupos étnicos y personas reconocibles con virtudes, defectos e intereses contrapuestos. Películas como Un hombre llamado Caballo, Pequeño gran hombre, Soldado azul y Las aventuras de Jeremiah Johnson son un ejemplo de este cambio en la década de 1970. Para la década de 1990, Danza con lobos y El último mohicano reflejaron la llegada de esta visión empática al público masivo, aun cuando la figura del “buen salvaje” terminó convirtiéndose en otro estereotipo.
Las historietas del Oeste europeas, incluidas obras maestras como la francesa Blueberry o la belga Comanche, siguieron trayectorias similares y, al igual que los antaño populares spaghetti westerns, los cómics del Oeste italianos tuvieron una evolución muy parecida. Series como Tex, Zagor, Historia del Oeste y Ken Parker se nutrieron del cine al tiempo que desarrollaban personajes indígenas diversos. Aunque continuaban siendo fantasías europeas, la mejora en las tramas convirtió a los pueblos originarios en actores de la historia, en contraposición a ser un simple telón de fondo o un enemigo único y sin rostro. En Yugoslavia, donde los cómics italianos tenían una enorme base de lectores, su lenguaje moral se volvió familiar para varias generaciones.
Anticolonialismo local
Los lectores yugoslavos no se limitaban a consumir aventuras traducidas. Dado que las importaciones de Occidente no bastaban para saciar el apetito por las historietas, la producción local se desarrolló en el período entre las dos guerras mundiales y continuó durante la era de la Yugoslavia socialista.
Por ejemplo, el dibujante Andrija Maurović (1901-1980) creó una amplia gama de cómics de aventuras y del Oeste de gran factura visual. A partir de 1978, la editorial Dnevnik de Novi Sad, encargó a guionistas y dibujantes locales la creación de episodios con licencia de El gran Blek, conocidos popularmente como Yu Blek. Asimismo, las editoriales Forum y Marketprint produjeron cómics de Tarzán entre 1983 y 1990, que se incorporaron a la franquicia global. Se trataba de una historieta comercial, distribuida en un país que se enorgullecía de haber sido cofundador del Movimiento de Países No Alineados y que celebraba públicamente su solidaridad con las luchas anticoloniales. Las giras de Tito por África y Asia proyectaban mensajes de paz y alianza con los Estados recientemente independizados. En este contexto, las historias sobre la resistencia a la conquista resonaban con la narrativa fundacional yugoslava de antifascismo partisano, liberación y coexistencia:
Esto hace que la década de 1990 resulte especialmente incómoda de recordar. Muchos que adoptaron o facilitaron las políticas nacionalistas se habían criado bajo los valores de “hermandad y unidad”, la solidaridad anticolonial y los héroes populares que protegían a los oprimidos, lo que demuestra que la infusión de los derechos humanos en la cultura popular no constituye una vacuna contra el fanatismo.
El discurso anticolonial perdura en la política nacionalista contemporánea, aunque a menudo de forma selectiva. Los crímenes coloniales de Occidente se invocan para retratar a “Occidente” como intrínsecamente ilegítimo y para responder a las críticas contra Rusia apelando al whataboutism (la falacia del “y tú más”), mientras que la conquista rusa a lo largo de Asia central, el Cáucaso y Siberia —y, más tarde, la rusificación de los pueblos asiáticos y europeos— queda fuera del encuadre.
Vojislav Šešelj, criminal de guerra condenado, ofrece un elocuente ejemplo serbio: tras describir a Estados Unidos como un Estado construido mediante la destrucción de su población nativa, instó a los serbios estadounidenses a votar por Donald Trump, en gran medida por la postura de este respecto a Rusia. El servicio de verificación de hechos Istinomer documentó luego la amplia mitología que los medios serbios construyeron en torno a Trump.
Variaciones de estas narrativas también están presentes en otros países de los Balcanes, contraste que se volvió más marcado tras la propia retórica expansionista de Trump respecto a Groenlandia y el canal de Panamá. Cuando la violencia colonial solo importa si la comete un adversario geopolítico, el anticolonialismo se convierte en una coartada en lugar de un principio.
Autóctonos en casa
Desde el proceso de construcción estatal del siglo XIX hasta la desintegración de Yugoslavia, las historias nacionales en pugna buscaron raíces cada vez más profundas. “Autóctono” se convirtió en un elogio, mientras que “recién llegado” o “huésped” pasó a ser una acusación. Los reclamos de quién llegó primero no causaron la violencia de manera mecánica, pero sirvieron para cubrir moralmente la asimilación, la expulsión y la limpieza étnica: si a los vecinos se los consideraba intrusos temporales, su expulsión podía presentarse como una restitución antes que como una injusticia. Las investigaciones sobre la formación de los Estados posotomanos demuestran cómo el desplazamiento, la redistribución de tierras y la homogeneización nacional estuvieron entrelazados desde fines del siglo XIX.
A partir de ese momento, los nacionalistas balcánicos tradujeron reiteradamente los relatos de continuidad en “derechos históricos”. Como herederas de entidades políticas antiguas o medievales, las naciones modernas supuestamente tenían derechos prioritarios sobre sus territorios. La Grecia moderna fue un ejemplo temprano, mientras que las historiografías rivales posteriores vincularon a serbios y búlgaros con imperios medievales, a los rumanos con la continuidad daco-romana y a los albaneses con la ascendencia iliria. La reciente “antigüización” afirmó la continuidad de los macedonios étnicos modernos con el reino de Alejandro Magno.
Sin embargo, los mapas de derecho histórico raras veces coincidían con las poblaciones mixtas que habitaban el territorio. La asimilación forzada, la migración forzada, el intercambio de poblaciones o la limpieza étnica fueron instrumentos fundamentales en construir los Estados-nación balcánicos desde la independencia de Grecia hasta las secuelas de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, y resurgieron más tarde durante las guerras yugoslavas (1991-2001). El vocabulario resurgió tras un incidente internacional en 2014, cuando un dron desplegó una pancarta que llevaba literalmente la palabra en inglés autochthonous (autóctono) sobre un mapa de la “Gran Albania” durante un partido de fútbol para la Eurocopa entre Serbia y Albania en Belgrado.
La investigación genética ha aportado a estas narrativas un vocabulario nuevo y aparentemente científico. Descubrimientos legítimos sobre el linaje —o estimaciones comerciales presentadas como ciencia— se interpretan de forma selectiva como prueba de que una nación moderna desciende directamente de una población antigua. Por ejemplo, la difusión en línea de las afirmaciones de teorías conspirativas pseudohistóricas que vinculan directamente a los serbios contemporáneos con la cultura prehistórica de la cultura Vinča —a los que califica como “el pueblo más antiguo de Europa”— contradice la evidencia científica sobre las migraciones eslavas.
Asignar a las etnias macedónicas y griegas porcentajes rivales de ascendencia genética del “antiguo ADN macedonio” reduce historias complejas y compartidas a meros certificados de autenticidad. La incertidumbre científica y siglos de mestizaje desaparecen; luego, se utilizan cifras seleccionadas para tildar a los vecinos de menos autóctonos, extranjeros o incluso racialmente inferiores. La genética de poblaciones puede arrojar luz sobre las migraciones y la ascendencia, pero no puede transformar culturas prehistóricas en naciones modernas ni decidir quién tiene mayores derechos sobre un territorio.
La movediza frontera entre “anfitrión” y “huésped”
Los Balcanes constituyen un caso dramático de cómo el odio justificado al nativismo contribuyó a alimentar guerras reales, pero “justificaciones” similares surgieron en otros lugares. Los movimientos contra los migrantes en Francia, Gran Bretaña o Alemania no necesitan atribuirse la descendencia de los primeros habitantes para llegar a una conclusión semejante: los recién llegados tienen menos derechos que los “nativos”.
El término Gastarbeiter de la Alemania occidental, que significa “trabajador huésped”, plasmó esta contradicción. A partir de la década de 1960, se reclutó a trabajadores de los Balcanes y Turquía porque se les necesitaba, pero no se asumió que obtendrían la residencia permanente ni la ciudadanía por naturalización. Incluso sus hijos y nietos podían ser tratados como huéspedes, mientras que los migrantes anteriores o sus descendientes pasaban a formar parte del “nosotros” consolidado y rechazaban a quienes llegaban después.
Por lo tanto, la paradoja más profunda es europea, no exclusivamente balcánica. En las historias sobre el Oeste norteamericano, “haber llegado primero” suele identificar a un pueblo desposeído que merece protección. En la política nacionalista, esa misma idea puede ser invocada por un grupo dominante como una licencia para excluir.
La historia y el sentido de pertenencia a una tierra son importantes, pero no deberían convertirse en un escalafón de la valía humana ni en un título de propiedad para la dominación étnica. La verdadera prueba de humanidad comienza cuando las personas cuyos derechos están en juego no son figuras lejanas en una película o en un cómic, sino los vecinos actuales.

title: A Viral Songwriting Challenge Shines a Spotlight on the Tradition of Hip Hop in West Virginia
content:
When Leeshia Lee got the idea to challenge artists to write a lyrical love letter to West Virginia, she had no idea it would create so much buzz. This spring and summer, the Dear West V. challenge went viral on social media. Submissions came in from all across the state.
“Clarksburg, Huntington, Charleston, hollers and hills that I’ve never heard of,” Lee said. “It was just great to see so many people take pride.”
Lee is from Charleston and is the cultural reporter with Black By God: The West Virginian. Black By God is a community news organization that centers Black voices from across the Mountain State.
“It is a way for us to change the narrative on how our stories are told,” Lee said. “It highlights the culture of Black people in West Virginia.”
Lee is also a former radio host, and over the years, she’s developed relationships with rappers, producers, and DJs from across the state.
“I decided that I wanted to challenge the artists in West Virginia all to write their version of a love letter to the 35th state.”
For the Dear West V. challenge, Lee chose a hip hop beat and all of the artists wrote a song to that same beat.
“I wanted to showcase the talent that is in West Virginia, because I believe there are thoroughly a lot of hidden gems here,” Lee said. “And on a large scale, mainstream scale, West Virginia doesn’t get the recognition that it deserves.”
For the challenge, Lee enlisted the help of Myles Satterfield, who goes by the artist name Myles T. Myles T is a hip hop producer who grew up in Charleston. He remembers listening to Lee’s radio show as a kid.
“Some of the local rappers, they were on the radio. And I was like, ‘Man, that’s cool. How do you do that?’” Myles T said.
Myles T is also the son of Crystal Good, a renowned Affilachian poet, and the founder of Black By God.
“My mother was a poet as well, so I was like, ‘Okay, you gonna write poetry, I’m gonna write raps,’” Myles T said. “But then eventually I gravitated more towards production.”
As a self-described nerd, Myles T says producing allowed him to explore his fascination with computers. When he was in college studying cyber security, he kept honing his skills in music.
“That was how I was paying rent. I was selling beats online to pay rent in college.”
These days, he lives in Los Angeles, working in cyber security and in music. He’s produced beats for industry heavy hitters like Big Sean and Wiz Khalifa. When Lee got the idea for the challenge, she reached out to Myles T.
“I asked him for a beat. And he sent me a couple but I chose the one beat,” Lee said.
Word about the Dear West V. challenge spread on social media. Artists wrote verses to Myles T’s beat, recorded themselves performing their songs, then submitted them to Black By God. They received over 100 submissions. Lee says many of the love letters expressed a sense of appreciation.
“I think that [in] the majority of the love letters, people paid homage to the neighborhoods that raised them.”
As Duke Johnson out of Huntington rapped:
See, I was raised here, the son of a African and a gringo.
Held it down from Moneyton to Mingo.
I’ve been in the projects, the trailer parks, nice houses, and hollers.
Met a lot of good folks that do what they can for a dollar.
Kind to our neighbor, respect in our behavior,
and we finally realizing that the coal ain’t gonna save us.
“There were some really deep moments in there too, where people talked about a lot of the loss that they saw, or a lot of the judgment that they got from their area, or how they don’t feel seen, or they don’t feel heard,” Myles T said. “There was so much in some of these verses.”
“Some of them were really, really political, talking about the environmental issues, the pharmaceutical industries…incarcerations,” Lee said.
Like Monstalung of Morgantown:
Dear West V, we have to do better
Places like McDowell got me writing this letter
High cancer rates throughout the state
The water’s bad, you can tell by the taste
They are cutting funding and programs for the people
Caging us up and calling us illegal
Nothing new, we’ve seen this sequel
Flipping the words and saying it’s not equal
Yo, shaking my head at the audacity
Like we ain’t surviving floods and catastrophes
So tell your family, tell your squad
That more than ever we need Black By God
Josh Mei, aka Spike Yee, is another artist from Morgantown who submitted a song to the challenge. “He referred to himself as AppalAsian,” Lee said. “And his love letter was very eye opening.”
“Growing up Chinese American [in Morgantown] in the 90s, you know, wasn’t the best experience. It wasn’t terrible, but it wasn’t the best,” Spike Yee said. “I still had a lot of self-identity issues.”
As a self-described socially awkward kid growing up in a traditional Chinese household, Spike Yee found inspiration in how hip hop artists presented themselves.
“It was like the bravado, the confidence that you have to show. These are all things that I really wanted as a child,” Spike Yee said.
It wasn’t until he got to college in Athens, Ohio, that Spike Yee started rapping. He began attending a monthly freestyle rap battle. At first, he was nervous to take the stage. But eventually, he found his stride.
“That rush became addicting. And so I started going back every time and I would just…keep battling. And then I started winning.”
Spike Yee is back in Morgantown now and is a known quantity in the hip hop scene there. He heard about the Dear West V. challenge through social media.
“I thought the beat was super dope, and I wanted to contribute a verse to the concept of a love letter to West Virginia. Just for myself.”
For Spike Yee, it was a chance to explore his complicated relationship with the state.
Growing up, I used to hate it here.
Jaded by the state of conditions,
and it would lead me to evade it in my later years.
Amount of times I wanted out, without a shadow of a doubt.
I had a paddle, but I couldn’t find a route.
Everybody said to go, so now he’s out on the run.
Headed west and saw the truth. Felt like the prodigal son.
Headed east back to my roots. Feel like I’m one of the ones.
Now let me hold it down in Morgantown. I’m second to none.
“I left so many times, and you know, I always came back,” Spike Yee said.
I spent so many years fishing for the answers. Like, when will it bite?
Just need a chance to be myself and take control of my life.
I feel serenity now. Take a look at how you raised him.
Chinese kid in Appalachia. I am AppalAsian.
In the land of almost heaven, watch for the throne.
The state accepted me and made sure I ain’t stepping alone.
It’s kind of crazy, never realized just where I belong.
So here’s my gratitude for giving me a home, West Virginia.
Another artist who submitted to the challenge is Nicole Johnson, aka CoCo Nicole. Growing up in Huntington, CoCo Nicole started rapping when she was in high school.
“You kind of roast each other when you’re in high school, right? Like, you always have jokes with your friend group. So as a way of doing that with each other, we would kind of freestyle and rap,” CoCo Nicole said. “So I really took a liking to it back when I was in probably ninth, tenth grade. Just doing that with the girls.”
She quickly discovered that rapping was a way to vent her emotions and document her life. Then in college, some friends invited her to record her songs.
“I never tried to sing at first, I just always knew I wanted to rap…and it just kind of came naturally,” CoCo Nicole said. “When I started projecting and putting that on the microphone, I always loved the way my voice sounds.”
As her confidence grew and her skills sharpened, CoCo Nicole started releasing her recordings and performing live. In 2024, she hit a career high when she opened for rapper Rick Ross in Ashland, Kentucky. But soon after that, she fell into a creative dry spell.
“I was like fresh out of having my baby, and I was postpartum. I just wasn’t inspired, I had a mental block from music. And I just felt like I wasn’t ever going to do it again,” CoCo Nicole said.
But then, her brother—who’s also a rapper—told her about the Dear West V. challenge. After seeing his submission and hearing the beat, she decided to write her own love letter.
“I was like, I’m getting back out there. I was like, I want to write, I’m inspired.”
Dear West Virginia, my words to you for birthing me.
How could I not appreciate a state creatin’ queens?
The type of women with ambition climbin’ hills of dreams.
We found our way next to the river where the money streams.
“I wanted to give thanks and give my love to West Virginia for creating the type of women that I know and I’m around, and even the type of women that raised me,” CoCo Nicole said.
Childhood in a wild hood.
Parents used to sacrifice, so we be all good.
Taught us morals and respect that go a long way.
I’ll take a country queen from here over anything.
For CoCo Nicole, the Dear West V. challenge reignited her creativity. She’s since written and recorded a handful of new songs and has even performed live again. “The creative juices are flowing,” she said.
For Leeshia Lee and Myles T, the response to the challenge was overwhelming. People from other states were following along online. So were people who Myles T says aren’t your typical hip hop fans.
“We’ll be in the gas station, and people be like, ‘Oh, y’all the ones doing the contest.’ And it’ll be like an old lady that I was like, ‘I had no clue that you would even see this. How did this even get in your radar?’” Myles T said.
CoCo Nicole says that the viral challenge galvanized the hip hop community across the state.
“The Dear West Virginia challenge really woke people back up,” she said. “I feel like what Leeshia and Myles have done is kind of waking people up to wanting to have more events, you know, to do things.”
Spike Yee agreed.
“It kind of showed everybody…we all exist. And we’re all here doing something that we love,” he said. “This is such a uniting factor for a bunch of people from so many different walks of life.”
Because the challenge was so successful, Leeshia Lee, Myles T, and Black By God decided to host an awards show this summer in Charleston. Tickets sold out, and everyone came dressed to impress for the black tie affair. Artists from the challenge were presented with a variety of awards. The categories included Most Heartfelt, Most Historic, and Best Female Performance, which CoCo Nicole was nominated for. In fact, she won.
“I prepared a speech for just in case I won, but I got up there and I forgot all my words,” CoCo Nicole said. “I was like, ‘I hope I sound good!’ Oh my god, I was so nervous.”
For CoCo Nicole, she hopes West Virginia’s hip hop community will continue to build upon the momentum that’s been generated from the Dear West V. challenge. She wants to see the Mountain State recognized as a hub for rap and hip hop.
“We see it happen in so many other big cities. I mean, Atlanta, LA, Houston. You see it happen everywhere else, but I feel like we have enough talent here to where if we all just come together and start pushing each other, it could be big. It could be a great thing.”
Through Black By God, Leeshia Lee and Myles T have plans to keep supporting West Virginia’s hip hop artists, with another awards show taking place this winter.
This article is part of the Living Traditions project, featuring an assortment of stories and podcasts about folklife in central Appalachia.

title: Global fund aims to end FGM, New York sees safest summer ever, Bhutan ends dog-transmitted human rabies
content:
Photo: Jessica Lea/DFID via Flickr (CC BY 2.0)
In today’s edition: a new fund has been launched with the aim of ending the practice of female genital mutilation, violent crime in New York City hits a historic low between June and August, and Bhutan has become the first country in South-East Asia to officially eliminate human rabies transmitted by dogs.
The aim of Her Horizon Fund is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending female genital mutilation within a generation. Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.
Source: The Guardian
Between June and August, New York City saw 195 shooting incidents, 249 shooting victims and 66 murders – the fewest in recorded history for each category. Major crime dropped by 6.6% citywide in August, with The Bronx leading the decline.
Source: CBS News
The WHO has validated Bhutan’s elimination of canine-transmitted rabies as a public health problem in the region. Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal once clinical symptoms appear, but deaths can be prevented by vaccinating dogs to curb the disease at its source. Additionally, the use of post exposure prophylaxis stops the virus from reaching the central nervous system after a bite.
Source: WHO
Tim Andrews received a kidney transplanted from a pig in January 2025, sparing him months of needing to go to hospital to have his blood filtered by a dialysis machine. The kidney continued to function until it was removed in October that year. Tim then needed dialysis for 82 days until he had an organ from a donor in January of this year. That organ has been working well.
Source: BBC News
Despite the Trump administration’s vocal opposition to renewable energy, the overwhelming majority of new solar power generation is taking place in conservative US states. Texas and Florida, the two largest Trump-supporting states by population, are in fact leading the way in the country’s adoption of solar.
Source: Grist
The laws, signed by the Democratic California governor on Thursday, bars social media companies from using infinite scroll and autoplay for users under 16. “This is about actually addressing the problem, the scrolling, the algorithms. This is about addressing the substantive issue around the engineering,” Gaving Newsom said at a news conference.
Source: The Guardian
Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said. The legislation comes a few months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s.
Source: The Guardian
How much exercise do you need per week? A new study suggests that the type of activity could make an unexpectedly big difference: according to research, just three minutes of intense sprinting reportedly trigger more measurable changes in the body than 90 minutes of moderate cycling.
Source: Science Daily
US farmers are increasingly turning to perennial grains which can withstand extreme weather and drought. Researchers at The Land Institute in Kansas are developing perennial versions of annual crops which can be planted once every couple of seasons, improving soil health and storing carbon.
Source: AP News
Family-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is striving to help Palestinians gain sovereignty over their food security. The project has two main aims. One is to collect and preserve the seeds of local plants that may thrive better in this landscape; the other is to create a node for seed distribution for farmers who need to save every possible penny.
Source: The Guardian

title: 6,000 People, 27 Villages & One Zero-Waste Mission
content: In Zemithang, Arunachal Pradesh, communities come together every Sunday to keep their Himalayan home clean. Every household contributes ₹50, while women riders collect the segregated waste and take it to a recycling centre. title: Dr Te Ripowai Higgins: An unrelenting champion of te ao Māori
content:
"Mō tēnei hōnore i homaihia nei, kei au te waimarie, nā te mea i a au e tipu mai ana e patua ana i te kura mō te kōrero i tō tātou reo. Ka mutu, koirā anake te reo i mōhio mātou."
Recognition like this is poignant, especially considering I was among the generations beaten at school for speaking our language, it's the only language we knew.
- Dr Te Ripowai Higgins, QSM, ONZM
Beaten for speaking te reo Māori at school, Dr Te Ripowai Higgins (Ngāi Tūhoe) dedicated her career to keeping her language and culture alive.
Her relentless dedication to a language she was punished for speaking has been recognised by the Governor-General at an investiture ceremony this week, where she received the Officer of the New Zealand Order of Merit (ONZM) for more than 43 years of service to education and Māori.
Dr Higgins reflected on the acknowledgement and shared her thoughts with Pūkāea.
"Mō tēnei hōnore i homaihia nei, kei au te waimarie, nā te mea i a au e tipu mai ana e patua ana i te kura mō te kōrero i tō tātou reo. Ka mutu, koirā anake te reo i mōhio mātou."
I find this type of recognition quite poignant, especially considering I was among the generations beaten at school for speaking our native tongue.
The assimilationist education system of the time prioritised English and contributed to the suppression and decline of te reo Māori.
But the punishment had the opposite effect on Dr Higgins.
She says kaumātua and kuia taught her generation to withstand those pressures and turn adversity into opportunity.
"Nā rātou i tohu, 'kia kaha koutou, ahakoa patua koutou, me ako koutou i taua reo. Kei te pai tō koutou reo Māori. Kua nui ake ngā Pākehā e haere mai ana, me ako koutou i tā rātou ake reo, kia mōhio ake tātou kei te aha ngā kōrero'."
They told us not to let the beatings break us; they helped us recognise that learning their language didn't mean we had to abandon our own. They said Pākehā would not stop coming, they told us we had to adapt and master their language so we would always know what they were saying."
The ability to navigate two worlds became a defining feature of Dr Higgins' career.
She went on to help establish initiatives that created pathways for te reo Māori in education, broadcasting and public life.
In 1982, she became a foundation board member of Te Ataarangi, the Māori language revitalisation movement.
She remained involved for 42 years, helping generations learn te reo Māori while sharing the approach with Indigenous communities overseas.
Her influence extended into Māori broadcasting.
She served three terms on the board of Te Māngai Pāho and was instrumental in establishing Te Upoko o te Ika, recognised as Aotearoa's first Māori radio station.
Those initiatives established foundations for the ongoing development of more education and media initiatives dedicated to fostering te reo Māori.
Dr Higgins says her aspiration is to ensure generations to come maintain pride in their identity.
"Karekau e tino aro atu ana ki ngā tohu pēnei. Ko te āhua kei te tino hiahia kia kitea, ko te whakakaha ake i te nui o ngā tāngata e kōrero Māori ana, heoi i tū atu I te reo, kia whakatauira ai rātou i te mana me te mōhio o ngā kuia, kaumātua."
Things like this have never interested me. The work I have done over the years is focussed on supporting the establishment of initiatives that encourage Māori to embrace their language, beyond that. I want future generations to take pride in their identity and represent their culture with integrity, I hope they, like me aspire to make their kaumātua and kuia proud."
Dr Higgins' daughter, Dr Rawinia Higgins is demonstrating the impact of her mother's work through her own role as Māori Language Commissioner, helping lead the revitalisation of te reo Māori.
Speaking to Radio New Zealand about the importance of Te wiki o Te Reo Māori, Higgins said the growing number of people learning the language is encouraging, and the commission's rangahau (research) continues to show that many New Zealanders see te reo Māori as a valuable part of the country's identity.
"This is a three generation kaupapa," she said.
"Every little step that each generation takes is really important."

title: Richmond Night Market prepares for its grand finale
content:
When the Richmond Night Market’s neon lights turn off for the last time on Sunday, the Metro Vancouver community will say goodbye to one of the region’s most vibrant cultural gatherings after 26 years.
The event, which ran on weekends from April to September, was founded by entrepreneur Raymond Cheung in 2000 to bring public night-time culture inspired by Asian night markets to the B.C. suburb.
Mr. Cheung announced the market’s permanent closing last month. He said the market’s lease near Bridgeport station was ending, and that the potential cost of taking on a new, pricier lease wouldn’t make sense for the business.
The market originally opened at Continental Shopping Centre in Richmond. Over the years, it moved to bigger sites, evolving into what organizers claim is North America’s largest night market. It drew more than one million visitors, tourists and locals alike, each year. The market hosted upwards of 200 vendors selling food, clothing and more in brightly lit stalls.
Since relocating in 2012 to its current location near Bridgeport station, the market became a major cultural and economic anchor in the region.
With its lease expiring and no affordable new site to welcome the large event, the only course of action seemed to be to close the market. “It’s a very mixed feeling,” owner Mr. Cheung said.
“The sad part, of course, is this is the end of the chapter. I didn’t expect this to last forever,” he said. “… But this market is about bonding, it’s about community – that’s what it is.”
For families like the Purbas, who drove from nearby Delta for their fourth visit this season, the closure cuts deep. “We’re sad that it is closing, but it is the last weekend we can attend, so that’s why we’re here,” Gagandeep Purba said.
The market’s reputation is known across borders. Jesica Vinson travelled from Seattle with her family to catch the final season. “Is there any way to save it?” she asked.
Behind the food stalls, however, many long-term vendors were feeling at peace. At Po Wah Dim Sum, Christopher Yee helped his mother, Lai Wah, wrap up a legacy of more than two decades running the family business. “My mom has been doing it for 26 years and she’s retiring this year,” Mr. Yee said.
Others, such as Francis Dela Chica of Bao Buns, have accepted the closing as bittersweet. He said that while it’s sad that the night market is ending, it was also the perfect incubator for small businesses like his own. “It was a good place to start, to test your products, to meet new customers.”

title: Child cancer groups call for concerted action
content:
It's one of the cruelest ironies in health and medicine. Pediatric sarcomas are among the rarest yet most aggressive forms of childhood cancer and some of the hardest to cure. Whereas many adult cancers are now treatable with new therapeutic strategies, such as immunotherapies, pediatric sarcomas have not seen nearly as many advances. Survival rates have remained largely unchanged for decades.
In 2014, parents from advocacy groups across Long Island, New York, who'd lost children to rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) banded together to form a coalition supporting a new research initiative aimed at better understanding this deadly disease so that one day a cure could be found.
The group met at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory's Banbury Center. This world-renowned think tank was built to bring together scientists, clinicians and patient advocates to launch initiatives like this one, focused on a particular area of research or public health.
Since that fateful first meeting, scientists have made progress not only in RMS but also in other sarcomas and childhood diseases. Likewise, what began as a small but dedicated coalition of RMS groups has grown into a full-fledged pediatric sarcoma movement. After more than a decade of progress, the movement returned to Banbury Center.
In 2025, the think tank hosted Pediatric Sarcomas: Targets for Therapeutic Development. The meeting was organized by CSHL Adjunct Professor Christopher Vakoc, now at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, and Kimberly Stegmaier, chair of the Department of Pediatric Oncology at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
"It was an intense and inspiring three days," recalls Phil Renna, founder of the Christina Renna Foundation, one of the advocacy groups that supported both Banbury meetings.
"So many ideas were proposed and discussed. Most importantly, we came away with a roadmap to help bring today's cutting-edge research from bench to bedside."
That roadmap recently appeared in an article in Genes & Development, published by CSHL Press. In the article, meeting attendees called for more collaboration in the spirit of the Banbury sessions.
The authors wrote that for today's pediatric cancer discoveries to eventually benefit patients, it would be crucial to "foster interdisciplinary partnerships among medical chemists, scientists, clinicians, advocates, and industry partners."
After outlining obstacles to progress, the group laid out three top priorities for the future: 1) creating an open-access platform for data and model sharing; 2) bridging pediatric and adult oncology through unified clinical infrastructure; and 3) fostering multidisciplinary collaboration.
"Together, these priorities underscore the need for a more interconnected research ecosystem that matches the complexity of the disease itself," the authors wrote.
"As emerging tools continue to reveal new vulnerabilities in pediatric sarcomas, the challenge ahead lies in translating this knowledge into durable therapies, guided by collaboration, shared infrastructure, and a sustained commitment to bridging discovery and treatment."
