title: Bio-RV, a Neonatal Rotavirus Vaccine Developed Through Bio Farma–MCRI Collaboration, Receives Marketing Authorization from BPOM
content:
Bio Farma officially received marketing authorization for Bio-RV on September 2, 2026. This regulatory milestone follows an extensive journey encompassing research, process development, preclinical and clinical studies, technology transfer, regulatory submission, and manufacturing preparation involving various national and international institutions.
The marketing authorization confirms that Bio-RV has undergone BPOM’s evaluation of its safety, efficacy, and quality in accordance with applicable regulatory standards and requirements. For Bio Farma and MCRI, this achievement shows how collaboration among research institutions, academia, industry, and global partners can translate into biotechnology innovation with the potential to deliver tangible public health benefits.
Bio-RV is a naturally attenuated live rotavirus vaccine administered orally. The vaccine is intended to prevent gastroenteritis, or acute diarrhea, caused by rotavirus infection. It is administered in a three-dose schedule: the first dose at 0–5 days of age, the second at 8–10 weeks, and the third at 12–14 weeks. These characteristics allow vaccination to begin during the neonatal period, establishing protection against rotavirus disease from the earliest stage of an infant’s life, at a time when families are in contact with their local health services
Bio-RV is particularly relevant as rotavirus remains one of the leading causes of severe diarrhea among infants and young children. Citing data from the Indonesia Rotavirus Surveillance Network for 2001–2017, the Indonesian Ministry of Health reported that rotavirus accounted for approximately 41–58 percent of diarrhoeal cases among children under five requiring hospitalization. Recurrent diarrhea may also impair nutrient absorption and increase the risk of growth disorders in children.
Bio Farma President Director Shadiq Akasya said that obtaining marketing authorization for Bio-RV reflects the company’s commitment to delivering vaccine innovations that address public health needs while strengthening Indonesia’s national capabilities in vaccine development.
“Bio-RV is not simply about introducing a new vaccine. Behind this achievement lies an extensive journey of scientific advancement, process development, preclinical and clinical studies, technology transfer, regulatory submission, and manufacturing preparation. This entire process has been made possible through collaboration among researchers, academia, industry, and global partners,” Shadiq said.
According to Shadiq, Bio-RV’s neonatal dosing schedule provides an opportunity to establish protection against rotavirus from the earliest stage of life.
“What we aim to deliver is protection for Indonesian children as early as possible, while ensuring that Indonesia has the capacity to independently safeguard the continuity of vaccine supply. This forms part of Bio Farma’s contribution to strengthening national health resilience and sovereignty,” he added.
Bio-RV originated from the RV3-BB vaccine candidate, based on a neonatal rotavirus strain developed by MCRI. The collaboration then progressed through clinical research and further development to prepare for Bio-RV production in Indonesia.
Human rotavirus was first identified in 1973 by MCRI Professor Ruth Bishop and Professor Ian Holmes from the University of Melbourne. Soon after, MCRI’s Professors Bishop and Barnes established a collaboration with UGM’s Professor Yati Soenarto, who was the first to confirm that rotavirus was the most common cause of diarrheal death and hospitalization in children in Indonesia. In 1982, Professor Bishop identified RV3, an unusual rotavirus strain that infected newborn babies without causing disease and appeared to protect them from subsequent severe rotavirus diarrhea.
Building on this discovery, MCRI Professor Julie Bines led the development of RV3-BB as a live oral neonatal vaccine, taking it from a promising naturally occurring strain through clinical development in Australia, New Zealand and Indonesia. This work provided the foundation for Bio Farma’s Bio-RV vaccine. The close 50-year collaboration between the teams at UGM and
MCRI has been pivotal to the clinical development of MCRI’s original RV3-BB vaccine and Bio Farma’s Bio-RV. The MCRI RV3-BB vaccine development was made possible through grants from the Gates Foundation and the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council. MCRI also acknowledges the Australian Government's enduring support for global health through the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
Several partners have also supported the collaboration between Bio Farma and MCRI, including Universitas Gadjah Mada (UGM), Universitas Airlangga through the Airlangga Integrated Research Clinic (AIRC), and PATH at various stages of development.
This collaboration has not only delivered a new vaccine but also strengthened Bio Farma’s capabilities to build Indonesia’s vaccine innovation ecosystem through cooperation among global research institutions, national academic institutions, and industry. Developing domestic capabilities across the Bio-RV development and manufacturing processes is expected to strengthen vaccine availability, reduce reliance on imported products, and support the sustainability of Indonesia’s National Immunization Program.
As part of the Danantara Indonesia ecosystem, Bio Farma remains committed to transforming national strategic assets and capabilities into tangible benefits for society while upholding good corporate governance, professionalism, and integrity. The development of Bio-RV represents a concrete contribution to improving quality of life through health innovation while strengthening Indonesia’s capabilities and competitiveness in the vaccine and life sciences industries.
This initiative aligns with Danantara’s purpose, “Transforming National Assets into Prosperity with Integrity,” particularly through efforts to improve quality of life and build a stronger Indonesia supported by robust national healthcare industry capabilities.
This achievement also reflects Bio Farma’s spirit of “Advancing Hope, Shaping the Future,” by turning hope into reality through health protection, science, innovation, and collaboration, while helping shape the future of healthcare in Indonesia and around the world.

title: HERITAGE & RESTITUTION OP-ED: We walk to remember what apartheid erased of Newlands and Claremont
content:
There is a temptation, on Heritage Day, to reduce our history to braais and bunting, a comfortable, sanitised celebration that costs us nothing and demands nothing. But for the families dispersed from Newlands and Claremont across the wind-blown expanse of the Cape Flats, heritage is neither comfortable nor abstract. It is the memory of a home from which they were torn, an ancestral landscape closer to the mountain that was declared, by the stroke of an apartheid bureaucrat’s pen, to be no longer theirs.
On Thursday, 24 September, the Newlands/Claremont Heritage, Environmental Justice and Restitution Society (NCHERS) will convene its fifth annual Walk of Remembrance through these streets. We walk because remembering is itself a form of resistance. The dispossession of Newlands and Claremont did not begin with the Group Areas Act; it reaches back to the 17th century, to the very foundations of colonial conquest at the Cape. But it was the apartheid forced removals of the 1960s that completed the work, emptying vibrant, mixed neighbourhoods of their people and scattering them to the periphery, out of sight of the leafy suburbs that rose in their place.
What was lost was not merely property. It was a way of living together. NCHERS was founded by two neighbouring houses of worship, St Saviour’s Anglican Church and the Claremont Main Road Masjid, precisely because they stand as living testimony to a community in which Christian and Muslim, and many others besides, lived in mutual coexistence. These sacred spaces are among the few remaining threads connecting the exiled to the homes they were forced to abandon. To this day, many who can no longer live in the area still travel back to worship here, drawn to the last tangible fragment of a stolen belonging.
In the Qur’an we are taught that God made us into nations and tribes that we might come to recognise and know one another (49:13), that diversity is a divine intention, not a problem to be engineered away. Apartheid’s spatial planning was, at its core, a theological heresy as much as a political crime: it declared that people created to know one another must instead be separated, ranked and removed. Our walk is a quiet repudiation of that lie.
This year we begin at the Newlands Cricket Ground and follow a route marked by three stops, each a wound and each a testimony. At Draper Square, off Main Road, former residents will recall the families and institutions that once filled that space, Talfalah Primary School, the Orpheum Bioscope, the ordinary infrastructure of a community that dared to flourish. Passing under the subway, we will pause outside the Stegman Road Masjid to honour the towering witness of Imam Abdullah Haron, who resisted the forced removals and the wider machinery of apartheid, and who was killed in an apartheid detention cell on 27 September 1969.
Our walk falls within days of that date, which this year marks the 57th anniversary of his martyrdom, and that his youngest daughter, Fatima Haron-Masoet, walks with us is a reminder that this history is not distant: it lives and breathes among us still.
Our third stop, at the Cape Town Athenaeum in Mariendahl Lane, honours the life of the mind. This was an intellectual hub, a meeting place for the Teachers’ League of South Africa and the broader Non-European Unity Movement, who understood that liberation begins in the mind long before it is won in the streets. Here teachers turned the instrument of their own subjugation against the regime, refusing to collaborate with tyranny and forging in their pupils a political consciousness that would accept nothing less than full liberation. The Unity Movement’s disciplined philosophy of non-collaboration and boycott, and its refusal of the very racial categories apartheid sought to impose, were among the most rigorous intellectual challenges the system ever faced. Among its foremost teachers was RO Dudley, a towering figure of the Teachers’ League; it is fitting that his son, Russell Dudley, today chairs NCHERS, with Fatima Haron-Masoet as his deputy, standing together to reclaim what was taken.
That this tradition has been all but written out of the popular story of our liberation is itself a form of erasure, a reminder that history is not only made in the places we destroy but in the memories we are permitted to keep. To stand here is to restore the Unity Movement to its rightful place in that history. Then we return, along the railway line and under the bridge, to where we began.
Make the invisible visible again
There is a deliberate lesson in walking these streets on foot. Injustice, when it is spatial, is designed to be invisible to those who benefit from it. One drives past Draper Street without a thought for the school that once stood there; one passes the mosque without knowing an imam was martyred defending his people. To walk slowly, to stop and to name what was taken, is to make the invisible visible again. It is to insist that these places have not always been what they are now, and need not remain so.
This is why NCHERS speaks not only of remembrance, but of restitution. Memory that does not reach towards justice is sentimentality. The families on the Cape Flats remain disconnected from their ancestral land, and the areas from which they were removed retain almost no markers of the lives that once thrived there. The slow, incremental erasure of this history is not accidental; it serves those who would prefer that the moral debt of dispossession quietly expire. Our task is to refuse that expiry, to keep the account open until it is honourably settled.
After the walk, we will gather at the Newlands Cricket Experience Museum to hear the journalist and author Dougie Oakes reflect on the history of anti-apartheid resistance through sport, and on the extraordinary role played by the non-racial South African Council on Sport and its founder, Hassan Howa, whose principle, “no normal sport in an abnormal society”, captured a moral clarity we would do well to recover. That we hold this gathering at a cricket ground, a place where the politics of race and belonging were once fiercely contested, is fitting. It reminds us that the struggle for a just society was waged on every terrain, including the playing field.
We invite Capetonians of every faith and none to join us. Come and walk. Come and remember the sons and daughters of Claremont and Newlands. Come and honour the legacy of Imam Abdullah Haron. And come to affirm, with your feet, a simple and stubborn conviction: that what was unjustly taken must be remembered, named, and one day, God willing, restored.
Heritage, rightly understood, is not a monument to the past. It is a demand upon the present.
The Walk of Remembrance takes place on Thursday, 24 September 2026. The NCHERS AGM begins at 9am at the Newlands Cricket Experience Museum (the Snakepit Building), with the walk departing the Newlands Cricket Ground at 9.30am, followed by Dougie Oakes at 11am. Refreshments and exhibitions will be available. DM

title: Reclaiming Indigenous Self-governance in Minahasa: Reviving Community Authority in a Modern Nation State
content: Reclaiming Indigenous Self-governance in Minahasa: Reviving Community Authority in a Modern Nation State tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 11:18 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Long before the concept of modern democracy emerged in ancient Greek political thought, the Minahasan Peoples had already developed their own system of governance rooted in consensus-based deliberation, equality, division of responsibilities, and collective accountability. Unlike societies structured around rigid social stratification, Minahasan society embraced the principle of human equality. Individuals were seen primarily based on the roles and responsibilities they assumed within their communities, rather than social status. Minahasan people earned respect because of the duties they fulfilled, the knowledge they possessed, or the responsibilities entrusted to them, a principle reflected in a Tontémboan proverb: “Si tou peleng masuat, mapute waya. Cawana se pakuru’an, cawana se paruku’an,” which means, “All people are equal; no person is meant to be worshipped, and no person is meant to worship another.” This understanding of equality became one of the fundamental pillars of Minahasan governance. Leadership was understood as a social responsibility entrusted by the people, and important decisions were not made unilaterally. Instead, they emerged through collective deliberation involving the community. Located in Tontemboan Indigenous Territory, "Watu Tumotowa Wangko" (The Great Altar Stone) or also called "Watu Rurumeran Ni Empung" (The Stone Throne of the God) or commonly known as "Watu Pinawetengan" (The Stone Where Division Were Made) contains etchings or engravings that symbolizes a directive or decision. Architecture of Minahasan Governance At the most fundamental level, Minahasan governance was rooted in the taranak, a kinship group or family clan. Within each taranak were three key figures who carried different responsibilities: the pahéndon tu’a, a person recognized for their wisdom and ability to make decisions for the benefit of all members of the clan; the wali’an un taranak, the ritual leader responsible for maintaining the spiritual relationship between members of the taranak, their ancestors, and the natural world; and the si lumulukaz or tétérusan, responsible for the physical security and protection of clan members. From the taranak, several family groups formed a wanua. A wanua was the primary space where the social, political, economic, and spiritual life of the Minahasan Peoples took place. It was the most fundamental unit of community where important decisions concerning collective life were made and implemented. Each wanua had a leadership structure composed of figures who carried specific functions. The tona’as umbanuа served as the primary leader of the community, the wali’an wangko’ led rituals and maintained the spiritual relationship of the wider community, the tétérusan wangko’ was responsible for the security and defense of the community, and the gumigirot carried out functions related to dispute resolution and justice. Beyond the wanua, the walak was based on geographical proximity and relationships between communities, while the pakasa’an was primarily formed through shared language, history, and ritual connections. There were also various tona’as who possessed specialized knowledge and expertise in particular fields, respected for their abilities and the responsibilities they carried for the benefit of the community. Even a young person could become a tona’as if they fulfilled the criteria known in Minahasan philosophy as sigha, enté’, wo wuaya—someone possessing intelligence, conscience, physical capability, and courage. Together, these interconnected structures formed a system of self-governance that emerged from within the community itself, growing from social relationships, collective responsibility, and the community’s own needs. Restoring a waruga (Ancient Minahasan stone sarcophagi) in a housing area. Not only this is the act of honoring our ancestor, it is also an action to show that despite the land has been bought by the housing corporation, it will always belong to the indigenous people. Photo by Rinto Taroreh. Displacement and Survival of Indigenous Governance Minahasan governance was disrupted by colonialism. The Dutch implemented a centralized, hierarchical administrative system to monitor and control territories, frequently appointing the heads of the walak as district heads within the colonial administration—a strategy that allowed the Dutch to expand their influence through figures already recognized and trusted by local communities. As authority became controlled by the colonial government, the position of the wanua as the center of governance and community life gradually weakened, while the walak began to transform into an administrative unit more aligned with colonial interests. The end of Dutch colonial rule did not automatically restore Minahasa’s Indigenous governance system. After Indonesia emerged as a modern nation State, it developed a governance structure based on nationally standardized administrative divisions. These new administrative boundaries did not always correspond with the social, cultural, and ethnic territories that had previously existed. In Minahasa, Indigenous territories that had historically developed through shared histories, languages, and cultural identities were divided across several administrative regions. Although Minahasan governance structures are no longer formally recognized within the State administrative system, traditional Indigenous self-governance has not completely disappeared. In many parts of Minahasa, village leaders are known as Hukum Tua, a position that has a historical connection to Minahasan leadership traditions, as they are directly elected by the village community. When issues arise that affect the entire community, a sidang adat, or Indigenous council meeting, will be convened as a forum for communities to reach decisions through deliberation. An important element of the sidang adat is the role of the taranak as the community’s basic social unit. Each taranak is represented by a pahendon tu’a, who attends as a representative of all members of their clan. During the council, the pahendon tu’a each carry a piece of tawaang, symbolizing that they have received a full mandate from their community to speak, express views, and make decisions on behalf of the taranak they represent. Decisions produced through this process are outcomes of community representation. Indigenous councils are generally led by three, five, seven, or nine Indigenous leaders; the number nine holds profound meaning as it is regarded as a symbol of human completeness. The use of an odd number of leaders also reflects the importance of balance and wisdom in decision-making processes, while ensuring that deliberations can reach agreements accepted by the entire community. Equally important, decisions made by Indigenous councils are binding and must be respected by all community members. Indigenous sanctions may take the form of fines in accordance with the provisions applicable within each community. However, the most severe form of sanction is not a monetary fine, but social exclusion from community life. In societies where social relationships are built on kinship, mutual cooperation, and a sense of belonging, losing acceptance within the community is a far greater consequence than material punishment. Minahasan Elders and representatives during a meeting. Reclaiming Identity, Rebuilding Governance The active involvement of Indigenous youth in shaping regulations is providing the foundation for recognition of their existence, through involvement in historical documentation, Indigenous territory mapping, revitalization of Indigenous institutions, and development of public policies. The Tomohon city government recently invited Indigenous youth to participate in drafting the Regional Regulation on Indigenous Peoples. If enacted, the instrument is expected not only to provide legal certainty for the Tombulu community, but also will ensure that local government development respects Indigenous rights and decision-making systems. This experience shows that reclaiming Indigenous self-governance does not mean just rebuilding past Indigenous governance, rather, creating spaces where Indigenous governance principles, community participation, social legitimacy, deliberation, and respect for Indigenous institutions can coexist alongside modern governmental systems. If successful, Tomohon will offer a model of how Indigenous communities and local governments can build an equal relationship within a democratic nation State. History has taken the Minahasan Peoples through colonialism, centralized governance, and urbanization. This journey has not completely erased how Minahasan society understands leadership, deliberation, and collective responsibility. What needs to be reclaimed are not the exact past institutional structures, but the right of Indigenous communities to participate in determining their futures. Indigenous governance is a living, social practice that ensures that the values that have sustained Minahasan society for centuries will continue to shape the future. Gerard Tiwow is a journalist belonging to the Tombulu’ Tribe of the Minahasa Peoples in Tomohon, Sulawesi Utara, Indonesia, and a former CS Youth Fellow. title: After two failed bids, Ipswich remains hopeful of becoming an NRL side
content:
Rugby league has a storied history in Ipswich, and local clubs are pushing for it to become home to the next NRL side.
The Ipswich Jets first made a bid to join the league 16 years ago.
The city's bid is facing strong competition from the Christchurch-based Southern Orcas.
After almost two decades and two failed bids, rugby league diehards in Ipswich are once again dreaming of a place in the NRL.
The league's 20th team is expected to be announced by the end of the year, with the Queensland city's bid facing strong competition from the Christchurch-based Southern Orcas.
"We don't underestimate the fight on our hands," Rugby League Ipswich Chairman David Nugent said.
"[But] don't underestimate an Ipswich person in a fight, we'll give it our all."
Rugby league has been inseparable from the cultural identity of the former coal-mining city since the early 20th century.
It takes hold of people early, often passed down through generations.
David Haug is a perfect example. At the North Ipswich Tigers clubhouse, it's easier to name what he hasn't done at the club.
"I've played since I was under nines … coached everything from under sevens through to A-grade, been on the committee and done everything from committee member to president," he said.
That tends to be how it goes in the former industrial city west of Brisbane.
Here the game takes hold early, often carried through generations.
Ipswich's community sports fields have been a consistent breeding ground of rugby league players.
From Dud Beattie in the 1950s, to Allan "Alfie" Langer in the 1990s, and Broncos NRLW captain Ali Brigginshaw today.
But none have been able to represent their home city at the top level.
"[Ipswich players] get to a certain age … and then get picked up by other Sydney clubs and they don't get a chance to actually come back and play for their city," Mr Haug said.
Player factory
It was this exodus of talent that sparked the first Western Corridor bid in 2010, which also included the Darling Downs city of Toowoomba.
"Our young kids were leaving home at 16 to live their rugby league dreams … and for every 10 that went down the Pacific Highway, nine came back with broken hearts," Ipswich Jets chair Steve Johnson said.
But Mr Johnson, who is spearheading the bid, believes the benefits of the Jets becoming the league's 20th team would spread far beyond Ipswich.
"With the expansion at the moment with PNG and Western Australia, [the NRL] needs more players and we will surely generate more players than we need."
"We'll become a player factory for the entire NRL."
University of Technology Sydney Sports Economics Professor Tim Harcourt said new clubs generally had to bring two things to the NRL: spectators and TV viewers.
"It's definitely rugby league heartland," Mr Harcourt said.
"And secondly, it's attractive economically to have more Brisbane derbies in a sense, because you'll have the Dolphins and Broncos, and then I guess the Jets."
But he believed the Ipswich bid's biggest competitor, the Christchurch-based Southern Orcas, was in a better position to become the NRL's 20th team.
He said Christchurch would be a more attractive destination for travelling fans, which the NRL would likely take into consideration.
"There's a lot of tourism to the South Island of New Zealand already, with Lord of the Rings and all the beautiful landscape."
"They've also got this brand new stadium which is fantastic for all sorts of sports and events, so they're kind of ready to go," Mr Harcourt said.
With no suitable stadium in Ipswich, the Jets would have to play at Brisbane's Lang Park.
The Jets are hoping to turn North Ipswich Reserve into a 12,000-seat rectangular stadium, but are yet to secure all necessary funding.
Eyes turn to next generation
Far removed from the boardroom machinations at Rugby League Central in Sydney, those who have spent decades working at the grassroots level consider an Ipswich NRL team through the eyes of local under-18s players.
"For me, the driving force is every kid involved in sport is one less kid on the street," Redbank Plains Bears President Jodie Elder said.
"For some kids it just means everything. It could be the highlight of their week to come to training."
Rory Morley-Davies plays for the North Ipswich Tigers under-15s side and started playing football at a young age.
"I don't think any other sport fulfils me like rugby does," he said.
"When [people in Ipswich] think of a sport, they don't think of anything other than rugby league."
"Everyone wouldn't want anything else, except for Ipswich to have a rugby league team, and I think it's a long time coming."

title: Mzilikazi commemorations grow into regional cultural spectacle
content:
Langalakhe Mabena, [email protected]
WHAT began as a commemoration of King Mzilikazi’s death anniversary turned into a major cross-border celebration of African culture and heritage on Saturday, as thousands of people from Zimbabwe and beyond converged at historic Mhlahlandlela in Bulawayo.
The gathering brought together Government officials, Bulawayo City Council leadership, amabutho, amaguqa, amatshitshi, cultural groups and members of the public, with visitors from South Africa, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and China also joining the celebrations.
The usually quiet historical site on the outskirts of Bulawayo was transformed into a vibrant cultural hub, with music, dance, traditional performances and colourful regalia creating a fitting tribute to the founder of the Ndebele nation.
The celebrations began at 7am with a cultural parade from Matshobana Township, led by amatshitshi, amaguqa, abafana and amabutho. Dressed in traditional regalia, the participants marched through some of Bulawayo’s iconic suburbs, including Matshobana, Nguboyenja, Mzilikazi and Makokoba, before proceeding into the city centre. The procession made a stop at the statue of the late Vice-President Dr Joshua Mqabuko Nyongolo Nkomo before continuing to the Large City Hall car park, from where participants were transported to Mhlahlandlela for the main ceremony.
At Mhlahlandlela, generations converged to celebrate the legacy of King Mzilikazi, with elderly participants, children and cultural groups adding colour to the festivities.
Born near Mkuze in Zululand in 1790, King Mzilikazi is remembered for his leadership in building the Ndebele nation after breaking away from King Shaka in 1823. He died on September 9, 1868, and was buried at Entumbane in Matobo, about 20km from Bulawayo.
This year’s commemorations marked 158 years since his death and highlighted the enduring cultural links between the Ndebele people in Zimbabwe and other Nguni communities across the region.
Matabeleland South Provincial Affairs and Devolution Minister Albert Nguluvhe, who was the guest of honour, said the huge turnout reflected the significance of King Mzilikazi’s contribution to the development of the Ndebele nation.
“Your presence is a reminder that we are gathered on sacred ground. We gather not to just remember a king but a builder. King Mzilikazi kaMatshobane was not just a warrior, he was a nation builder, a unifier and a custodian of identity,” he said.
Minister Nguluvhe said culture remained central to how communities and the country conducted their affairs.
“Culture is the way we resolve conflict. It is the way we farm, it is the way we treat our elderly, it is how we lead and how we govern,” he said.
The commemorations also emerged as a platform for strengthening cultural ties beyond Zimbabwe’s borders. Royal guest Dumisani Mthembo Dube, chairman of the Umkhosi WeNxwala ceremony in Zambia under the kingship of Mpezeni, said attending the event had allowed him to learn more about Ndebele history and culture.
“It is a great thing for the nation to unite to revive African culture. It’s a great honour that I was invited to be part of this event. Coming from Zambia to Bulawayo to celebrate the King Mzilikazi commemorations gave me purpose because I am here to learn the history of our forefathers and further learn the way of life for the Ndebele nation.
“This was a great expedition, and what I learnt here, I will share it with other Nguni people in Zambia,” said Mr Dube.
Adding star power to the commemorations were South African entertainment personalities, including Maskandi musician Khuzani Mpungose and stars of the popular television series Shaka iLembe, Dawn Thandeka King and Mpilo Mbatha, who played Mkabayi and Mzilikazi respectively.
Khuzani, who has a large following among Maskandi fans, popularly known as the “blue nation”, said he was overwhelmed by the reception he received in Bulawayo.
“It’s my first time being in Zimbabwe, KwaBulawayo, and I am shocked by what I am seeing here. Being welcomed with such love is a beautiful gesture that I believe is mostly reserved for the kings and queens. Such a gesture humbles me.
“The cultural songs at this ceremony were sung in isintu, a great common thing that we do in KwaZulu. Basically, my experience here confirmed that indeed we are one people,” said Khuzani.
For acclaimed actress Dawn Thandeka King, the visit was equally personal, with the actress describing her return to Bulawayo as a homecoming. King previously visited the city earlier this year for Imiklomelo kaDakamela before travelling to Nkayi, where she immersed herself in local culture and interacted with communities.
“Being here already feels like home. Earlier this year, I was here and went to Nkayi, where I had a great cultural experience. Instead of staying for a short period of time, I had to stay much longer because I found purpose in this city, holding acting classes and doing other business.
“My return is to continue my cultural journey and discovery in this beautiful city. My roots are connected with the Khumalo people, and I felt like royalty to be invited for this great day, celebrating the legacy of King Mzilikazi,” she said.
Chief Dakamela of Nkayi, who delivered the closing remarks, said the massive turnout demonstrated that communities remained committed to preserving their cultural identity.
“What I see here is an embrace of who we are. I am proud that people came in their numbers to celebrate this day. This was King Mzilikazi’s dream when he created the Ndebele nation. I am sure he is happy wherever he is, because we united today to preserve his dream and legacy.
“This event was a success because of the people. Amabutho or chiefs were not going to make all this such a success alone. It is the people who left everything behind to come together and unite for this event,” said Chief Dakamela.
The main ceremony ended at 5pm, but the cultural celebration continued into the evening at a local leisure spot where the Maskandi Music Festival, headlined by Khuzani, took over.
Other performers included Bhila, Gazelimnyama and Imfanomsuthu, alongside Maskandi and Imbube artistes.
The scale and diversity of this year’s commemorations demonstrated that King Mzilikazi’s legacy extends beyond a historical remembrance, continuing to provide a cultural bridge connecting communities across Zimbabwe and the wider Nguni world.
Meanwhile, the Mthwakazi kaMzilikazi Cultural Association (MMCA) has hailed this year’s commemorations as a resounding success, expressing gratitude to the thousands of people who turned out to honour the legacy of King Mzilikazi, the founding father of the Ndebele nation.

title: The 'forgotten' model village where 19th-Century workers escaped overcrowded slums
content:
The 'forgotten' model village where 19th-Century workers escaped overcrowded slums
- Published
While Port Sunlight on the Wirral is a well-known example of an industrial model village where workers lived to escape Victorian slums, another model village close by actually predates it by more than three decades.
Bromborough Pool, founded in 1853, is less well known than Port Sunlight, and local historian Elizabeth Davey said "even Wirral residents are not quite sure what is there".
The garden village, a planned community, was founded by Price's Patent Candle Factory to enable workers to escape overcrowded and disease-ridden industrial slums.
Mike Christiansen, who has researched its history, said it was a "forgotten village", despite being the second such village to be created in Britain.
Christiansen works for the Autism Together charity, which was given three Grade II-listed buildings in the village by former owners Riverside Housing.
These are the village school, the village hall and St Matthew's Church.
Christiansen, who does occasional tours of the village, said he "made it my mission" to learn more about the village after he became manager of the charity's cafe there and people would come in and ask questions about its history.
He said Bromborough Pool was the first model village to have gardens attached to the houses.
The village once had a wall around it and "at 11 o'clock every night, the gates would be closed, so if anyone wasn't back in the village by 11 o'clock, then they'd have to hop over the wall," he said.
Christiansen said Bromborough Pool appeared to have been a "dry village" at one time and so residents "definitely had to go further afield if they wanted to go to the pub".
Wirral Council archivist Will Meredith said industrialists such as the Wilson family at Price's Patent Candles "were paternalistic towards the workers" at a time when others could be exploitative.
He said it must have been difficult, though, as "what we have got here is you've got your boss in the factory where you work who is also your landlord".
Meredith said Bromborough Pool was "not as fancy as Port Sunlight but it's just nice terraced housing".
Another listed building that remains in the village is the Clock Tower, which once housed offices, and is now owned by Wirral Methodist Housing Association and used for residential accommodation.
James and George Wilson, owners of Price's Patent Candle Company, bought 61 acres of land when they wanted to build a new factory at Bromborough Pool to expand on their operation in London.
They purchased the land from the Lord of Bromborough Manor for £12,267 and 10 shillings, Christiansen said.
He said the main ethos of the village was ensure the welfare of its workers, particularly in relation to religion, education, horticulture and sport and "so the village had public buildings to encompass all these values".
Other model industrial villages built in Britain around this time include Saltaire near Bradford in West Yorkshire in the mid 19th Century and Bourneville, built to house workers from the Cadbury factory in the 1890s in Birmingham.
It was founded 35 years before industrialist William Hesketh Lever's company began building Port Sunlight down the road in 1888.
Bromborough Pool village was created at a time when many people would have lived in overcrowded, insanitary conditions, Davey said.
Christiansen said a former fever hospital was also built in the village to treat sailors on the River Mersey who had contracted diphtheria and typhoid.
This later became the Price's Social Club and is now in private ownership.
My childhood memories
Bromborough Pool village has a place close to my heart as it is where my nan and grandad Rene and Tom O'Hara lived from the 1970s up until 2000.
They moved there from Rock Ferry when Tom began working at what became Unilever's Unichema factory.
He and Rene were given a tied cottage and actually ended up living in two different cottages on Manor Place in the village during their time there, as a result of phased refurbishment of the houses during the 1980s.
While I do not think my cousins and I really appreciated the history of the village while growing up, it now fascinates us and my cousin Ruth Molyneux and I went on a tour put on by the custodians of several of the village's buildings - the Autism Together charity - as part of Heritage Open Days.
A vivid childhood memory for Ruth and I is spending time in their beautiful cottage gardens.
I loved making "perfume" from rose petals and water, while Ruth enjoyed tasting freshly picked peas from the pod grown by our grandad.
We also enjoyed walking around the village and watching cricketers on the green, along with trips past the allotments to a long gone playground located behind the school.

title: Outback town marks 60th anniversary of plane crash that claimed 24 lives
content:
Winton remembers deadly Ansett-ANA Flight 149 crash 60 years on
In short:
Ansett-ANA Flight 149 crashed near the outback Queensland town of Winton on September 22nd 1966, killing all 24 people aboard.
The crash triggered one of the largest aviation investigations in Australia's history.
As the Winton community and loved ones of those who died pay their respects, the daughter of one of the pilots continues to work on an oral history project to document the crash and its fallout.
Sixty years ago, what was meant to be a short flight between two Western Queensland towns ended in one of Australia's deadliest aviation crashes.
Conditions were favourable when Ansett-ANA Flight 149 took off from Mount Isa, bound for Brisbane via Longreach, on September 22, 1966.
But 30 minutes into the flight an engine was on fire and the aircraft was put into an emergency descent before breaking apart in the air and crashing onto a cattle property 19 kilometres west of Winton.
All 24 people on board died.
As the small outback community nearly 200 kilometres north-west of Longreach gathered to mark the 60th anniversary, they remembered the lives that were lost and the impact the tragedy had on the aviation industry.
Community mourns
Winton Mayor Cathy White said the crash greatly affected the community.
"Sixty years on, there are people here that remember it like it happened yesterday," she said.
"I think we should always come and remember [together]."
At the ceremony on Tuesday locals and the families of those who died paid their respects.
Elizabeth Gillam, the daughter of co-pilot John Gillam, was 18 months old when her father died.
"It was a defining feature of my life," she said.
"When the crash happened, my mum went from being a stay-at-home mum to being the breadwinner, so everything changed."
Dr Gillam said it was important to hear the stories of other people affected.
"All of these families, all of these people in the Winton community were brought together by this one singular event," she said.
"So many lives were changed."
Anne O'Leary's father, Ken Cooper, piloted the plane.
She said his loss significantly changed the dynamic of her family's life. Her mum had no choice but to go to work and the family home was sold to make ends meet.
Ms O'Leary said her two younger brothers followed in their dad's footsteps and became pilots themselves.
"I became a teacher. My older brother and I do not like to fly, but we do manage that," she said.
Ms O'Leary attended the 25th anniversary, which she said was "cathartic and gave them closure".
"After 60 years it's more about meeting other people, sharing stories and dedicating the memory to them," she said.
Extensive investigation
The tragedy led to one of the largest aviation crash investigation in Australian history.
State Library of New South Wales historian Peter Hobbins said the Air Safety Investigation Branch (the predecessor to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau) launched an investigation and the federal government ordered an independent inquiry.
"[It] ended up costing the Commonwealth an estimated $1.12 million, in 1967 terms," he said.
Dr Hobbins said the investigation and the following independent inquiry concluded that a small "blower" motor that helped deliver air into the cabin had worn out and caught fire, also igniting one of the engines.
That caused parts of the plane to melt before the wing broke off, tearing the roof open on descent.
Dr Hobbins said the crash attracted the attention it did because there had been two other similar crashes in Australia that decade.
"I think to have an accident as severe as the one at Winton pushed hard against that sense of comfort that Australians were starting to assume about airline travel," he said.
Dr Hobbins said the inquiry drove home the need for better monitoring and servicing intervals, and that the investigation reinforced Australia's dedication to becoming a world leader in aviation safety.
"For the last nearly 60 years, it actually has been incredibly safe," he said.
"I think a lot of the roots of that [safety] culture were set in the 1950s and the 1960s."
Documenting oral history
Dr Gillam believes there are lessons to be learned from the crash and has spent the last decade working to document them.
After the 50th anniversary she started an oral history project to collect testimonies from anyone who remembered the days and weeks following the tragedy.
As part of that research Dr Gillam spoke with investigator Don Wally.
"He was able to explain in great detail what had happened," she said.
Dr Gillam's project is ongoing and she is keen to speak with other people who have been affected, not just to capture what happened on that day in 1966, but to learn more about the wider ramifications, including how the families were compensated in the aftermath.
"All of these are important to capture, for history, to work out how we can do things better."

title: ‘It’ll never be the same’: Regina family seeks justice for Rebecca Wilson
content:
Friends, family and loved ones of 37-year-old Rebecca Wilson gathered outside Regina’s Legislative Building Friday evening to remember and honour her life.
Wilson, referred to as ‘Becca’ or ‘Becky’ by those who knew her, was described by family as a devoted older sister, a woman of faith and someone of strong character. Her sister, Katie Wilson, said Rebecca was a creative person who spent a lot of time painting and writing.
“As her sister, there’s a huge gap now and I’ll never be able to fill it the same way,” said Katie Wilson. “It’ll never be the same.”
The family took turns speaking about Rebecca Wilson, describing her as funny, loyal and a huge loss for the family. Wilson said the circumstances around the death make the loss that much more difficult.
Get daily National news
“She didn’t just die. She didn’t just pass away from some sickness or anything or some freak accident. She was murdered,” said Wilson.
Police are investigating.
Rebecca Wilson’s mother, Wendy Lerat Lynn said Wilson, who was the oldest of five, always embodied the trait of advocating for others.
“She took on being the big sister,” she said. “She did that on the playground too with other kids. She kind of was like that.”
Lerat said her daughter’s laugh was contagious and wanted people to remember Wilson as faithful, funny and an amazing human being.
“The way she ended, it didn’t do her any justice at all,” said Lerat.
Signs at the vigil called for justice for missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls. Lerat said what happened to her daughter is not an isolated incident.
“I understand there’s different degrees and understanding of murdered and missing Indigenous women,” said Lerat. “The more that people start to talk about it maybe it’ll become something that people will actually see.”
Rebecca Wilson was the victim of an aggravated assault on Aug. 14. She was found in an alley in the 1400 block of Wascana Street and died from her injuries on Aug. 30.
“There needs to be something more that is addressing why these women are being murdered,” said Lerat.
No arrests have been made in Wilson’s death.
“Our family will not stop, I will not stop. It is my mission to find truth for my sister, we will know the truth. The truth will come to light, it’s just a matter of when,” said Wilson.

title: Low-cost phone lessons keep children learning during emergency school closures across five countries
content:
The COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns forced people to find ways to get things done remotely. Companies developed systems that made working from home run smoothly. Educators also had to shift to mobile phones and group video calls to get their lessons across and make sure students didn't lose out on their progress. This exposed the need for education systems to be more resilient and adaptive to local and global disruptions.
A recent Nature study explored how low-tech mobile phone programs could keep children learning when schools close because of major emergencies such as disease outbreaks, extreme weather or natural disasters.
Across India, Kenya, Nepal, the Philippines and Uganda, researchers conducted large-scale randomized trials to test remote-learning methods delivered through simple mobile phones.
Adding a weekly, one-on-one, 20-minute phone-call tutorial to text messages led to significant gains in basic math skills across all five countries. Students learned roughly three times more when they received phone calls tailored to their learning level.
The combined phone-call and SMS tutorial program cost just $11 per child. For every $100 spent, it generated 3.6 years of high-quality schooling, putting it among the top 10 most cost-effective education interventions ever evaluated, out of 150 studies worldwide.
Learning must go on
Nearly 25% of the world's population lives in countries where education is at risk of disruption because of political, medical or climate emergencies. A recent report estimated that around 222 million children face regular disruptions to their education, losing precious opportunities to learn and worsening the existing global learning crisis, in which fewer than half of primary-school-age children in low- and middle-income countries can read a simple story or do basic arithmetic.
When schools shut down, education systems need fast, low-cost and flexible ways to keep kids learning. However, rigorous evidence on what actually works during emergencies is rare.
Mobile phones have permeated into most nooks and crannies of the world where humans reside, leading researchers to explore them as a tool for reaching primary school children during emergencies. Wherever there are mobile phones, people can connect via text messages and phone calls, which might feel less efficient than the internet, but more than 70% of households in low-income countries have the former and only 15% have the latter.
Hello, it's math
To find out whether a single mobile-phone-based emergency education strategy could work in different parts of the world, researchers needed a coordinated, multicountry trial. Between December 2020 and July 2022, more than 16,000 households with primary school students from the five countries participated in the remote-learning experiment. Researchers randomly assigned students to different groups to compare levels of remote support.
Students in the control group received no remote tutoring during the trial period. Families in the SMS-only group received weekly text messages containing basic math problems and practice reminders. This group was not tested in India. Students in the phone call and SMS group received the weekly text messages plus a 20-minute, one-on-one phone tutoring session each week for 8–12 weeks.
The phone calls were built around targeted teaching. Each week, instructors used a short assessment during the call to determine what the child could do, then designed the math lesson around those specific needs instead of simply following the grade-level curriculum. At the end of the trial, researchers tested progress using the standard Annual Status of Education Report tool.
Economic yet effective
They found that weekly live tutoring calls paired with text messages delivered large learning gains in basic math across all five countries. On average, students in the phone tutoring program gained 0.321 standard deviations in learning, meaning their gains were three times larger than those of the median education intervention evaluated globally.
The combined phone-call and SMS program led to a 92% jump in the number of students who could correctly solve division problems. Students also improved on more advanced skills, including fractions, where performance increased by 6.4 percentage points.
Uganda and the Philippines saw the biggest improvements, where long school closures left children with few opportunities to continue learning. In Uganda, phone tutoring helped fourth graders make up all the learning they had lost during the pandemic and even outperform fifth graders who did not receive the program.
The researchers found that the approach worked just as well when delivered by government teachers as by nongovernmental organizations, giving them confidence that it can be scaled through public education systems.
The results show that by deploying a low-cost mobile-based intervention strategy, education systems can maintain learning amid disruptions across diverse settings. The approach is now moving into classrooms across Karnataka, India, supporting learning during the school year and keeping children connected when monsoon closures shut schools.

title: 'A good model going forward': New Zealand opens first Maori co-managed marine reserves
content:
Five no-take marine reserves took effect in Aotearoa New Zealand after more than 10 years of work, marking a significant step in ocean protection and establishing a shared management arrangement between Indigenous leadership and the Department of Conservation.
The July 1, 2026 rollout differs markedly from a previous attempt to create a sanctuary through central government action alone, an effort that later collapsed in disputes over Māori rights.
Here's what to know
Kelp forests, rocky reefs, tidal lagoons, offshore canyons, and other seabed habitats are among the environments the reserves are meant to protect within Te Au Roa o Te Rakihouia, a planned marine protection network.
As Mongabay reported, these are the first marine reserves in the country with formal joint management by Indigenous people and the government, including shared decision-making and a co-run ranger team.
This outcome comes after the failure of New Zealand's 2015 Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary proposal, a plan for a vast marine protected area in northern waters that opponents said moved ahead without proper Māori consultation and conflicted with fishing rights recognized in earlier agreements.
"This is the only example of its type in the country and … could well be quite a good model going forward," Edward Ellison, a Kāi Tahu leader who is one of the network's six governors, told Mongabay.
Together, the five reserves span 119 square miles, or about 0.01% of New Zealand's waters. According to the Department of Conservation, their addition brings the share of the country's waters that are highly protected to 0.46%, and 20.38% have "some form of protection."
More background
Planning began in 2014 with a forum that included representatives from conservation, tourism, science, and commercial and recreational fishing, along with Kāi Tahu participants.
Ellison said some of the early meetings were held in marae, Māori gathering places, to help others better understand how Kāi Tahu work collectively. "That set a really great base and people felt comfortable and understood," he told Mongabay.
Healthy marine ecosystems can help support fisheries, cultural practices, research, education, and jobs tied to restoration and stewardship. The reserves are too small to dramatically change New Zealand's global protection figures, but the model could still inform future conservation efforts.
What's being done?
These five reserves represent just the opening stage of the wider network. Beyond these first sites, the network is intended to include six marine reserves, five mixed-use Type 2 marine protected areas, and one kelp protection area. One reserve, Te Umukōau, is still pending after a legal challenge from the Otago Rock Lobster Industry Association led to a boundary review in December 2025.
According to Mongabay, the Department of Conservation earmarked about 7 million New Zealand dollars (about $4 million) for the network from 2023 to 2027. That funding is helping support six full-time marine rangers employed through the Kāi Tahu tribal council and working alongside the department.
Brendan Flack, a customary fisheries guardian for the Kāi Tahu hapū Kāti Huirapa, leads that ranger team. Their work includes ecological monitoring, restoration, education, surveillance, and seaweed research — including efforts that could create local income streams.
"The purpose is also to retain memory, location, kōrero associated with these places, and build on that going forward for future generations," Ellison said in an official launch video. "It's a model that helps broker the way forward," Ellison told Mongabay.
Where can I learn more?
Other island communities are expanding marine protection while tying conservation to local stewardship. These stories from Dominica, Hawaiʻi, and Zanzibar show how reserve design, Indigenous leadership, and tourism limits can shape ocean protection beyond New Zealand.
• Dominica has created the world's first sperm whale reserve to protect habitat and store carbon.
• On Oʻahu, Native Hawaiian communities are restoring traditional fishponds to rebuild food security and stewardship.
• Off Zanzibar, residents and conservation groups limited the number of reef visitors to 80.
Marine protection often works best when ecological goals are matched with community authority. That makes them useful parallels as Aotearoa tests a co-managed model with implications beyond these first reserves.
