title: Group to showcase Domboshava heritage at Bira reMbira
content:
Herald Reporter
DOMBOSHAVA’S Mbira Dzepadombo Ensemble will be among featured groups at this year’s Bira reMbira National Festival, bringing the area’s rich mbira traditions to the national cultural showcase at the Glamis Arena on Friday.
The third edition of Bira reMbira, which starts at 10am on September 25 and runs through to the morning of September 26, will bring together leading “gwenyambiras” master mbira players in a celebration of traditional acoustic music, spiritual heritage and the country’s mbira value chain.
The festival is being held under the theme “Roots to Markets – Empowering Makers, Players and Markets”, according to the Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture’s official festival brief.
The festival is being held with support from the Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture and the Ministry of Tourism and Hospitality Industry.
For Mbira Dzepadombo, the festival provides an important national platform to showcase the cultural traditions of Domboshava while highlighting ongoing efforts to preserve and pass on mbira knowledge to younger generations.
The ensemble was initiated by Dr Pearson Pfavayi, a tourism and cultural heritage advocate who recognised the deep cultural and spiritual connection between mbira music and the Domboshava community.
The group has been selected as one of the featured ensembles at Bira reMbira 2026 in recognition of its artistry, cultural preservation work and performance standards.
It will be led by master “gwenyambira,” Sekuru Thomas Chiombera, alongside Percy Dandiro, David Matiza and Nokutenda Kadzima.
Dr Pfavayi said the group’s participation was part of a broader effort to ensure that mbira remains a living cultural tradition rather than merely a historical artefact.
“Mbira is a sacred art form and a foundational pillar of our Zimbabwean cultural heritage that we must actively honour, preserve and identify with. Through Mbira Dzepadombo, we seek to safeguard these ancient rhythms while creating opportunities for people to learn, experience and appreciate their cultural significance,” he said.
The group’s activities are closely linked to Basecamp Domboshava, which serves as the home of Mbira Dzepadombo.
Situated at the foot of the historic Domboshava Caves and granite mountain, Basecamp Domboshava brings together cultural heritage preservation, community arts and adventure tourism.
A Mbira Training Centre is set to commence training on October 10, offering structured lessons to local youths, national students and international visitors in traditional mbira tuning, crafting and playing techniques.
The training centre forms part of the broader cultural activities being developed at Basecamp Domboshava, which also operates alongside Domboview Adventures, providing a base for guided cave hikes, team-building activities, art gallery sales and traditional food experiences.
Dr Pfavayi said the forthcoming training programme would help strengthen the inter-generational transmission of mbira knowledge.
“By establishing Mbira Dzepadombo and our dedicated Mbira Training Centre at Basecamp Domboshava, our mission is to preserve traditional knowledge and skills while opening the mbira experience to young Zimbabweans, visitors and international audiences,” he said.
The 2026 Bira reMbira festival will feature a wide range of artistes and mbira groups, including Victor Kunonga, Feli Nandi, Andy Muridzo, Duramazwi, Nyamasvisva Nemaungira Enharira, Amadhuve, Sasha, Kurai Makore, Mangwenya, Diana Samkange, Vee Mhofu, Texas Tekenya, Jah Lemmy, Gushungo, Jaka Band, Lioness Shumbakadzi, Ntswai Ntswai Arts, Brity Yonly, NzombeHuru Mbira Ensemble, Pauline Mafriq, Tatu Maluba, Dzambira, Mbira Dzenharo, Ambuya Mavhu Mbira Group, Chikwata 263, Batroy Movement, Nemachinda Ehondo Crew, Nina X and Zariyah Roots Band, Professor Muzvinafundo, Sekuru Gore and Mazana Movement, Ruyamuro Mbira Crew, Rose Wembira, Madzimambo Edu Mbira Family, Culture Livingstone, Dzimbanwe Mbira Crew, Pastoral Entertainment Group, Masimba Evanhu Mbira Group, Madzinza Embira, Dzamawuruka Mbira Band, Sekuru Mushore Mbira Custodians, Chishawasha Nhare Mbira Group, Izwi Remhondoro Mbira Group, Mbira Dzepadombo, Jangu Wiriranai Arts and Mbira Group and Nelson Tswatswa.
The extensive line-up reflects the organisers’ intention to bring together established musicians, emerging performers and traditional mbira ensembles under one platform.
Festival organiser Benjamin “Benjie” Nyandoro said Bira reMbira was designed to create a meeting point for musicians, cultural practitioners, audiences and the wider creative economy.
“Bira reMbira is more than a music event. It is a platform for Zimbabweans to celebrate their heritage while creating opportunities for musicians, instrument makers, cultural practitioners and young creatives. Our intention is to connect the roots of mbira with markets so that those who preserve and promote this heritage can also find sustainable opportunities within the creative economy,” he said.
The festival will provide a free-to-the-public cultural experience and will feature established and emerging mbira musicians, school ensembles and young creative collectives.
There will also be exhibitions showcasing mbira instruments, national fabric, herbs and medicinal plants, indigenous foods and other expressions of Zimbabwe’s diverse cultural heritage.
A major feature of this year’s festival will be a special tribute honouring the late Mbuya Stella Chiweshe, one of Zimbabwe’s foremost mbira practitioners and cultural ambassadors.
The Ministry’s official brief states that the festival will honour her through dedicated performances of her songs in a commemorative segment highlighting her influence on contemporary mbira practice.
Her artistic journey, leadership and longstanding commitment to the mbira tradition inspired generations of musicians, cultural practitioners and mbira custodians.
The tribute will form part of a broader celebration of Zimbabwe’s living heritage, with performers using the festival to demonstrate how the mbira continues to evolve while remaining rooted in traditional practice.
For Mbira Dzepadombo, the Bira reMbira appearance will be followed by another community-focused engagement when the ensemble is scheduled to perform at the Pinktober Breast Cancer Awareness Event on October 31.
The performance will form part of activities supporting cancer survivors and breast cancer awareness.
The continued involvement of Mbira Dzepadombo in cultural, tourism and community initiatives reflects the group’s broader objective of using mbira as a vehicle for cultural education, heritage preservation and community engagement.
The Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture has said Bira reMbira complements the Government’s broader cultural development agenda by creating platforms for heritage preservation, youth participation, creative enterprise, skills development, market access and cultural diplomacy.
As Glamis Arena prepares to host the overnight cultural gathering, Mbira Dzepadombo will carry with it the sounds and traditions of Domboshava, giving audiences an opportunity to experience a living heritage that continues to evolve while remaining rooted in Zimbabwean cultural identity.

title: El maestro que hizo de Iberoamérica y Europa una casa común
content:
El maestro que hizo de Iberoamérica y Europa una casa común
Tras ocho años al frente de la Organización de Estados Iberoamericanos (OEI), el educador español Mariano Jabonero deja este diciembre una institución convertida en una red de cooperación “muy americana”, con 23 países integrantes, más de 600 proyectos anuales, millones de beneficiarios y reconocida con el Premio Princesa de Asturias. Su última batalla es también una idea política: América Latina no es la periferia de Occidente, sino una de sus partes esenciales
En El Salvador, país que por entonces lloraba las 80.000 almas que se había tragado su guerra civil, se le acercó un día un campesino:
—Gracias por enseñarme a usar el ordenador.
Mariano Jabonero (San Martín de Valdeiglesias, Madrid, 1953), que llevaba desde 1984 asistiendo al Gobierno en tareas de cooperación con Latinoamérica, había recibido el encargo de capitanear un proyecto de cooperación con apoyo español en el plan de paz y reconstrucción institucional allí. Extrañado, miró al hombre que tenía a su frente y le respondió:
—Disculpe, pero no hemos entregado ordenadores.
—Este es mi portátil —indicó el campesino, sacando del bolsillo un bolígrafo— Ahora sé escribir y contar. Ya no volverán a engañarme.
La anécdota es de 1992, pero la moraleja sigue igual de vigente: “En los países con alta alfabetización, los ingresos per cápita se duplican. Es el primer paso para una sociedad libre”, explica Jabonero, sentado en la sala de reuniones de la sede de la Organización de Estados Iberoamericanos (OEI) de Madrid, ahora que se despide, tras ocho años, de su cargo de secretario general. Lo que sigue es el balance de lo logrado en ese período por parte de quien, antes que ninguna otra cosa, se reclama “maestro”. Resuena con gravedad el sustantivo cuando lo pronuncia, acarrea su voz el orgullo del verdadero sentimiento de pertenencia. Porque en cuarenta años no ha cambiado su convencimiento de que es en el aula, entre pupitres y pizarras, donde se construye ciudadanía; de que el diálogo y la democracia se aprenden.
Un repaso a la labor de ocho años
Acción siempre sobre el terreno
La Organización de Estados Iberoamericanos (OEI) es la mayor red multilateral de cooperación en la región, con 23 Estados miembro. En la imagen, una actividad de la Noche Iberoamericana de l@s Investigador@s, celebrada en Montevideo (Uruguay) en 2023
Fotos: Cedidas por OEI
Trabajando por el futuro
Uno de sus principales ámbitos de actuación es la educación, entendida también como la formación que dará futuro y empleo a los beneficiarios de estos programas. En la imagen, una alumna de la Escuela Taller de Asunción (Paraguay), impulsada por la OEI en colaboración con la Agencia Española de Cooperación Internacional para el Desarrollo (AECID)
Más científicas iberoamericanas
La igualdad de oportunidades y la inclusión de la mujer en el ámbito de la investigación y la ciencia es uno de los grandes retos regionales en Iberoamérica, y como tal tratan de afrontarlo los proyectos de la OEI. En la fotografía, un instante del programa Mujeres en ciencia celebrada en 2023 en Montevideo (Uruguay)
Energía limpia (y justa)
La sostenibilidad y la suficiencia energética son un desafío de presente y futuro, como señala Jabonero. Con financiación europea, la OEI desarrolló el proyecto Energytran para impulsar una transición justa y limpia entre Europa y América Latina. La imagen corresponde a una instalación de placas fotovoltaicas en Ciudad de México, en 2024
COP30 (Brasil)
Uno de los grandes hitos recientes fue la organización por parte de la OEI, en colaboración con el Gobierno de Brasil, de la COP30, la cumbre anual de Naciones Unidas sobre el cambio climático, celebrada en noviembre de 2025 en Belém (Brasil), en la que se adoptaron 56 decisiones consensuadas, incluida una hoja de ruta para el abandono del uso de los combustibles fósiles. Reunió a más de 300.000 asistentes: el mayor proyecto organizado en la Amazonia
Alfabetización, la base
Los tres ejes principales de actuación de los proyectos de la OEI son la educación, la ciencia y la cultura. Pero, para todos, el primer paso fue el lograr que Iberoamérica sea una región con un 98% de alfabetización. En Honduras (en la imagen), la OEI contribuyó a la declaración del país como “Territorio libre de analfabetismo” en 2025
Un balance inmaculado
Durante los último ocho años, el periodo durante el que el pedagogo Mariano Jabonero ha estado al frente de la secretaría general de la OEI, la institución ha puesto en marcha 2.500 proyectos en los 23 países integrantes, que han impactado en la vida de un total de 22 millones de personas. “Nuestro equipo está formado por excelentes profesionales, actuamos con transparencia y autonomía. Tenemos un enorme arraigo y, sobre todo, logramos que la cooperación suceda, lo que hace que todos los países y beneficiarios confíen en nosotros”, explica Jabonero
Este diciembre deja Jabonero una OEI que, alejada del papel asistencial y burocrático que pudo tener en sus comienzos (se creó en 1949), se ha convertido en un bien público regional de utilidad indiscutida, que, bajo su gestión, ha impulsado más de 600 proyectos anuales en educación, ciencia, cultura y educación en derechos humanos y democracia para más de 22 millones de beneficiarios, una organización de gestión transparente (“podemos rastrear en directo adónde ha ido el dinero de una factura pagada en Honduras”) que trabaja sobre el terreno en los 23 países que la integran; una OEI, remarca Jabonero, “muy americana, pero sin injerencia ni un solo dólar de EE UU”. “Al principio la financiación procedía sobre todo de España. Ahora el porcentaje de aporte español es mínimo. Hemos logrado que se entienda como un invento de la región y para la región”.
Un profesor filósofo forjado en la Transición
Jabonero nació en un pueblo del suroeste de Madrid y su juventud es la de quien, frente a los estertores represivos y violentos de la dictadura de Franco, anhelaba “la llegada de un régimen de libertades y tolerancia”. Fue su conciencia social la que, en un tiempo tan efervescente, lo condujo hacia los estudios de Filosofía y Ciencias de la Educación.
“Recuerdo la publicación del primer número de EL PAÍS, en mayo de 1976. Lo compré en un quiosco en Campamento [barrio del distrito La Latina de Madrid donde se asentaban cuarteles de militares y guardias civiles]. Mi primer destino como maestro fue allí cerca, en un colegio público de Aluche”. Para entonces, Jabonero ya había viajado a Francia, y a su regreso la mitad de la carga clandestina de su mochila eran libros aquí prohibidos: “La poesía española censurada o a pensadores como Paulo Freire los leí en panfletos ciclostilados”.
Repite una cita célebre, atribuida a uno de los padres de esta Europa nuestra, Jean Monnet: “Si tuviera que volver a empezar [a construir la Unión Europea, se refiere], empezaría por la cultura”. Pedagogía, educación y sociología son para Jabonero caras del mismo cubo. A finales de los años 70, obtuvo, frente a 850 candidatos, una de las 18 plazas a inspector de Educación, momento en que descubrió lo que realmente entrañaba el derecho a la educación, la enorme responsabilidad sobre sus hombros: “el sistema, las políticas públicas, tienen que lograr que el alumnado pueda sentarse en el aula y aprender lengua o matemáticas en condiciones óptimas; y eso incluye desde la rehabilitación de escuelas rurales que no tenían ni baños ni agua corriente en aquel tiempo hasta la garantía de que esos niños y niñas hubieran podido desayunar en casa antes de venir al colegio”.
No podemos perder de vista el valor de la Educación como elemento corrector de las desigualdades de cuna, esa fe democrática que hoy Jabonero observa a su alrededor “tristemente cansada, agotada”, expresa, tomando las palabras del filósofo germano-coreano Byung-Chul Han. Los siguientes pasos, como en un destino inexorable, fueron los que modelaron al pedagogo indispensable que Jabonero es hoy: pasó por el Ministerio de Educación, llegaron El Salvador, Argentina, Colombia y la cooperación —la literatura del bum fue su llave hacia eso que a Martín Caparrós le gusta llamar Ñamérica—, dio clase en la Complutense, trabajó para Unesco, dirigió la Fundación Santillana, ejerció de consultor para gobiernos de todo el continente… hasta que en 2018 y por unanimidad fue elegido, durante dos mandatos, secretario general de la OEI.
Sentirse en casa: por qué Iberoamérica es Occidente
Cola de un cine. En París o en Berlín. Si, entre el tumulto de voces, Jabonero oye la suave cadencia del colombiano o el marcado deje del español caribeño dice que no puede evitar girarse y trabar conversación. “He vivido en muchos países de Iberoamérica y siempre me he sentido en casa”. Le apena la concepción errada que todavía, dice, se tiene en España de los vecinos del otro lado del Atlántico: “Respecto de la tierra de dictaduras, guerras y pobreza que pervive en cierto imaginario, el cambio ha sido brutal: 98% de alfabetización, es la zona donde más ha crecido la matriculación en estudios superiores, 33 millones de estudiantes, en el 70% de los casos de familias donde los progenitores no pasaron por la universidad”.
Todavía pesan la inequidad o sus economías, demasiado dependientes de la venta de materias primas: “El litio boliviano está en manos de empresas chinas; el cobre se produce en Chile y Perú, pero se cotiza en Estados Unidos; las flores ecuatorianas se venden en Ámsterdam”. Pero están, cuenta, “a un salto de constituirse en verdaderas sociedades de conocimiento, como lo son las más competitivas”.
Entre los hablantes de español y portugués —esta última, la lengua cuyo uso más crece en África— sumamos 850 millones de personas en el mundo. Se trata de un potencial incontestable, que motiva el alegato que quiere lanzar “sin caer en demasiada retórica”: por lengua, por historia, por derecho, por cultura, por religión “América Latina no es la periferia de Occidente, sino una parte más de su núcleo”.
Reputación y futuro
¿Qué méritos motivan un galardón como el Princesa de Asturias de Cooperación Internacional de 2024 o el premio Anna Frank del pasado marzo? ¿Cómo navega la OEI para que gobiernos de todos los colores la valoren por igual en sus 77 años de acción? “Hemos sabido estar a la altura de las circunstancias”, responde Jabonero. Y enumera algunos ejemplos de por qué sus proyectos de cooperación han generado un inmensurable impacto en la zona: fue, por ejemplo, un costarricense becado por la OEI para doctorarse en la Universidad de Sevilla quien redactó la Ley de Cuidados de su país.
Durante la pandemia, unos 180 millones de estudiantes latinoamericanos quedaron excluidos de las aulas y aproximadamente la mitad no tenía una conexión a internet suficiente. La OEI produjo entonces cientos de contenidos digitales, ayudó a los sistemas educativos nacionales a mantener la actividad y concedió miles de becas para formar a profesores universitarios que hasta entonces trabajaban casi exclusivamente con cuaderno y tiza. En una de las escenas más insólitas de aquel periodo, programas educativos de televisión mexicanos llegaron a emitirse en Guinea Ecuatorial.
Si la democracia se tambalea, hará falta más democracia y más consenso. Eso defiende a capa y espada Jabonero para un futuro en el que identifica varios desafíos que no admiten complacencia: la transición digital —una tecnología al servicio de todos—, la transición verde —nuevas y sostenibles fuentes de energía que no subyuguen a los habitantes del Sur Global— y, sobre todo, una transición justa, sin perdedores, imposible si no se recupera esa vieja e inquebrantable fe en la Educación. Cómo no va a creer en su poder este maestro que vio cómo un campesino podía cambiar su mundo con un boli.

title: In Queens, Immigrant Women Sew a Truer Atlas
content:
In Queens, Immigrant Women Sew a Truer Atlas
The largely undocumented Latin American women of New York’s “costureros,” or needlework circles, are creating a countermap to archive the stories of their lives.
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.
How can we delve into the archives of the present? Is it possible to unveil and touch the documents that communities are creating today to record and remember their history, or does understanding only arise with the passage of time? When does an object become an archive?
For the past two years, I have been working with two immigrant-led costureros: circles of women from all over Latin America that gather to create textiles together. Located in different community centers in Northwestern Queens in New York City, these spaces have become a safe haven for many undocumented, working-class immigrants who are enduring racial profiling and persecution under the current immigration crackdown. Amid this terror, the intimacy and secrecy of the costurero set a table where gossip and generosity sit side by side with threads and needles.
The first group, BordeAndo, was founded in 2018 as a community engagement initiative of the Queens Museum, though it soon grew beyond the institution to become an independent collective. Its name plays with multiple meanings in Spanish: bordar (to embroider), borde (border or frontier), and the suffix -ando, which evokes movement or walking. Most of its members come from the Ecuadorian highlands (la Sierra), though others are from the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, and Mexico. They range in age from 30 to 83 and have lived in the United States for between 10 and 50 years.
Las Comadres Bordadoras was founded in 2021 in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic by two Mexican immigrants, who sought to bring women out of isolation and foster a mutual support network. Their name, also difficult to translate, gestures toward camaraderie and kinship. The comadre refers specifically to women who are, in their words, “a midpoint between friend and family.” The comadres come from Mexico, Cuba, El Salvador, Uruguay, Colombia, Ecuador, and Argentina; range in age from 35 to 75; and have lived in the United States for between two and 30 years. They mostly embroider Mexican cloth napkins, but all forms of needlework are welcome. This costurero calls itself “nomadic” because it has moved around community gardens, public libraries, and schools in the area since its conception. Both circles are intergenerational, international spaces of confluence for transnational, working-class, largely undocumented immigrant women.
Last year, BordeAndo and Las Comadres Bordadoras were the protagonists of Thread of Voice / Un hilo de voz at the Queens Museum. The exhibition, which I curated, featured Andrés Altamirano’s photographs of the costurero members along with film by documentarian Eleonora Privitera. The visual narrative and documentation of this project was also done in collaboration with Altamirano.
I see these costureros as living archives — as sites where craft traditions converge, and concrete embodied and material practices connect geographies of affect and displacement, like a woman knitting a stitch learned by her grandmother back home or another embroidering a napkin for the altar of a dead loved one whose grave she cannot visit because of her migratory status. “Text” and “textile” share an etymological root — the Latin verb texere — that reveals both that texts are woven and textiles written. In this sense, textiles are texts that we have forgotten how to read, encoded with bodily gestures, storytelling practices, and materialities that could, if safeguarded, be called archives.

title: Terreiro Carijós, no Recife, recebe encontro entre Patrimônios Vivos da cultura pernambucana
content:
A memória e os modos de fazer da cultura popular pernambucana estarão no centro de uma programação gratuita realizada nesta quarta-feira (16), na Zona Norte do Recife. A partir das 16h, o Terreiro da Tribo Indígena Carijós do Recife, na Mangabeira, recebe uma roda de conversa com mestres, mestras e representantes de grupos tradicionais. Às 19h, as atividades continuam na Bomba do Hemetério, na Rua Guanabi, nº 382, com oficinas, exposição de objetos e elementos tradicionais e apresentações de manifestações da cultura popular.
Com uma programação que combina conversa, formação e apresentações artísticas, o projeto “Carijós acolhe os Patrimônios Vivos de Pernambuco em seu Terreiro” propõe um encontro entre diferentes expressões que integram o patrimônio cultural do estado. Entre os participantes estão o Coco de Umbigada, a Ciranda Dengosa, o Urso Cangaçá de Água Fria, o Maracatu Nação Raízes de Pai Adão e a própria Tribo Carijós do Recife.
A primeira atividade será dedicada à troca de experiências. Na roda “Partilha de Saberes”, com mediação de Jacira França, Superintendente de Patrimônio Imaterial da Fundarpe, representantes das manifestações convidadas compartilham trajetórias, lembranças e conhecimentos relacionados às práticas culturais que preservam.
Participam da conversa a Cacica da Tribo Carijós, Mãe Beth de Oxum, do Coco de Umbigada, a Mestra Cristina Andrade, da Ciranda Dengosa e do Urso Cangaçá de Água Fria, e representantes do Maracatu Nação Raízes de Pai Adão.
A escolha do Terreiro Carijós como ponto de partida também coloca em evidência a trajetória da própria tribo, reconhecida como o grupo de caboclinho mais antigo de Pernambuco. A partir desse espaço, o projeto amplia a programação para outras manifestações e cria um momento de convivência entre diferentes formas de expressão da tradição popular.
Na segunda parte do encontro, o público poderá participar de oficinas conduzidas pelos mestres e mestras envolvidos na iniciativa. A proposta é ir além da apresentação dos grupos e possibilitar um contato mais próximo com técnicas, objetos, linguagens e conhecimentos associados a essas manifestações.
A programação inclui ainda uma mostra de artesanato, figurinos e adereços tradicionais. O conjunto de atividades será complementado por apresentações do caboclinho Carijós do Recife, do Coco de Umbigada, da Ciranda Dengosa e do Maracatu Nação Raízes de Pai Adão.
Para o produtor geral e elaborador do projeto, professor Clébio Marques, reunir essas referências em uma mesma programação é uma forma de favorecer a circulação dos conhecimentos entre os próprios grupos e entre o público.
“Mais do que apresentar manifestações tradicionais, a iniciativa aposta no encontro como ferramenta de preservação. Ao juntar diferentes linguagens em diálogo, o projeto contribui para aproximar novas gerações desses conhecimentos e reforça a importância de manter vivos os modos de fazer”, defende.
Realizado com incentivo do Edital Multilinguagens 2025 da Política Nacional Aldir Blanc (PNAB), o projeto conta com apoio da Secretaria de Cultura de Pernambuco, do Ministério da Cultura e do Governo Federal.

title: $58m Aboriginal cultural centre opens at Darwin Waterfront
content:
Darwin's $58m Larrakia Cultural Centre opens to the public after 24-year wait
In short:
The Larrakia Cultural Centre on the Darwin Waterfront has opened its doors to the public, more than two decades since the idea was first developed.
The project cost $58 million and its design was inspired by a cultural centre in Whistler, Canada, and others around the world.
What's next?
Aboriginal Investment NT says it hopes the project will create more economic opportunities for Larrakia people.
A centre showcasing the culture, history and art of the traditional owners of the Darwin region, the Larrakia people, has opened to the public after 24 years of planning and development.
The $58 million Larrakia Cultural Centre, situated at Stokes Hill Wharf on the Darwin Waterfront, opened its doors for a sunrise tour this morning.
The idea for the centre was conceived in 2002, and negotiations between the Larrakia Development Corporation (LDC) and Northern Territory government on granting the waterfront location and developing the venue lasted from 2005 to 2022 before construction began two years ago.
LDC chair Mark Motlop said the new centre would "fill a void" in cultural education in Darwin.
"People rock up in Darwin, they want an Aboriginal experience and they want a Larrakia experience," he said.
"In the past we haven't had that, we've had dribs and drabs … this is a one-stop shop."
Centre takes worldwide inspiration
Mr Motlop said he had travelled the world looking at similar venues during the centre's planning phase, and that its design was influenced by cultural centres in Canada, Alaska and New Zealand.
"We had to get a model that was going to be sustainable and we didn't want this to be the golden goose that goes looking for funding later on," he said.
"It had to be a commercial model, and Whistler [in Canada] had that."
Alongside a museum space and art displays, the centre in Darwin includes meeting and office spaces, a retail shop, a cafe and a restaurant.
Aboriginal Investment NT chief executive Nigel Browne said he hoped the centre would not only provide cultural benefits to Larrakia people, but lasting economic gains as well.
"There's a cohort of full-time staff that are employed within the cultural centre … but there's a much bigger scope here,"he said.
"There'll be opportunities moving forward for Larrakia to engage in business and branch out from the centre itself.
"Over the years we've had a number of Larrakia people running their own tourism businesses … I'm sure that opportunities will come into the future to have those individuals linked with the cultural centre."
Cultural items and interactive displays
Mr Browne said the centre "takes the shape of the ancestral being", a bird in flight, which is "attached to the Larrakia sacred site" at the nearby Stokes Hill.
On display are 23 cultural items that have been repatriated to Larrakia land from interstate and overseas, as well as a replica of the Larrakia peoples' 1972 petition to Queen Elizabeth II for land rights and political representation.
There is also an interactive display where Larrakia people and visitors can learn about the history of the nine Larrakia family groups.
"A lot of people [in Darwin] will have come across or met or even fallen in love with Larrakia people over the years," Mr Browne said.
"Now's the opportunity to really come to one place where they can get a fuller appreciation of Larrakia history, of the story of Larrakia and what it's meant for Larrakia people ever since [George] Goyder sailed into our harbour in 1869."
The centre's cultural liaison officer, Donella Young, said she felt "so privileged" to see it finally come to fruition.
"It talks about culture, country, land rights and women and men that served in World War I and World War II and the Black Watch," she said.
"It also still talks about how the Larrakia community is still thriving to this day."

title: Brasil registra a menor taxa de analfabetismo da história: menos de 5%
content:
Brasil registra a menor taxa de analfabetismo da história: menos de 5%
O Brasil conseguiu derrubar a taxa de analfabetismo para menos de 5% pela primeira vez na série histórica da PNAD Contínua. A taxa caiu de 5,3% no ano anterior para 4,9% dos brasileiros em 2025. Isso em relação a jovens com 15 anos ou mais que não sabiam ler nem escrever. Isso significa quase 600 mil analfabetos a menos.
O resultado é o menor desde 2016, quando começou a série atual da Pesquisa Nacional por Amostra de Domicílios Contínua, do IBGE. Naquele primeiro levantamento, o índice era de 6,7%.
Nesta semana, o Ministério da Educação voltou a destacar o avanço e divulgou novos dados sobre a Educação de Jovens e Adultos, a EJA. Em 2025, mais de 2,25 milhões de estudantes estavam matriculados nessa modalidade em quase 30 mil escolas brasileiras. O número é ótimo, mas o desafio ainda é grande.
Nordeste concentra maior número
A queda, porém, não ocorreu de maneira uniforme no país. O Nordeste ainda concentrava 4,8 milhões das pessoas analfabetas em 2025, mais da metade do total brasileiro. A taxa na região era de 10,6%. No Norte, o índice ficou em 5,7%. Depois aparecem Centro-Oeste, com 3,3%, Sul, com 2,4%, e Sudeste, com 2,3%.
A idade também pesa bastante no resultado. Dos 8,4 milhões de brasileiros que não sabiam ler nem escrever, 4,9 milhões tinham 60 anos ou mais. Isso representa 58% do total de pessoas analfabetas do país.
Entre os brasileiros com 60 anos ou mais, a taxa de analfabetismo chegou a 13,8%. Se forem consideradas apenas as pessoas de 15 a 59 anos, o índice nacional cai para 2,6%.

- Professor adotou três irmãos para mantê-los juntos e 3 anos depois, eles são os melhores alunos
Quem é considerado analfabeto?
Pelo critério utilizado pelo IBGE, é considerada analfabeta a pessoa que não consegue ler e escrever um bilhete simples.
A taxa nacional saiu de 6,7% em 2016 para 4,9% em 2025. O dado de 2025 é o mais recente disponível e foi divulgado originalmente pelo IBGE em junho. A pesquisa passou por reponderação com base nos resultados do Censo 2022.
O MEC atribui parte do avanço dos indicadores à ampliação das políticas de alfabetização e da EJA. O Pacto também reúne ações do Programa Brasil Alfabetizado, formação de professores e expansão da educação profissional para jovens e adultos.
Mais de 2 milhões voltaram a estudar
Um dos caminhos para reduzir esses números é a Educação de Jovens e Adultos. Dados divulgados pelo MEC nesta quinta-feira, 10, mostram que 2.252.069 estudantes estavam matriculados na EJA em 2025. Eles estavam distribuídos por 29.696 escolas públicas e privadas.
A rede pública concentra a grande maioria: 2.084.947 matrículas em 28.204 escolas.
O Nordeste também possui a maior rede de atendimento da modalidade. Foram 1,2 milhão de matrículas em 2025. O Sudeste registrou 493,6 mil; o Norte, 255 mil; o Sul, 192,9 mil; e o Centro-Oeste, 105,2 mil.
Como voltar a estudar
Para quem deixou a escola e quer retomar os estudos, o governo federal criou o CadEJA, plataforma que registra o interesse por uma vaga na Educação de Jovens e Adultos.
Pessoas a partir dos 15 anos podem procurar uma oportunidade para concluir o ensino fundamental. Para o ensino médio, a idade mínima é de 18 anos.
No CadEJA, o interessado seleciona a opção “Quero voltar a estudar”, preenche os dados solicitados e aguarda o contato de um operador, que orienta sobre as oportunidades de matrícula disponíveis na região.
O sistema foi instituído pela Portaria nº 275 de 2026 e faz parte das ações do Pacto Nacional pela Superação do Analfabetismo e Qualificação da Educação de Jovens e Adultos.

title: Translational Hepatology From Bedside to Global Policy: How Robust Clinical and Translational Research Reshapes Global Practice Guidelines and Patient Outcomes.
content: Over four decades, translational hepatology has evolved from empirical observations into an evidence-driven discipline. This review synthesizes key bedside discoveries, mechanistic studies, prospective cohorts, cross-regional health-economic evaluations, and landmark randomized controlled trials (RCTs) by our team that have helped to reshape regulatory drug approvals, Boxed Warnings, and international practice guidelines across APASL, AASLD, and EASL. First, clinical trials established the biphasic model and risk predictors of immunosuppression-induced hepatitis B virus (HBV) reactivation, proving that pre-emptive nucleos(t)ide analogue (NUC) prophylaxis prevents liver failure and antineoplastic disruptions. Second, multinational Phase III registration trials of finite 48-week pegylated interferon alfa-2a (Peg-IFN α-2a) in chronic hepatitis B (CHB)-combined with intrahepatic cccDNA kinetics, adoptive immunity transfer, and 30-year Asia-Pacific Markov health-economic modeling-established response-guided rules and validated finite Peg-IFN switch/add-on strategies as clinically dominant and cost-effective. Third, prospective cohorts uncovered direct-acting antiviral (DAA)-induced HBV reactivation during HCV clearance, establishing mandatory regulatory Boxed Warnings and pre-DAA screening. Fourth, the Phase III HIMALAYA study and pooled Greater China (Mainland China, Hong Kong, Taiwan) cohorts validated the STRIDE regimen (single-dose tremelimumab plus regular durvalumab) as frontline dual immunotherapy for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (uHCC), establishing marked survival benefit in HBV-predominant populations (median OS 25.26 vs. 14.09 months) alongside a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-free standard for cirrhotic portal hypertension within APASL guidelines. Finally, translational insights across metabolic dysfunction, COVID-19, ACLF, artificial intelligence (AI), and functional cure frameworks inform the APASL 2026 "treat-all" CHB paradigm.

title: New grant funds study of California’s traditional health care practices
content:
A landmark effort to bring Indigenous healing practices into the formal health care system is about to face its most rigorous scientific scrutiny yet. The University of California, Riverside has received a $1.25 million grant from the California Department of Health Care Services to conduct a statewide evaluation of California’s traditional health care practices benefit, a pioneering Medicaid initiative that allows Indigenous healing services provided through Indian health clinics to be reimbursed through Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program. The project marks a critical step in understanding how culturally grounded healing can be integrated into mainstream care for communities that have long faced disproportionate health burdens.
The evaluation will be led by Claradina Soto, who is Navajo and Jemez Pueblo, an associate professor of social medicine, population, and public health in the UCR School of Medicine. Soto joined UC Riverside earlier this year after a decade at the University of Southern California, where the project was first housed, and she brings with her a long record of community-engaged research on substance use prevention and Indigenous health. Under her leadership, the initiative will bring together tribal leaders, clinicians, health organizations, and state partners to collect and analyze data on the benefit, including how it is implemented, what barriers and facilitators shape its delivery, how services reach patients, and what participants themselves experience.
The stakes of the evaluation are rooted in a painful public health reality. California was prompted to create the traditional health care practices initiative by disproportionately high rates of opioid overdose and substance use deaths among Native American communities. Those disparities reflect generations of historical trauma, limited access to culturally appropriate care, and health systems that were often designed without input from Indigenous peoples. By embedding traditional healing into the state’s Medicaid infrastructure, California is attempting to address substance use not only with clinical tools but with practices that connect patients to community, culture, and identity.
The mechanics of the benefit are notable in the landscape of American health policy. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the federal agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services that administers the Medicare program, approved the California Department of Health Care Services to cover traditional health care practices for Medi-Cal members in Drug Medi-Cal Organized Delivery System counties. That approval came through an amendment to California’s Section 1115 waiver, a special federal agreement that allows states to test new, flexible ways of running their Medicaid programs, coordinating physical and behavioral health, and funding unique care initiatives. Through this waiver structure, services that would normally fall outside the scope of reimbursable medical care can be financed through the state’s Medicaid program.
California is one of only a few states approved to reimburse traditional healing services through Medicaid, which makes the initiative a nationally significant model for integrating Indigenous healing into health care. The services covered under the benefit are culturally grounded and diverse: ceremonies, one-on-one support from traditional healers, talking circles, prayer, and other healing approaches that complement clinical care, including treatment and recovery services for people with substance use disorders. Before the benefit was established, many Indian health clinics relied on grants or other temporary funding sources to offer these services, leaving them vulnerable to funding gaps and forcing healers and clinics to piece together support year after year. Medicaid reimbursement, by contrast, offers a durable, systemic financing mechanism that recognizes these practices as legitimate components of care.
Soto emphasized the historical weight of the moment. “This has been more than 10 years in the making, so it’s a major milestone,” she said. “California is one of only a few states where traditional healers can be reimbursed through Medicaid, creating an important opportunity to evaluate how these services are implemented and their impact on communities.” The decade-long path to the benefit reflects persistent advocacy by tribal communities and their allies, who argued that healing practices sustained for millennia deserved recognition within the systems that now serve Indigenous patients. The evaluation grant represents the next phase of that journey: turning policy achievement into evidence that can sustain and expand the work.
As principal investigator, Soto will oversee an evaluation design that combines multiple methods to capture the complexity of the benefit across the state. The project will include interviews with clinic providers and traditional healers, who can describe how the reimbursement system works in practice and where it creates friction; focus groups with community members, who can speak to the cultural fit and perceived value of the services; and surveys of patients receiving traditional healing services, which will generate quantitative data on experiences and outcomes. Guiding the entire effort will be an advisory board composed of tribal representatives, clinicians, and tribal and urban Indian organizations, ensuring that the research remains accountable to the communities it studies, a principle increasingly recognized as essential in Indigenous health research.
The significance of this work extends well beyond California’s borders. As one of the first systematic evaluations of a Medicaid-reimbursed traditional healing benefit, the project is positioned to inform national conversations about Indigenous health care and culturally grounded approaches to wellness. “The project represents a significant opportunity to contribute to national conversations about Indigenous health care and culturally grounded approaches to wellness,” Soto said. “By partnering with tribal communities, health care providers, and the DHCS, we hope to identify best practices that strengthen access to traditional healing and improve care for Native communities.” Other states watching California’s experiment will look to the evaluation’s findings as they consider whether similar benefits could work in their own Medicaid programs.
The evidence generated by the evaluation is expected to serve two audiences simultaneously. In California, it will help inform future policy decisions by the Department of Health Care Services, showing policymakers which implementation strategies succeed, which barriers must be addressed, and how the benefit might be refined or expanded. Nationally, it will provide a roadmap for other states interested in integrating Indigenous healing practices into their health care systems, offering concrete data on implementation processes, service delivery models, and participant experiences rather than leaving them to navigate uncharted territory. Soto noted that the evaluation will generate evidence on how the benefit is implemented across diverse communities and health care settings, a critical consideration in a state as large and varied as California, where tribal nations, rural clinics, and urban Indian health programs all operate under different conditions.
For the communities at the center of the initiative, the evaluation carries the promise of validation and sustainability. Traditional healing has always been central to Indigenous well-being, but its marginalization from formal health financing has limited access for many patients seeking recovery from substance use disorders. If the evaluation demonstrates that reimbursed traditional healing services improve engagement, recovery outcomes, and community health, it could cement the benefit as a permanent fixture of California’s Medicaid program and inspire a wave of adoption across the country. What began as a response to a devastating crisis of opioid overdose and substance use deaths may ultimately reshape how the American health care system understands healing itself, recognizing that for many patients, recovery begins not in a clinic exam room but in a ceremony, a talking circle, or a conversation with a healer who shares their culture and their history.

title: Destaca desprivatización de agua y restitución de tierras a indígenas
content:
Miércoles 2 de septiembre de 2026, p. 3
Con la reforma integral a la Ley de Aguas Nacionales, que revirtió el saqueo de este recurso en el país y modificó la visión del líquido como mercancía, se logró la desprivatización de poco más de “5 mil millones de metros cúbicos del recurso, suficiente para abastecer durante un año a más de 90 millones de personas”, afirmó la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum durante su segundo Informe de gobierno.
Por otro lado, tras señalar que, con la reforma constitucional para reconocer a los pueblos indígenas como sujetos de derecho público, se les han canalizado 25 mil millones de pesos a 19 mil comunidades, la mandataria resaltó que, con los gobiernos de la Cuarta Transformación, se les han restituido 13 mil hectáreas de tierra a los pueblos rarámuri, yaqui, seri, wixárika, ódami y otomí. Adelantó que está en proceso el retorno de 177 mil 632 hectáreas adicionales.
En el capítulo social de su informe, reivindicó la concepción del Estado en cuanto a su papel en la distribución de la riqueza: “no podemos esperar que los beneficios del crecimiento lleguen por sí solos a todas las familias. El Estado tiene una responsabilidad rectora: planear e impulsar el desarrollo, garantizar los derechos sociales, fortalecer una distribución justa de la riqueza, fortalecer los sectores estratégicos”.
Al destacar que en 2026 se distribuirá un billón de pesos en los diferentes programas sociales, Sheinbaum afirmó que es una nueva manera de entender al Estado, no como espectador de las desigualdades, sino como instrumento de justicia. Uno de los mayores cambios con su movimiento es “haber convertido el amor en política pública, y la política pública en derechos que le pertenecen al pueblo de México”. Hizo un recuento de las partidas asignadas a adultos mayores, pensiones para personas con discapacidad, apoyo a jóvenes, becas y respaldo a mujeres.
Sheinbaum resaltó que la reforma en materia de aguas permitió entregar 12 mil 346 títulos de concesión a comunidades, pequeños y medianos productores, así como asignar agua a los municipios que antes tenían que pagar por ella a particulares. Citó los casos de Mexicali y Tijuana, que ya tienen la concesión directa de la Comisión Nacional del Agua, cuando antes tenían que pagar a particulares.
Se refirió a la política laboral, la cual, destacó, ha representado una “primavera” en materia de derechos para los trabajadores, porque el salario mínimo mensual pasó de 2 mil 800 pesos en 2018 a 9 mil 582 pesos en 2026, un incremento de 154 por ciento en términos reales. En la frontera norte, el salario mínimo alcanza 13 mil 409 pesos.
Al señalar que hay 42 millones de beneficiarios de los programas sociales, aseguró que estos no son concesiones del poder, sino una forma de reconocer la dignidad y el esfuerzo de millones de mexicanos.

title: Indigenous 'turtle women' help save endangered freshwater turtles in the Amazon
content:
On the banks of the Aguarico River in the Ecuadorian Amazon, a group of Indigenous Siekopai women are combining traditional knowledge and modern technology to help a threatened native turtle recover.
Their efforts center around charapa turtles (Podocnemis unifilis), also known as the yellow-spotted Amazon River turtle, Mongabay Latam’s Astrid Arellano reported. The animal’s populations have declined due to hunting adult turtles, harvesting eggs from nests, and pollution from garbage, oil, and gasoline.
“Sometimes we see plastic, garbage bags,” Janeth Piaguaje, a Siekopai community leader of the project, told Mongabay Latam. “We also see dead animals floating down the river. We can’t control all of that, but we do make a significant effort to clean the beaches where we work.”
Boat traffic is also eroding riverbanks, and climate change has caused water levels to rise, flooding the flats where turtles make their nests. Charapa turtles are listed as vulnerable by the IUCN, the global conservation authority.
To help the turtles recover, a group of seven Siekopai women, who call themselves Tari Nomiowa’i, or “turtle women,” patrol the riverbanks looking for turtle tracks and nests. When they find nests, the women carefully collect the eggs, a skill Piaguaje said she learned from her father.
“He taught me how to handle the eggs, how to see on what dates and in what months the turtles lay their nests,” she said.
The women document the date, time, location, and number of eggs in each nest using the Epicollect5 app, a field data collection tool.
Then they take the eggs to an incubation facility where they are protected from predators, flooding, and pollution. Once the eggs hatch, the women continue to care for the baby turtles for another month, feeding them cassava, sweet potato, and taro leaves.
Their painstaking work has paid off.
Over the 2025-26 nesting season, the women collected 235 eggs and successfully hatched and released 208 hatchlings into the Aguarico River over March and April this year. The group invited the local community, including schoolchildren, to participate in the turtle release and attend workshops.
“A little girl said, ‘I’m going to take care of them, I’m going to tell them not to touch the eggs,’” Piaguaje recalled.
A driving force behind the work of the Tari Nomiowa’i is their culture and the ancestral belief that the turtles are a link between the visible and spiritual worlds, each swimming with protection from Koouwajëo, the spiritual chief, mother, and ancestral guardian of the turtles.
“I want Koouwajëo to be proud,” said Piaguaje. “When we protect turtles, we don’t just care for a species; we honor the spirits of the river, strengthen our culture, and maintain the sacred pact between our community and nature.”
