title: Pueblo a’uwẽ-xavante denuncia megaproyectos en Brasil
content:
Este artículo de Djalma Ramalho (Aranã Caboclo) se publicó originalmente en el sitio web de Cultural Survival el 17 de agosto de 2026. Global Voices lo reproduce editado con autorización. Lee más sobre la campaña.
Este artículo es parte de la serie «Spotlight» de Global Voices de agosto de 2026, «Derechos indígenas«. Esta serie ofrece una visión de las vidas y experiencias de los pueblos indígenas con el fin de establecer vínculos entre regiones, destacar las experiencias indígenas y contar historias de líderes, activistas, miembros de la comunidad y otras personas. Puedes apoyar esta cobertura con una donación.
Bajo un cielo muy cargado, en la costas del lago Léman en Ginebra, palabras rojas cortan el paisaje. Delante de la jet d’Eau of Bains des Pâquis, la emblemática fuente de Ginebra, aparecieron dos mensajes: “Dejen que los a’uwẽ-xavante sigan soñando” y “Alto a los megaproyectos que fragmentan Ró, el territorio a’uwẽ-xavante”.
La intervención se dio en la inauguración internacional de una campaña encabezada por líderes, comunidades y organizaciones a’uwẽ-xavante durante el Mecanismo de Expertos sobre los Derechos de los Pueblos Indígenas de Naciones Unidas en julio de 2026. Son un grupo indígena de la región centro oeste de Brasil, con una población de cerca de 25,300 personas. Según el censo de 2022, Brasil tiene 1.69 millones de personas que se identifican como indígenas de 391 etnias.
Mientras los representantes gubernamentales debatían políticas y normas internacionales en Naciones Unidas, la delegación indígena ocupó espacios públicos para transmitir un mensaje: no puede haber desarrollo legítimo cuando realizarlo depende de destruir las condiciones materiales, espirituales y políticas que sostienen la existencia de un pueblo.
Soñar no es una metáfora
Para el pueblo a’uwẽ-xavante, soñar es una dimensión concreta de la vida social, espiritual y política. En su investigación sobre el desempeño de los sueños entre los a’uwẽ-xavante, la antropóloga Laura Graham demuestra que los sueños establecen relaciones entre vivos, ancestros e inmortales. Las canciones que se reciben durante al sueño se difunden con la comunidad y pueden convertirse en actuaciones colectivas que reúnen narrativa, música, danza, memoria y continuidad cultural.
En un episodio documentado por Graham, un anciano cuenta que recibe canciones de creadores ancestrales dirigidas a los vivos, así que al cantarlas colectivamente, los a’uwẽ seguirán existiendo como a’uwẽ. Por lo tanto, el soñador no aparece como el dueño individual de una creación, sino como un mediador de conocimiento que pertenece y circula entre el pueblo como un todo, y se vuelve parte del legado vivo de la comunidad.
En años recientes, según los líderes que han gestionado la campaña, los sueños también empezaron a transmitir advertencias relacionadas con crecientes presiones en sus territorios. Por tanto, la expansión de ferrocarriles, carreteras, proyectos hidroeléctricos, monocultivos y otros proyectos a gran escala no se entiende meramente como una transformación física del entorno, sino como una amenaza a las relaciones que hacen posible recibir, transmitir y aplicar este conocimiento.
Entonces, defender el derecho a soñar es defender las condiciones territoriales que hacen que soñar sea posible.
Ró: Cerrado, mundo, territorio y vida
La palabra «ró» no tiene un equivalente completo en la traducción convencional de “territorio”. La geógrafa Maria Lucia Cereda Gomide explica que ró puede significar simultáneamente “cerrado, mundo, nuestra tierra, todo”. Se refiere a una complejo territorial y cosmológico que se extiende desde el espacio de la aldea al cerrado [bioma en el centro de Brasil], y comprende sus aguas, animales, plantas y los espíritus que viven en este mundo. Ró es una red viviente de relaciones. Abarca cazar, recolectar y pescar; aldeas antiguas, tierras de sepultura, ríos y caminos, plantas medicinales; lugares ceremoniales y presencias ancestrales que sostienen la vida colectiva.
Una nota técnica de la Asociación Antropológica brasileña, publicada en 2025, enfatiza que la territorialidad a’uwẽ-xavante depende de prácticas como recorrer el cerrado, recolectar raíces, frutas y fibras, pescar, cazar y circuitos de reciprocidad que conecta familias, clanes, grupos etarios y diferentes tierras indígenas. Por tanto, la fragmentación territorial compromete el acceso a recursos naturales y la capacidad de realizar ceremonias, transmitir conocimiento y mantener las relaciones sociales y cosmológicas a través de las cuales los a’uwẽ se constituyen como pueblo. También va más allá de relaciones que no se pueden contener dentro de los límites administrativos trazados por el Estado.
Entonces, el mensaje proyectado en Ginebra –“Dejen que los a’uwẽ-xavante sigan soñando”– es un pedido para proteger la integridad de ró y por la continuidad de su propia existencia. Hiparidi Top’tiro, líder a’uwẽ-xavante, dice en el documento de la campaña: “Cualquier proyecto que afecta a uno de nuestros territorios es un problema para todo el pueblo a’uwẽ-xavante”.
Territorios, vidas y sueños cortados por pistas
El pedido central de la campaña es proteger los derechos del pueblo a’uwẽ-xavante ante la construcción del Ferrocarril de Integración Centro Oeste (FICO), también conocido como EF-354. El Gobierno brasileño lo ha presentado como un proyecto estratégico para reducir costos logísticos y expandir el transporte ferroviario de carga, y es parte de un corredor más amplio diseñado principalmente para trasladar soya, maíz y otros productos de la región. Al avanzar el proyecto sin garantizar una consulta adecuada, libre, previa e informada, el Estado brasileño no ha logrado proteger los derechos de los pueblos indígenas.
La vía de FICO es un proyecto federal de aproximadamente 1641 kilómetros (1020 millas) bajo la responsabilidad de Infra S.A. La empresa minera Vale está construyendo la primera sección, que recorre 363 kilómetros (226 millas), entre Mara Rosa, en el estado de Goiás, y Água Boa, en el estado de Mato Grosso, como compensación por la renovación prematura de otra concesión. Estudios y procesos administrativos relacionados con la ruta han identificado los territorios xavante dentro de su zona de influencia, lo que plantea serias preocupaciones sobre el impacto territorial, ambiental, social y cultural.
En mayo de 2026, la propia Infra S.A. informó que aproximadamente 80 kilómetros (50 millas) de la parte final de la porción de la sección que actualmente está en construcción dependía de que se completara el Plan Ambiental Básico – Componente Indígena (PBA-CI) y de negociaciones con las comunidades xavante. Esto deja en claro que la relación entre el ferrocarril y los territorios indígenas no es meramente indirecta, sino un asunto central que afecta la implementación del proyecto.
La nota técnica emitida por la Asociación Antropológica brasileña establece que el ferrocarril afecta zonas de ocupación tradicional, tierras reclamadas que aún no se han demarcado, ha juntado zonas, aldeas antiguas, tierras de sepulturas, ríos navegables y sitios sagrados. El documento recomienda suspender la construcción y la licencia de instalación hasta que se haya hecho una consulta adecuada, y alterar la ruta para que el ferrocarril no cruce territorio a’uwẽ-xavante.
El informe de defensa de la campaña Dejen que los a’uwẽ-xavante sigan soñando, iniciada en Ginebra, sostiene que FICO no puede evaluarse meramente como una línea ferroviaria aislada. Es parte de una arquitectura más amplia de carreteras, ferrocarriles, cursos de agua, y exporta corredores que probablemente intensifique los flujos de mercadería, ocupación no indígena y presión económica en territorios ya fragmentados.
Consulta en disputa
En febrero de 2026, la Coordinación de Organizaciones Indígenas de la Amazonía Brasileña (COIAB) denunció irregularidades en el proceso de consulta relacionado con FICO. Según la organización, las reuniones programadas para algunas tierras indígenas se hicieron a intervalos muy cortos, lo que dejó a las comunidades con poco tiempo para tener debates internos de acuerdo con sus propios procesos de toma de decisiones. También hay documentadas denuncias de presiones a líderes indígenas, falta de asistencia técnica independiente y dificultades de comunicación entre comunidades distribuidas entre territorios que históricamente han estado fragmentados. El Ministerio Público Federal inició un procedimiento administrativo para dar seguimiento al proceso de consulta.
La Organización Internacional del Trabajo (OIT) y la Declaración de Naciones Unidas sobre Derechos de los Pueblos Indígenas establece que los Estados deben consultar y cooperar de buena fe con los pueblos indígenas después de aprobar proyectos que afectan a sus tierras, territorios o recursos, para obtener su consentimiento libre, previo e informado.
La consulta no solo significa informar a una comunidad que un proyecto procederá, sino también respetará sus cronogramas de toma de decisiones, sin coerción y su capacidad de retener el consentimiento de medidas que pudieran comprometer su futuro.
A Europa: el colonialismo solo viaja por tren y autos eléctricos
La intervención en Ginebra tiene un peso simbólico particular. La ciudad es sede de la Oficina de Naciones Unidas y de numerosas instituciones relacionadas con el sistema internacional de derechos humanos. A los representantes indígenas se les da poco minutos para presentar conflictos territoriales delineados por décadas de violaciones.
La campaña también desafía las contradicciones de la llamada transición ecológica. Ferrocarriles, corredores logísticos, operaciones mineras y proyectos de infraestructura a gran escala se presentan frecuentemente como instrumentos necesarios para construir una economía con bajo carbono. Pero cuando avanzan sin la participación efectiva de los pueblos afectados, pueden reproducir mecanismos coloniales que perduran: apropiación territorial, concentración de beneficios económicos y transferencia de costos ambientales y sociales a pueblos indígenas y comunidades tradicionales.
La proyección delante de Jet d’Eau confronta esta paradoja. Europa, históricamente implicada en la colonización de territorios indígenas, sigue conectadas con estas regiones por medio de redes de finanzas, consumo, minería, agroindustria e infraestructura de exportaciones. Cambiar la fuente de energía sin transformar estas relaciones no es suficiente. Una transición que sigue amenazando territorios indígenas como zonas de sacrificio puede ser tecnológicamente nuevo, pero sigue siendo políticamente colonial.
Para los a’uwẽ-xavante, un territorio fragmentado no significa simplemente reducir el espacio físico. Significa interrumpir caminos, canciones, ceremonias y recuerdos, y relaciones ancestrales. Ningún megaproyecto puede decir que representa el futuro si su existencia depende de destruir los sueños de quienes siempre han cuidado la tierra.

title: ‘Unlock your DNA’: More young S’poreans taking up dialect classes
content:
‘Unlock your DNA’: More young S’poreans taking up dialect classes
- More Singaporeans are learning Chinese dialects to reconnect with their heritage and strengthen family bonds.
- Clan associations report rising enrolments in dialect classes, with creative, fun methods used to make learning engaging and culturally rich.
- The government supports dialect learning alongside Mandarin, promoting cultural roots and local Chinese identity through various activities and programmes.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – When Eldred Wee started learning Hainanese at the Hainan Hwee Kuan in December 2025, the 34-year-old had practically no grasp of the language despite both his parents’ strong fluency.
His parents, who are both Hainanese, divorced when he was around nine, and he grew up speaking English with his mother.
“My dialect and culture were never handed to me.
“I am choosing as an adult, for myself and for my son, to rebuild a generational link that was broken,” said the entrepreneur.
Wee wants his four-year-old son, Eden, to know Hainanese. At home, he makes it a point to use simple Hainanese phrases like “boh gai dit” (thank you).
“My motivation is identity, intergenerational bonding and belonging,” he said.
The film Dear You may have sparked renewed interest in Teochew and dialects in general, but clan associations across Singapore told The Straits Times their dialect classes have become more popular in recent years.
Learners, who used to be mainly middle-aged and older, have become much younger, with many in their 20s to 40s.
For instance, Kong Chow Wui Koon’s (KCWK) advanced Cantonese class sizes doubled between 2022 and 2026, while the Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan (SHHK) Cultural Academy has seen participation for its Hokkien classes jump about 15 per cent over the past three years.
Meanwhile, Char Yong (Dabu) Association started its Hakka class in April, with 19 students. Its second run has been expanded to 26 students, and there are three people on the waiting list.
Veteran radio newscaster Nigel Lim, who has been teaching Teochew at the Teochew Poit Ip Huay Kuan since 2003, noted the rising enrolment and the clear demographic shift.
“China has grown stronger, and more are seeking roots. Many are realising that speaking their dialect helps them connect with overseas relatives and even Chinese business partners,” he said.
For 20-year-old Joshua Loh, it was a Hakka song sung by a musician in a Shanghai cafe that inspired him to take up lessons at the Char Yong (Dabu) Association in 2026.
“He (the musician) told me something that really stuck: If you speak Hakka, you unlock your DNA. Learning Hakka has given me a sense of grounding, and I hope more young people get to experience that too,” said the polytechnic student.
He also hopes this can strengthen his relationship with his grandparents, whom he visits every other week.
“They would correct me if my pronunciation was different from what they grew up with,” he said. “It has become a nice bonding ritual between us.”
Accessible routes to cultural roots
Lim, the Teochew instructor, said the Government’s recent easing of its policy on dialect content is actually good for Singaporeans’ use of Mandarin.
In his Mandarin speech at the National Day Rally on Aug 23, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced that there would no longer be a cap on the number of screenings of dialect films, as long as a Mandarin-dubbed version is available.
He also spotlighted clan associations’ efforts to promote dialects here through classes and cultural activities, and said the Government will continue to support these efforts.
While the Government previously discouraged dialects to streamline communication across diverse Chinese groups, Lim believes dialects have the ability to unify, rather than fragment.
“Learning a Chinese dialect can actually boost one’s Mandarin, as mastering a dialect’s complex tones and structures makes Mandarin easier to grasp,” he added.
There are also students like Tan Song Ya, whose interest in Cantopop and Hong Kong dramas prompted her to enrol in a Cantonese class at KCWK in July.
“Perhaps I should be learning my own dialect, Hokkien, after this,” said the 34-year-old engineer, who grew up speaking English and Mandarin.
A budding interest in one’s dialect can also become an abiding interest in Chinese history and culture, noted Kong Chow Cultural Centre head and Cantonese instructor Wong Chee Meng.
“For the class in Chinese history and culture, many students enjoy learning classical poetry, especially Tang poetry, in Cantonese, because the richness in rhymes and tonal patterns often cannot be replicated in Mandarin,” he noted.
Clan associations here said they are experimenting with different ways to build on this momentum of interest in dialects.
For instance, the central plot device of Dear You is qiaopi, which were letters sent home by overseas Chinese along with remittance money. The letters were written with Chinese ink and traditional script, which flowed vertically from top to bottom.
SHHK has since incorporated this into its dialect programmes. It also organises intergenerational activities where youth and seniors are grouped together to make traditional food such as bak chang (glutinous rice dumplings) and to learn classic Hokkien songs together, said its marketing manager Jeremiah Soh.
Tapping into Singaporeans’ gastronomic obsessions, many of the lessons also touch on the dishes unique to each dialect group.
“Food is especially effective because it brings people together. We discuss dishes such as Hainanese chicken rice, kaya and yi bua, a Hainanese glutinous rice snack,” said Hou Wenxue, a teacher at Hainan Hwee Kuan.
“These dishes give students a way to understand the history and environment behind the culture.”
Meanwhile, KCWK’s elementary-level Cantonese class focuses on phrases for real-life situations, such as ordering food in a restaurant.
Lim said dialects also offer a stress-free way to access and appreciate one’s culture and traditions as there are no exams.
“There are also no strict standards to follow, as Singapore’s dialects are not ‘pure’ and have been influenced by other languages here.”
Hakka instructor Wong Chin Fee agreed. “Even in Dabu county, there are variations of the same Hakka dialect,” he said.
“I always tell my students: Just speak up and don’t be afraid of making mistakes.”
Students told ST that besides tapping on food, music and pop culture, what will sustain interest in dialects here is having more opportunities to use these languages in daily life.
This can include having more events where everyone attempts to speak in the same dialect, whether they are karaoke and movie nights or cooking classes.
“If dialect becomes something that we encounter more naturally in our everyday lives, I think more young people would be curious enough to give it a try,” said polytechnic student Alexis Foo, 18, who is learning Hakka.
“Sometimes, preserving a culture starts simply by making it easier for people to participate in it.”

title: La capa de ozono se recuperará en 40 años gracias al Protocolo de Montreal, según expertos
content:
La capa de ozono, el manto natural que protege la Tierra de la radiación ultravioleta, se está recuperando lentamente y la ciencia estima en unos cuarenta años el tiempo aproximado para completar ese proceso, según subraya Naciones Unidas en el Día Internacional de la Preservación de la Capa de Ozono, el 16 de septiembre.
La protección de la capa de ozono se acordó en el marco del Convenio de Viena (1985) y posteriormente, con el Protocolo de Montreal (1987), se establecieron las obligaciones para la eliminación de las sustancias que destruyen ese manto natural, los gases clorofluorocarbonados (CFC).
En 2016, con la firma de la Enmienda de Kigali, se acordó además la reducción gradual de la producción y consumo de gases hidrofluorocarbonos (HFC), utilizados en la refrigeración y para el aire acondicionado.
Ahora el Día Mundial del Ozono conmemora los 10 años de la Enmienda de Kigali, acordada dentro del Protocolo de Montreal, y hace hincapié en la relación entre protección del ozono y salvaguarda del clima.
Fueron dos científicos, el ingeniero químico mexicano Mario Molina-Pasquel Henríquez y el químico estadounidense Frank Sherwood Rowland, los que descubrieron en los años setenta que los gases CFC destruían la capa de ozono.
Ambos fueron galardonados con el Premio Nobel de Química en 1995, junto al químico neerlandés Paul Jozef Crutzen, quien también estudió la formación y descomposición del ozono.
Gracias a sus estudios, la comunidad internacional se puso de acuerdo para la firma del Protocolo de Montreal y agilizar la prohibición de CFC, gases muy utilizados en sistemas de refrigeración, aerosoles (lacas de peluquería, desodorantes, insecticidas o pinturas), espumas aislantes o disolventes industriales, que aún persisten en la atmósfera.
En 1985, los científicos Joe Farman, Brian Gardiner y Jonathan Shanklin, del Instituto Antártico Británico, detectaron un gran agujero en la capa de ozono sobre la Antártida que se abre y se cierra de forma cíclica todos los años.
Menor agujero y evidencia científica
Según un informe de la Organización Meteorológica Mundial (OMM) de septiembre de 2025, la capa de ozono va “camino de recuperarse” y en 2024 el agujero “fue menor” que en años precedentes.
La OMM asegura, no obstante, que es un proceso que “aún tardará varios decenios”, un periodo que científicos de la NASA y de la Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica (NOAA, por sus siglas en inglés) fijan en 40 años.
Según explica a EFE el investigador del Centro Atmosférico de Izaña de la Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet) de España, Alberto Redondas Marrero, “la capa de ozono se está recuperando y tenemos evidencias claras de que el Protocolo de Montreal está funcionando”.
El también responsable del Centro de calibración de ozono y la red de observación de ozono (EuBrewnet) indica que los resultados preliminares del estudio Ozone Assessment que forman parte de la evaluación científica de 2026 —que se publicará a finales de año— “muestran una recuperación clara del ozono en la alta estratosfera entre 2000 y 2024 y prácticamente en todas las latitudes”.
Explica que los resultados del estudio se presentaron en un “reciente congreso en Davos celebrando los primeros 100 años de la medida de ozono” y subraya que “el balance conjunto es muy significativo”.
Redondas asegura que el Protocolo de Montreal “está permitiendo recuperar la capa de ozono y, al mismo tiempo, ha evitado una cantidad importante de calentamiento global”, mientras que la Enmienda de Kigali “completa ese éxito reduciendo ahora el impacto climático de los gases que sustituyeron a las sustancias destructoras del ozono”.
Por eso, afirma, “10 años después de Kigali, el Día Mundial del Ozono de 2026 pone especialmente de relieve que proteger la capa de ozono y proteger el clima son objetivos distintos, pero estrechamente relacionados”.
No obstante, recuerda que “la recuperación es mucho más lenta que su destrucción” y, para que la recuperación sea completa, se necesita tiempo “porque los CFC permanecen en la atmósfera durante muchas décadas”.
Las proyecciones indican que “podríamos volver aproximadamente a los niveles de 1980 hacia 2040 para el promedio global, mientras que en la Antártida tendremos que esperar hasta la década de 2060”, sostiene el experto, según reportó EFE.

title: On Yom Kippur I was shot protecting my synagogue, now I carry the torch. - Sponsored Content
content:
One year ago on Yom Kippur, my life changed forever. I was shot while protecting the doors of Heaton Park Synagogue in Manchester during a terrorist attack. Badly injured, I underwent seven hours of surgery and spent the next ten days in hospital. I survived. Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz, two remarkable men I think about every day, tragically did not.
Since the attack, I have looked for ways to honour life and remember those we lost. So, when I was invited to join the 2026 International March of the Living, I welcomed the opportunity to march alongside Holocaust survivors and fellow survivors of antisemitic attacks. Together, we set off on the march.
As the shofar was blown, we began the 3.5 km walk from Auschwitz to Birkenau. Israeli flags were waving and 8,000 people walked with us.
They did not beat us.
The March gives you the extraordinary opportunity to spend time with survivors who rebuilt their lives and now educate the next generation. As Elie Wiesel said, “When you listen to a witness, you become a witness.”
I wasn’t the only one there carrying scars of my own. I met Hannah Abesidon and Eva Wietzen, survivors of the Bondi Beach attack, and Abbie Talmoud and Catherine Szkop, who witnessed the murders of their friends Sarah Milgrim and Yaron Lischinsky in Washington, D.C. We were asked whether these experiences had made us afraid to be visibly Jewish. I was wearing a kippah, Abbie a Magen David, Hannah a Chai necklace. We all gave the same answer: we were proud to be Jewish, and our pride had only been strengthened.
Together, we lit the first torch at the March’s closing ceremony in Birkenau, dedicated to combating antisemitism, alongside Sylvan Adams, President of the World Jewish Congress–Israel, and Ambassador Yehuda Kaploun, the U.S. Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism.
In a symbolic moment, the next torch was lit by the international law enforcement delegation, who had come to pledge their commitment to “Never Again – Not on Our Watch.” I was privileged to address the delegation, and I told them that members of my synagogue were killed and I was injured because hatred had moved from social media and marches into real life. Hate is not abstract. It has consequences, and I am living proof.
The community doesn’t feel any safer a year on from Heaton Park. There are more gates and more security than we have ever had. Any event we hold does not have the address displayed on the poster. Our kids go to schools that look like fortresses. Every Jewish building has to have security.
Combating antisemitism is not the responsibility of the Jewish community alone. As history has shown, when radicalisation or hate targets Jews first, it threatens the freedom, safety, and human rights of society as a whole. We all have a responsibility to speak up and challenge antisemitism wherever we see it.
We did not march only against antisemitism. We also marched for Jewish life and Jewish pride. In Tykocin, I experienced one of the most inspirational moments of the trip. In the synagogue there, built in 1642, we prayed Mincha, then danced, holding hands and singing V’hi She’amdah with survivors. A testament that Jewish life would not just survive but thrive.
This instinct to dance rather than surrender was already familiar to me from Yom Kippur. While I was undergoing surgery, our rabbi, Daniel Walker, made the decision that we would carry on and refuse to let the terrorists win. Not a single prayer was missed. The first time I was able to return to my synagogue was Simchat Torah, where we danced like we had never danced before, with defiance. Even in the darkness and the pain, we carry on, and we dance.
As the plane lifted off from Warsaw, I made a silent promise to myself: I will be back.
I invite you to join me.
Join the March of the Living or help someone else make the journey.
Yom Kippur will never be the same for me. But I know that, as a community, we will carry on. This Yom Kippur, we will return to our Shul. Yes, we are different, but we are still here and we are saying the same prayers that we carried on saying last year. On the March, we prayed, sang and danced in the very places where the Nazis tried to wipe us out, alongside the very people they tried to murder. And we are continuing a story that has endured in every generation, despite those who have tried to stop it.
May we all be inscribed in the Book of Life, and may the memory of all those murdered because of antisemitism be a blessing.

title: Filmmaker Georgina Lightning set out to change how Indigenous people were seen and heard
content:
Georgina Lightning was the first North American Indigenous woman to write, direct, produce and star in a feature film. She was a woman ahead of her time when it came to storytelling. Her film Older Than America (2008), starring a young Bradley Cooper, was one of the first feature films ever made about the horrors of residential school. The film won multiple honours, most notably a best director prize for Ms. Lightning at the 2008 American Indian Motion Picture Awards.
The film was released two years before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission began its cross-country truth-gathering events and the wider public became aware of the atrocities against Indigenous children at those institutions.
On Sept. 5, Ms. Lightning was killed in an accident doing what she loved – filming. Ms. Lightning was working on her latest project about Indian relay horse racing. She was in Enoch Cree Nation, Alta., when a horse left the track, striking Ms. Lightning, who was in the media pit with a camera. Ms. Lightning’s neck was broken and she was not able to be revived, according to her close friend Jodi Calahoo-Stonehouse. Ms. Lightning was 63.
A citizen of Samson Cree Nation whose traditional name was White Bear Woman, Ms. Lightning was driven in her storytelling to change how Indigenous people were seen and heard, both in front of and behind the camera.
“I watched my mother break down so many barriers and fight for what she wanted,” said Crystle Lightning, Ms. Lightning’s only daughter.
She was born Georgina Lynn De Jong in Edmonton on July 4, 1963 to Bernice and George De Jong. Although Georgina suffered abuse at the hands of her father when she was young, family remained the most important thing to her. She was the middle child of three sisters and her love of family was instilled in her by her mother.
She had her first child at the age of 17, but her relationship with the child’s father did not last. She later married and had two more children, but left her husband after experiencing abuse.
Ms. Lightning was determined to make a better life for herself and her children. As a single mother, she moved to Los Angeles in the early 1990s to pursue a career in acting. She attended the American Academy of Dramatic Arts and was the only student with children. She became the valedictorian of her class. Her children: Cody, Crystle and William Lightning were all under the age of 10 at the time. Ms. De Jong, the children’s grandmother, moved to L.A. with the family.
Crystle Lightning recalls that her mother got her an agent when they arrived in L.A., and she landed her first big role as a teenager in the 1995 film 3 Ninjas: Knuckle Up. But she said her mother did not push her into the spotlight and gave her the opportunity to choose what she wanted to do when she turned 18.
“When I graduated high school, she had the talk with me: ‘You’re 18 now. What do you wanna do? Mama can’t be taking you to your auditions any more,’” Crystle Lightning said.
However, the elder Ms. Lightning never stopped supporting her children and the pursuit of their dreams. But eventually Hollywood took a backseat to home, and in 2012 Georgina Lightning returned to Alberta where she continued her career and began building a film family in Edmonton. After her return, she acted in a dozen TV productions, including Blackstone, Trickster and Three Pines, as well as several films.
It was her dream to see that city become the Indigenous film capital of Turtle Island (North America), and she had been working toward that goal for several years, meeting with mayors, provincial ministers and members of the film community.
Ms. Lightning’s life journey is reflected in the films and television series she appeared in. In Older Than America, which she co-wrote with Christine K. Walker, Ms. Lightning was inspired by her own family’s story of relatives being forced to attend Indian residential institutions, the abuse they suffered and the resulting wounds that they carried with them.
Her father, George, a residential school survivor who didn’t talk about his childhood, died by suicide. This event led her on a quest to find out more about him, which in turn led her to researching residential schools.
When she returned to Alberta, she immediately met with Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse, now an NDP Alberta MLA. At the time, Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse was hosting and producing Acimowin, an Indigenous radio show on which Ms. Lightning appeared several times as a guest. So it was only natural that they became close friends, calling one another sister.
“She just left America with a broken heart and had some mental health, depression battles and came home for healing and wanted to film and share that journey of healing, of recovery and the reality of suicide in our community and in our lives,” Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse said.
The resulting documentary project has been a decade-long journey. It began with the working title Fantasies of Flying, according to the Internet Movie Database (IMDb). It will now be renamed Grandmother’s Medicine and Crystle Lightning and Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse will finish Georgina Lightning’s work.
The film looks at “where we’re at, what it’s taken to get us from the injury of the Indian residential school, and what it has taken to recover from genocide, which is Grandmother’s Medicine,” Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse said.
On the Tuesday before her death, Ms. Lightning visited Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse and made her friend promise to work with Crystle. They are currently working together as co-hosts of a film on climate change by the younger Ms. Lightning. Now, they will work together to finish her mother’s projects as well.
“You honour your family with the highest integrity by fulfilling their legacy. I’m very busy with my work but she’s my sister and we loved each other deeply and she was just as much there for me,” Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse said.
That is who Ms. Lightning was; always there for her family and friends. No matter what she was working on herself, she found time to support, mentor and talk with people. Ms. Lightning even renovated Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse’s kitchen during the pandemic.
“When I ran for national chief [of the Assembly of First Nations in 2021], she was over every day helping me and wearing a ‘Vote for Jodi’ shirt and hat. She’s been my biggest cheerleader,” Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse said.
Elle-Máijá Tailfeathers agrees. Ms. Tailfeathers is also an actor, writer, director and producer who acted with Ms. Lightning on the TV series Three Pines.
“I remember this one particular day, I was struggling to hit an emotional beat I needed for the character. I was in the scene with Georgina. So it wasn’t her coverage, it was my coverage. My character knocked on her character’s door and had to deliver some challenging news. I struggled with the first couple of takes and then Georgina recognized that I was struggling. And I think it was the third take, I knocked on the door and she opened the door and she had tears streaming down her cheeks,” Ms. Tailfeathers said.
“And she was just in this deeply vulnerable open place as an actor, delivering what her character might be feeling. And it just ruptured me, it opened me right up and it brought me to where the character needed to be in the scene. It was just so generous of her to do that for me and for the story, because she wasn’t on camera.”
As a younger filmmaker, Ms. Tailfeathers looked up to Ms. Lightning and watched her work. When they met, the two became friends.
“I always felt she supported my career, she offered gentle and generous guidance. And she was just such a warm and bright soul, and so fierce as well,” Ms. Tailfeathers said.
That seems to be the consensus of the life Ms. Lightning led – she was generous. Even when she struggled with her own battles, she prayed for others’ health when she sundanced. She battled lymphoma cancer with traditional and Western medicines but had been in remission for the past year.
Yet, she seemed to know her time was limited. After Robert Redford’s death in September, 2025, Ms. Lightning posted on social media: “What’s up with these past few months? Creator has been calling on so many Heroes that included my mother Bernice - all this loss really makes you do a check in with yourself … Am I spending my time efficiently, effectively, because life is really so so short.”
When asked what Ms. Lightning’s legacy will be, Ms. Calahoo-Stonehouse and Ms. Tailfeathers agreed it would be her children – two of whom are formidable and talented actors.
Mr. Lightning’s film Smudge the Blades had its world premiere on Sept. 12 at the Toronto International Film Festival, while Crystle Lightning continues on with her musical Bear Grease, which she created with her husband, Henry Andrade, a rapper known as Red Cloud. She will also see to it that her mother’s final four projects will be completed, including the one on the Indian relay horse racing.
“But her legacy is also just her path of kindness that she forged and her path of just being fierce. She was this tiny woman, but she just carried so much spirit within that tiny body,” Ms. Tailfeathers said.
Crystle Lightning said she will remember her “fierce momma bear love” for her family, including her four grandchildren. And that is why she worked so hard to blaze trails, break down doors, and keep them open for others to walk through.
“It sounds so cliché, but like literally chasing your dreams down. Nothing’s gonna be handed to you. Nothing. Especially being an Indigenous woman in this industry, you have to just sometimes create your own opportunities because sometimes we won’t ever get the chance that we’re waiting for. That’s what she showed me.”

title: Thousands flock to traditional ox race, floating market festival in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta
content:
The 2026 Ro Pagoda Traditional Ox Racing Festival officially opened on Sunday morning in An Cu Commune, An Giang Province, drawing 32 top pairs of oxen from the Seven Mountains area.
Ox racing is a long-standing cultural and sporting tradition among Khmer people in the Mekong Delta and has become a local tourism attraction in the Seven Mountains area.
Truong Thi Hong Tham, a visitor from Ca Mau Province, said it was her first time attending the Ro Pagoda ox racing festival.
The visitor was impressed by the skill of both the oxen and their handlers, as spectators cheered loudly as the pairs raced toward the finish line.
Nguyen Duy Phong, chairman of the An Cu Commune People's Committee, said the festival provides an opportunity for local residents to strengthen community ties and preserve Khmer cultural traditions.
The commune also hoped the event would help promote tourism in the Seven Mountains area to domestic and international visitors, he said.
The festival also featured a photo exhibition showcasing ox racing and the cultural life of people in the Seven Mountains area, along with the presentation of 100 bicycles to disadvantaged students and an exhibition of local OCOP (One Commune One Product) products.
Flood-season festival draws crowds in Hong Ngu
Also on Sunday, thousands of residents and visitors headed to a more than 2km-long embankment in Hong Ngu Ward, Dong Thap Province for the second edition of the Sac Nuoc Vung Bien festival.
The festival celebrated the Mekong Delta's annual flood season with activities including a floating market, boat racing, and duck-catching games.
Every year, from around August to December, water from the upper Mekong River flows into the Mekong Delta, turning vast areas into a sea of water.
Unlike a sudden flood, the water rises gradually, filling rivers before spilling over their banks and into the fields.
For Mekong Delta tourism and local communities, the annual flood season is seen as a gift from nature, bringing fertile alluvial soil and an abundance of fish, shrimp, fruits, and other local produce.
Dozens of decorated boats and sampans were arranged along the main festival area, creating a floating-market setting where visitors could sample local food and drinks and take photos.
Vo Nguyen Huy Nam, a local resident, said he was proud that Hong Ngu had developed a tourism event centered on the flood season, a distinctive feature of the area.
Phan Thi Hue, another local resident, said she sold roasted field shrimp with coconut water, teas and canarium products at the festival.
The event not only created a lively atmosphere and helped local vendors sell their products, but also conveyed a message about protecting the environment so that the annual flood season remains clean and healthy, she said.
Nguyen Thi Kim Yen, deputy chairwoman of the Hong Ngu Ward People's Committee, said this year's activities were designed to bring the flood season closer to residents and visitors through hands-on experiences.
Visitors could explore a floating market, enjoy don ca tai tu performances, join team boat races, and take part in other activities celebrating rural life during the flood season.
The festival also included an experiential program and a photo contest highlighting the beauty of Hong Ngu.
“The market tells the story of local produce. The boats tell the story of life on the waterways. Folk songs and traditional music tell the story of culture. Local dishes tell stories of memories. And the smiles of Hong Ngu people tell stories of kindness, friendliness, and hospitality,” Yen said.
“Through these familiar elements, we are not only creating a lively festival but also gradually building a distinctive cultural and tourism product for Hong Ngu.”

title: As climate disasters multiply, Indigenous governance offers a way forward
content: Indigenous lands from Canada to Ecuador to Nepal are increasingly being hit by catastrophic storms, fires, and floods. Worse, these climate disasters often come one after the other as overlapping crises rather than isolated incidents. Still, despite the ongoing destruction, Indigenous peoples continue to prove that they have the knowledge and skills to respond, if only global powers will let them. Even amid growing recognition by scientists and policymakers of the power of Indigenous expertise to respond to climate change, the key role that Indigenous governance plays in those knowledge systems has not received as much respect. That’s according to a new report from Land Is Life that highlights the global success of Indigenous climate adaptation and resilience amid escalating crises. The report also says supporting Indigenous governance through legal recognition, financing, and partnerships — none of which are occurring on a large scale — is the best way to reduce climate disaster risk worldwide. “We show that it’s not that they are only the most impacted, but they are already implementing effective solutions,” said Luisa Castañeda Quintana, the executive director of Land Is Life, a global nonprofit dedicated to Indigenous self-determination. “When it comes to adaptation, we don’t really need to create new structures or systems. We just need to see what is working.” The report adds to an expansive body of research showing that Indigenous self-determination, land stewardship, and cultural knowledge and practices are proven climate solutions. The report, released today, offers dozens of examples. In Kenya, Indigenous Endorois and Tugen women cultivated drought-resistant varieties of sorghum, millet, and other key foods that provided some of the region’s only harvests in years with severe drought. In Brazil, Coordination of Indigenous Organizations of the Brazilian Amazon — the nation’s largest regional Indigenous network — helps organize fire management and response. It also provides training and mobilizes response teams. The report is based on detailed case studies and more than 200 survey responses from 46 countries spanning six ecosystems: forests, mountains, drylands, freshwater systems, grasslands, and coastal. Castañeda Quintana said a broad global study was essential to show climate change and environmental disasters are not limited by national or even ecological boundaries, and responses to them must transcend borders. It also is essential to recognize that disasters do not arrive one at a time. More than 80 percent of survey respondents said that they face two or more at once, and over 90 percent reported rising frequency. For example, in 2019, the Kichwa People of Sarayaku in the Ecuadorian Amazon faced devastating floods along the Bobonaza River, destroying crops and homes. Daniel Santi, who is the president of the community, which numbers roughly 1,600 and inhabits more than 500 square miles, said that his people were able to respond effectively because of their strong governance structures that were already in place. In other words, self-determination and governance allowed them to decide how best to prepare for, and respond to, a crisis. “This organization makes it possible to confront any problem and any threat,” Santi said. The report argues that the combination of Indigenous governance and knowledge is what makes these adaptation strategies so effective. Knowledge rooted in the land can be put into action immediately. Sarayaku elders, for example, noticed rain and lightning patterns at the river’s headwaters that signaled possible flooding and were then able to warn the community. Sarayaku structure includes clear decision-making processes, mechanisms to address the most urgent needs like housing for families with destroyed homes, and dedicated representatives to communicate status updates and needs with external authorities. According to Santi, these responses are guided by minga, a Kichwa term for solidarity and collective responsibility. But many countries do not legally recognize Indigenous peoples or their governments, refuse to use Indigenous languages for emergency alerts, and continue to criminalize Indigenous culture. Those conditions can weaken the impact of Indigenous knowledge and governance. Read Next As climate change threatens their lands, Indigenous nations demand more power at the UN Dionne Phillips Santi believes Indigenous peoples have a lot to teach the world about adapting and responding to climate change, but communities like his need support as it continues to accelerate. He is calling for greater legal protections for Indigenous land and authority, as well as resources and partnerships that embrace Indigenous knowledge and decision-making. In Peru’s Ausangate Regional Conservation Area, Quechua communities joined a conservation organization to document environmental indicators, improve community monitoring, and pursue other efforts that combined Indigenous knowledge with Western research. According to the report, this is an example of how productive partnerships increase resilience. The report also found other shortcomings in many of the world’s mitigation and adaptation strategies. They include climate initiatives that focus on short-term benefits, rejecting Indigenous self-governance and imposing external authority on communities, and drawing on or celebrating Indigenous knowledge without supporting the people who provide it. Despite growing evidence that shows Indigenous land stewardship is effective and that providing Indigenous communities with direct financing helps with global climate adaptation, funding and legal security remain insufficient. “It’s always the lack of resources and the lack of access to funding that makes it so difficult for us to work, especially when climate change makes us the most vulnerable,” said Anisha Buda, who is from the Kaike Magar community and is a program officer at the national Indigenous Women Forum in Nepal. Rather than outlining a specific template for Indigenous governance, the report urges governments, philanthropists, and policymakers to foster the conditions that allow Indigenous communities to thrive. Flexible and direct funding is one of those key conditions. Land Is Life released the report during New York Climate Week specifically to call out the need for more direct financing for Indigenous communities. Despite billions of dollars pledged around the world, barely any of that money is earmarked for Indigenous peoples. And even when it is, Indigenous leaders say that they still don’t receive it. “It’s also so frustrating, right?” said Buda. “Because there are so many projects that are supposed to be for Indigenous peoples, but they are implemented by non-Indigenous organizations and non-Indigenous peoples.” With the U.S. and European countries pulling back billions of dollars from climate commitments in recent years and wars in Iran and Ukraine stretching global resources, Indigenous leaders worry they will be left even further behind. “We are in a moment where resources are scarce,” said Gisela Hurtado, the report’s author. “Where can we put the little money that we have? Where can we put it to make it much more effective? And for me, for the report, the idea is put it into what already is working.” As the climate continues to change and the world experiences escalating impacts, Hurtado says the Indigenous responses outlined in the report offer a way forward. “What they are seeing in the territories, we’re going to see it also in the future,” Hurtado said. “They are the ones that are much more connected with the Earth to know what is going to happen in the future.” This story was originally published by Grist with the headline As climate disasters multiply, Indigenous governance offers a way forward on Sep 23, 2026.

title: Keeping Indigenous Memory Alive Through Music, Language, and Storytelling
content: Keeping Indigenous Memory Alive Through Music, Language, and Storytelling Country South Africa agnes Wed, 09/23/2026 - 10:02 Issues Languages and Cultures Program 5 Main Image By Byron Tenesaca (Kichwa Kañari, CS Staff) Across Indigenous communities, culture is not something preserved only in museums or history books. It lives in songs, languages, instruments, stories, dances, and the knowledge carried from one generation to the next. But as globalization, displacement, and other pressures reshape Indigenous communities, many of these traditions are at risk of being lost. Indigenous youth are using their own voices and creative practices to keep their cultures alive. Through Cultural Survival’s Indigenous Youth Fellowship Program, young Indigenous leaders are developing projects that strengthen cultural identity and create new ways for their communities to share and transmit ancestral knowledge. In South Africa, musician, educator, and composer Asakhe Cuntsulana is using music, research, storytelling, and community engagement to help ensure that Indigenous musical traditions remain living practices passed on to future generations. Reviving the Sound and Story of the uHadi For South African musician, educator, and composer Asakhe Cuntsulana, music is a way of remembering, healing, and reconnecting with community. As a member of the amaXhosa community, Asakhe has built his work around Indigenous music and the stories it carries. His studies in music at Rhodes University, combined with his work with artists and cultural historians, have enabled him to explore how traditional African sounds can speak to contemporary audiences. Through his work as founder of IThala leAfrika, he promotes Ubuntu, arts, and literature while creating spaces for people to reflect on and celebrate Africa’s diverse cultural heritage. At the heart of Asakhe’s work is the uHadi, the traditional Xhosa bow harp. For generations, Indigenous instruments and the music surrounding them have carried histories, spiritual knowledge, relationships with nature, and ways of understanding the world. Yet much of this knowledge is increasingly vulnerable as younger generations are influenced by globalization and changing cultural practices. For Asakhe, preserving the uHadi is therefore about much more than saving an instrument. It is about protecting the stories, techniques, meanings, and relationships that give the instrument its cultural significance. His project also brings the uHadi into dialogue with the Adungu, a traditional harp from Uganda, creating a pan-African exchange around Indigenous musical traditions. By connecting musical practices across African communities, Asakhe’s work explores how traditional instruments can serve as bridges between histories, cultures, and generations. This vision is at the center of Ingoma yoHadi (Song of the Harp), a project that brings together music, research, storytelling, and publication. Asakhe is developing a music album featuring compositions that blend the sounds of the uHadi, Adungu, and other traditional instruments, while a companion book will document the instruments’ histories, oral narratives, playing techniques, and roles in traditional and contemporary music. The project builds on preliminary work that began in 2024 through live performances and the development of the concept. By bringing together musicians, cultural historians, and visual artists, Asakhe hopes to create a living archive that can reach both community members and wider audiences. Rather than treating Indigenous music as something fixed in the past, the project recognizes tradition as something that can continue to evolve while remaining connected to its cultural roots. The project will also create opportunities for knowledge to be shared directly within communities. Through local workshops, participants will learn how to play the uHadi and Adungu while exploring their cultural significance. Multimedia materials, exhibitions, online platforms, and public engagements will further extend these stories beyond the performance space. For Asakhe, this is a way of ensuring that Indigenous music remains a living practice rather than becoming something remembered only through historical records. By combining performance with documentation, education, and storytelling, he is creating opportunities for younger generations to encounter traditional music not simply as an artifact of the past, but as a source of creativity and connection in the present. Ingoma yoHadi is ultimately an invitation to hear the voices of the ancestors in traditional instruments while making space for younger generations to create their own songs.

title: In her second novel, Amanda Peters returns to the stories of Nova Scotia’s Mi’kmaq women
content:
Sometimes the briefest of conversations is all it takes to ignite an entire storyline. That’s what happened for author Amanda Peters, who just released her second novel, The Birthing Tree, earlier this month.
In it, Peters traces one woman’s journey to protect the land, the traditions and the memory of the Mi’kmaq women who came before her – and to decide which parts of her inheritance she will carry into the future.
Like Peters herself, who is of Mi’kmaq and settler ancestry, the novel’s protagonist, Aliet Paul, returns to the rural Nova Scotia community where she grew up. As Paul begins unravelling her family history, each revelation pulls her deeper into a web of long-guarded silences.
The Birthing Tree is Peters’s second book, following her debut novel The Berry Pickers, which won the Andrew Carnegie Medal for Excellence in Fiction and the 2023 Barnes & Noble Discover Prize. It was also a finalist for the Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize and the Amazon First Novel Award.
While reeling from her debut novel’s accolades, Peters realized she was still drawn to the rolling hills and generational storylines of Nova Scotia’s Annapolis Valley. An offhand comment uttered decades ago by her grandmother sparked an idea, and a two-week writing residency in the mountains of Banff was enough for the book to take shape.
From her home in the Annapolis Valley, where she teaches English at Acadia University, Peters spoke to The Globe and Mail about inspiration, traditional Indigenous practices and riding the waves of creativity amid economic uncertainty.
In this story, a tree is the first character we meet and it becomes a central symbol throughout the book. Where did this idea come from?
It was inspired by my Nan and something she told me. It just stuck with me so fiercely. She was living with dementia and one day she turned from the window and said to me, “Do you know that tree down by the water?” I didn’t know what she was talking about, so I said, “Yeah, sure, Nan.” And she said, “That’s where we used to give birth.” And then she was back to the window, and I couldn’t get anything else out of her. It just sat with me forever, that tiny 10-second conversation.
You write a lot about family secrets and intergenerational dynamics. Why do you keep coming back to those themes?
They say “write what you know,” which I don’t always agree with, but I have very large families on both sides and there have always been a lot of stories passed down to me about previous generations. That inspires me. I’m a sucker for nostalgia and tradition, so I think I fall back on that.
Midwives – and their work – figure quite prominently in this story.
I was lucky enough to work with midwives in Nova Scotia when I worked briefly for the government, and I think they just inspired me. I watched my nephew be born, and it was the most miraculous thing I’ve ever seen. I think everybody should have the opportunity to choose safely and wisely how they give birth, especially now, when women’s bodies and reproductive rights are in so much jeopardy.
In the book, we also learn about other traditional health practices, such as the use of willow bark for its painkilling properties.
To me, it’s not just about midwifery; it’s about all traditional Indigenous practices, a lot of which have been outlawed in the past, and some of which have been erased altogether. I encourage readers to see the beauty of our Indigenous practices and traditions, get curious and do a little bit of research. I tell this to my students all the time: Readers of fiction are just better people, because readers of fiction have increased empathy, scientifically. When you’re reading fiction, you get to step into another person’s world.
Nova Scotia’s arts and publishing landscape has been under some pressure, including elimination of Nova Scotia’s Publishers Assistance Program as part of a provincial austerity budget released earlier this year. How do you encourage your students to persist in telling those stories?
I just tell them to keep writing. Don’t let any of that stop you, if it’s something you love and want to do. It may not be something you end up doing full-time, but don’t give up on it. The Berry Pickers came out when I was 46 years old, so you never know when your time is going to come.
This interview has been edited and condensed.
Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that Amanda Peters teaches theatre as well as English at Acadia University. She teaches only English.

title: Hebron’s Jewish community finishes restoring tomb belonging to ancestors of biblical King David
content:
Hebron’s Jewish community completed a four year restoration of the Tomb of Yishai and Ruth atop Tel Hebron in the West Bank on Tuesday.
The work was spearheaded by the community’s international spokesperson, Yishai Fleisher, a member of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party.
He also serves as a member of the Efrat Local Council, and is a widely recognized English-speaking voice for Israel abroad, with his YouTube channel having more than 300,000 subscribers.
The tomb is believed by Jewish sources to be the burial place of the biblical King David’s father, Yishai, and his great-grandmother, Ruth the Moabite.
“The location of the site in Hebron, city of the Patriarchs and Matriarchs, the first acquisition of the Jews in the Land of Israel, made by our forefather Abraham, carries important spiritual significance,” explained Fleisher. “There is a connection between the Tomb of Yishai and Ruth and the Cave of the [Patriarchs].”
“The sources state that there are four 'wheels' in the Chariot of the G-d: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David. Why specifically David? Because David is the one who fulfills the dream of the Patriarchs and Matriarchs, the dream of a united and strong people in their land, living in holiness."
Bringing Safed to Hebron
Fleisher, working closely with a team of historians and artisans, drew up a design drawing on the turquoise color usually associated with Safed, departing from the site's traditional browns and greens.
"We wanted to bring the sanctity of Safed's turquoise into the heart of Hebron," Fleisher said.
The graves of Yishai and Ruth themselves were redesigned using stone, calligraphic inscriptions, a Star of David, and a wheat motif to represent Ruth's biblical story.
Renovations for the tomb, as well as the establishment of a new synagogue and study hall at the site, were completed using mainly local Hebron stone, wrought iron, and wood.
The project cost roughly one million dollars fundraised by Fleisher from donars around the world.
Connecting site to younger generations
Additionally, a chamber dating back to the Byzantine and medieval periods was restored and converted into a a working studio, where a scribe writes on parchment using traditional methods, in view of visitors.
The completed site also includes shaded seating areas, water fountains, restrooms, a small event hall, a courtyard, parking, and direct access to the Tel Hebron archaeological park.
"If young people saw the place as it used to be, they wouldn't connect to it, and they wouldn't feel that this is a place of holiness,” Fleisher stated. “My view is that these places we love, places that are our heritage, need to be beautiful, need to expand the heart, to believe that this is truly something great.”
“I'm looking forward to applying my experience in beautifying Hebron to beautifying the whole Land of Israel through the Knesset.”
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

title: Sacks, Matkas & Bows Become Sports Gear at Madhya Pradesh’s Baiga Olympics
content: There are no synthetic tracks here. No floodlit stadium. No branded jerseys, expensive sports shoes or professional training camps. Instead, there are gunny sacks, earthen pots, ropes, bows and arrows, mud, wooden sticks and the physical skills that have travelled through generations of the Baiga community. In Baihar, in Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district, these everyday objects become sporting equipment during the Baiga Olympics — a tribal sporting and cultural festival designed around the traditional games of the Baiga people. The event was first organised in Baihar in 2015 by the Balaghat Tourism Promotion Council, with the stated aim of showcasing traditional Baiga games and helping conserve the community’s cultural heritage. Later editions have brought together Baiga participants from Madhya Pradesh and neighbouring states. A 2020 edition, for instance, was planned over three days and invited Baiga communities from parts of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Jharkhand and Andhra Pradesh. But who are the Baigas? The Baigas are one of Madhya Pradesh's Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs)-a special category created to identify tribal communities facing particularly severe socio-economic and infrastructural disadvantages. India currently recognises 75 PVTGs across 18 states and the Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The classification has historically been based on indicators including low literacy, economic vulnerability, geographical isolation, dependence on subsistence livelihoods, and stagnant or declining population trends. The Baiga are among the PVTGs listed in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. The term itself has an important history. These communities were earlier officially referred to as “Primitive Tribal Groups”, but the terminology was changed to PVTG in 2006–07 because the word “primitive” was considered inappropriate and value-laden. They have traditionally lived in close relationship with the forests of central India, particularly across areas of Madhya Pradesh and neighbouring Chhattisgarh. In Madhya Pradesh, large concentrations of the community are found in districts including Mandla and Balaghat. Their relationship with the forest goes well beyond livelihood. Baiga communities have traditionally depended on forest resources for food, medicine and other necessities, while maintaining extensive knowledge of local plants and their uses. And then there are the games. Long before the word "Olympics" was attached to them, many of these activities were simply part of community life. The Baiga Olympics takes those games out of the village setting and puts them into a common arena. So, what exactly happens at the Baiga Olympics? The answer is wonderfully different from what one might expect from a conventional sporting meet. Take Bora Daud. Instead of sprinting down a professional track, participants climb into gunny sacks and race. The humble sack becomes the equivalent of a piece of sporting equipment. Then there is the Matka race, where participants race while balancing earthen pots. It turns an everyday object into a test of balance, coordination and speed. From Matka Daud and Bora Daud to Bhalafenk, Dhanushbaan, Kabaddi and Kho-Kho, the games blend tradition with sport. Photograph: (Madhya Pradesh Tourism/Shutterstock) Bhalafenk, or spear throwing, draws on the physical precision associated with traditional hunting skills. Dhanushbaan, involving the bow and arrow, is another important traditional contest. The Madhya Pradesh government lists it among the Baiga Olympics' traditional "hunter games". There is also Vajni Khel, described as a traditional form of wrestling; Rassa-Kashi, the tug-of-war; and running events including relay and Tritangi races. The official list of competitions has included Matka Daud, Bora Daud, Tritangi race, relay race, Bhalafenk, Vajni Khel, Lipa-Poti, kabaddi, kho-kho, volleyball, Rassa-Kashi and Dhanushbaan. Earlier editions have also featured games such as Gobardanda. What do you need to compete? Not much by modern sporting standards. A sack for Bora Daud. An earthen pot for the Matka race. A spear for Bhalafenk. And, most importantly, the knowledge of how to use them. A special torch also forms part of the event. According to the Balaghat district administration, the torch travels through different districts before reaching Baihar, with a promotional vehicle accompanying it and inviting Baiga youth to participate. The event was first organised in Baihar in 2015 by the Balaghat Tourism Promotion Council. Photograph: (Government of Madhya Pradesh) The participants, too, are not necessarily professional athletes. The Ministry of Tourism describes the event as one where both young and older members of the Baiga community can participate, rather than restricting competition to trained athletes. A participant does not need years of specialised coaching, a sponsorship deal or access to a stadium. A skill learned through community life can become the basis for competition. Why does something like this matter? Because indigenous cultures can disappear quietly. The Baiga Olympics offers one way of keeping some of those practices visible. People from Baiga community are all set to welcome you to take a sneak peek into their world with Baiga Olympics, Balaghat. The 3 day fiesta from 4th-6th Jan will showcase the rich culture of Baiga tribes of Madhya Pradesh.#MPTourism pic.twitter.com/nsFQWyLVUD — Madhya Pradesh Tourism (@MPTourism) January 2, 2020 There is also an important question of dignity. For years, tribal communities have often been represented primarily through poverty, remoteness or deprivation. The Baiga Olympics attempts to shift the frame. An Olympics without an Olympic-sized budget That may ultimately be the most compelling part of the Baiga Olympics. The event borrows the language and spectacle of a global sporting competition, the torch, competitions, teams, spectators and prizes but changes the meaning of what counts as an athlete and what counts as sport. The Baiga Olympics does not attempt to reproduce the world's Olympics in a forested corner of Madhya Pradesh. It builds a sporting platform around what the community already knows. Sources: ‘Balaghat to host two-day Baiga Olympics to promote tribal culture’: By Hindustan Times, Published on 18 March 2015 ‘Baiga tribe: cuisine and culture’: By Madhya Pradesh Tourism, Published on 12 May 2022 ‘Baiga Olympics’: By Government of Madhya Pradesh

title: Entre descobertas históricas e pioneirismo, Fiocruz foi fundamental para consolidação do SUS
content:
A história da Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (Fiocruz) confunde-se com a própria trajetória do desenvolvimento da ciência e da saúde pública no Brasil. Nascida na Fazenda de Manguinhos, no Rio de Janeiro, a instituição construiu uma trajetória secular marcada por descobertas científicas, combate a epidemias e inovação tecnológica a serviço do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS).
Origens e a Reforma Sanitária no Rio de Janeiro
A trajetória teve início em 25 de maio de 1900 com a criação do Instituto Soroterápico Federal, criado para fabricar soros e vacinas contra a peste bubônica sob a direção técnica do bacteriologista Oswaldo Cruz e direção geral do Barão de Pedro Affonso. Ao assumir a direção geral em 1902 e, em seguida, a diretoria geral de Saúde Pública em 1903, Oswaldo Cruz liderou campanhas sanitárias que erradicaram a febre amarela e a peste bubônica da capital federal.
As medidas sanitárias enfrentaram forte oposição popular, culminando na Revolta da Vacina em 1904 após a instituição da obrigatoriedade da vacina antivariólica. Apesar dos reveses políticos, o Instituto expandiu sua atuação pelo interior do país por meio de expedições científicas pioneiras.
Rebatizada como Instituto Oswaldo Cruz em 1908, a instituição ganhou projeção internacional. Um dos marcos científicos mais importantes ocorreu em 1909, quando Carlos Chagas descreveu o ciclo completo da tripanosomíase americana (doença de Chagas). Em 1920, Chagas assumiu o Departamento Nacional de Saúde Pública, reorganizando os serviços sanitários em todo o território nacional.
Pioneirismo científico
Ao longo do século XX, a instituição acompanhou as profundas transformações políticas do país. Em 1937, iniciou a produção da vacina contra a febre amarela em parceria com a Fundação Rockefeller, tornando-se posteriormente responsável por cerca de 80% da produção mundial desse imunizante. Em 1954, foi criada a Escola Nacional de Saúde Pública (Ensp), que mais tarde receberia o nome do sanitarista Sergio Arouca, cujos estudos foram fundamentais para desenhar as diretrizes do SUS.
Durante a ditadura militar, a instituição sofreu o “Massacre de Manguinhos” em 1970, episódio em que dez renomados cientistas tiveram seus direitos políticos cassados e foram aposentados compulsoriamente. No mesmo período, a instituição foi reestruturada, passando a denominar-se Fundação Oswaldo Cruz em 1974. Em 1976, foram criados os laboratórios de Bio-Manguinhos e Far-Manguinhos, impulsionando a produção de vacinas, diagnósticos e medicamentos para a saúde pública.
Com a redemocratização na década de 1980 e a gestão de Sergio Arouca, os cientistas perseguidos foram reintegrados. Em 1987, equipes da Fiocruz alcançaram outro feito histórico: o primeiro isolamento do vírus HIV na América Latina.
Expansão, inovação e resposta a emergências sanitárias
No século XXI, a Fiocruz consolidou sua expansão nacional e internacional. A Fundação inaugurou novas unidades regionais (como a Fiocruz Ceará), escritórios no exterior (Moçambique), o laboratório permanente Fioantar na Antártica e o Canal Saúde. Na área de pesquisa, realizou o sequenciamento do genoma da vacina BCG em 2006. Em 2016, a socióloga Nísia Trindade Lima tornou-se a primeira mulher eleita presidente na história da instituição.
A Fiocruz manteve papel de destaque no combate a emergências de saúde pública, atuando na pandemia de Influenza A (H1N1) em 2009 e na epidemia de zika e microcefalia (2015/2016), na qual identificou a presença do vírus em casos da má-formação congênita e desenvolveu kits de diagnóstico diferencial.
O combate à covid-19
Ao comemorar 120 anos em 2020, a Fiocruz foi nomeada referência da OMS para Covid-19 nas Américas. Em resposta à crise sanitária, construiu um complexo hospitalar de emergência em menos de dois meses, produziu testes moleculares em larga escala e coordenou o ensaio clínico internacional Solidariedade no Brasil.
Por meio de acordo de transferência tecnológica com o Reino Unido, a instituição assumiu a produção da vacina contra a covid-19, entregando mais de 150 milhões de doses ao SUS em 2021. Em 2022, disponibilizou as primeiras doses da vacina produzidas com o Ingrediente Farmacêutico Ativo (IFA) 100% nacional, garantindo a autossuficiência do Brasil. A instituição também assinou parcerias para a produção local de antivirais orais e desenvolveu testes diagnósticos múltiplos para vírus respiratórios.

title: Inside India’s first transwomen rescue squad, trained in Kolhapur
content:
In the last week of August, a group of people gathered at Rajaram Lake, pulled on orange life jackets, checked their ropes, and spent 10 days practising rescue drills in the water. It looked like routine disaster-response training – until you learned who they were. This is India’s first transgender disaster management and rescue team, and for its members, the life jacket has come to mean something far bigger than safety gear.
The Kolhapur District Disaster Management Authority has trained over 2,500 volunteers in the last decade. In 2019, it created the state’s first all-women rescue unit, the ‘Aapda Sakhi’ team, which now counts more than 500 trained volunteers. But ahead of this year’s monsoon, officials decided to try something unique.
“We thought, why not train a transwomen team,” said Prasad Sankpal, District Disaster Management Officer, Kolhapur. “So a first-of-its-kind transgender disaster management and rescue team initiative was begun in the country.”
The first batch of 10 transwomen, all associated with the Kolhapur-based Maitri NGO, went through their inaugural training module from May 26 to 28. Since then, the district has trained 15 transwomen in total, with fresh rounds of practice held every three months – the most recent a 10-day exercise at Rajaram Lake in the last week of August.
Recruits learned rescue swimming, how to operate an inflatable rescue boat, dry and wet lifesaving techniques, motorboat handling and maintenance, and First Aid and CPR.
“So far the results are excellent,” Sankpal said. “The institutional strengthening is already visible – the volunteers now help victims of road accidents without any instructions.”
For the women themselves, the initiative is about something the training manual doesn’t cover.
“Even today, people see us as sex workers or beggars,” said Mayuri Alvekar, founder of Maitri NGO, who brought the other volunteers on board. “I believe that such opportunities of working with the administration would help promote inclusivity and give us space in mainstream society, while changing the perspective towards us. We have been helping people during disasters or rescue needs but faced discrimination. However, now we are getting recognition and, most importantly, an identity.”
“To take the initiative further, I have also created a similar volunteer team in Dhule and Parbhani,” Alvekar added.
Suhasini Devmane, another team member and Maharashtra’s first transgender tourist guide, spent eight years as an ayurvedic panchakarma expert while hiding who she was.
“Despite a desire to contribute to society, many of us had previously been unable to participate in social initiatives due to a lack of opportunities,” she said. “For over eight years, I had to hide my identity – else I would have lost my job, and my financial situation didn’t allow for that risk then. I believe this training will not only change society’s perspective towards transgender people but also boost the self-confidence of individuals within the community.”
Shivani Gajabar, who is currently pursuing a Master of Social Work degree at Shivaji University, Kolhapur, says the acceptance hasn’t fully arrived yet.
“Even today, transgender community members feel alienated from mainstream society,” she said. “Though giving us a platform in the disaster management rescue team is a welcome step and would help bring inclusivity – and we all would give our best while saving lives – I feel there is a long way ahead to fill the gap. Even when I go regularly to attend classes, no one sits on my bench. I’m all alone.”
Her family cut off contact when she left home in Class 7. “They used to think I could not do any considerable work,” she said. “However, now, being part of the disaster management rescue team, my family members have started communicating with me again.”
The administration isn’t stopping at floods and drowning rescues. “There are around 30 categories of man-made and natural disasters, including wildlife rescues involving snakes and crocodiles in Kolhapur, and the transwomen volunteers will gradually be trained for these as well,” Sankpal said.
One gap the authorities want to close: money. The volunteers currently work for free. “We are also planning to deploy them for crowd management during upcoming festivals such as Navaratri, Anant Chaturdashi, and the Jyotiba Yatra among others. Also, efforts are underway to grant home guard status to the transwomen volunteers, which would come with an honorarium,” Sankpal told The Indian Express.

title: ‘I’m coming home’: Last words haunt a 9/11 daughter 25 years later as she builds a legacy in his honor
content:
"I'm getting out. I'm coming home."
Those were the final words of William Lawrence Fallon Jr. before he was killed in the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center 25 years ago.
He worked as an IT manager for Cantor Fitzgerald and was just 38 years old when he was killed.
I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES
His daughter Kayla Fallon Smith was 8 years old when she learned her father would not be coming home.
Before the attacks, Smith, now 33, said her father – who always commuted into work early – would call the house phone in the morning to wish her and her sister well before they would head to school.

He went in early so he could leave earlier in the afternoons to take her to dancing school after her school day.
"That was the kind of man he was. I remember he would get up and work out in the morning before even going to work, so you'd hear the weights dropping in the house. I do remember that as a kid," Smith said.
Those quick and light-hearted morning phone calls to his daughters set the tone for the day.
"He would tell us what the skyline looked like. Sometimes it would be cloudy below him and he couldn't even see the street, but it'd be sunny up there," she said.
FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE
Smith remembers hearing her father's voice for the last time on Tuesday, Sept. 11, 2001.
"I spoke to him on the house phone that day, as I always did," she said, to which he said on the phone, "Have a good morning," she said.
"I'm sure I said something like, 'I love you, have a great day'," Smith said.
Her dad called again that fateful morning – sometime after the first tower was hit.
SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE
This time, her mother answered the phone.
"He said something to the degree of, 'I'm getting out, I'm coming home,' and that was it," she said.
Smith's mother replied and said, "What are you talking about?" He responded and said, "Turn on the news."
After that he hung up.

His family never heard from him again.
"Those words haunt me a little bit," Smith said. "Every year, grief is different. It doesn't go away. It's a myth when people say that time heals all wounds; it doesn't."
In the last 25 years of growing up without her father, Smith has turned her pain and grief into purpose. She's devoted her life to helping others living with grief and mental struggles.

Smith is a licensed mental health counselor who founded Trails of Purpose – a nonprofit organization that provides free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members, veterans, first responders and their families.
"As I was getting my graduate degree, I started to experience equine-assisted therapy, and I really—it just clicked for me," she said.
She went on to say, "I never experienced that as a kid, and I had a lot of trauma therapy growing up. The resources were abundant for 9/11 victims, and I never experienced equine therapy."

She started her organization in 2019.

"I needed a place to just be when my brain always felt on fire. I think I've created that, and it's seeming to resonate with other people."
Trails of Purpose has offered 30,000 hours of free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members and first responders.
"The horses, and the connection that they have when when words don't seem to to come, the horses can just be with you," she said.

"I created the thing that I think I needed: community and understanding, and a place that's safe, and quiet, and a respite," she said.
As she helps others heal, Smith said she'll never stop sharing her father's story.
